theory_blocks.title: Distance-time graphs
theory_blocks.body:
In a DISTANCE-TIME graph, time is on the horizontal axis and distance from the start is on the vertical axis.

- A SLOPING LINE means the object is moving. The GRADIENT is the SPEED: $\text{speed}=\dfrac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}$.
- A HORIZONTAL line means the object is STATIONARY (speed $0$).
- A line sloping DOWNWARDS means the object is coming back towards the start.
- AVERAGE SPEED $=\dfrac{\text{total distance travelled}}{\text{total time taken}}$, including any time spent stopped.

theory_blocks.title: Three distance-time mistakes
theory_blocks.body:
- Reading a horizontal line as "moving at constant speed". On a DISTANCE-TIME graph it means [[red:NOT MOVING]].
- Using the final distance from the start instead of the TOTAL distance travelled. A return journey to the start has distance-from-start $0$, but the object still travelled the full out-and-back distance.
- Counting each square as $1$ unit. Always read the scale: a small square might represent $0.1$ hours across and $10$ km up, or any other value.

theory_blocks.title: Conversion graphs
theory_blocks.body:
A CONVERSION GRAPH changes one unit into another (currencies, temperatures, kilograms and pounds). Any value can be converted in either direction by reading across and down (or up and across) using ruled construction lines.

If the line does NOT pass through the origin (e.g. $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $32^\circ\text{F}$, not $0^\circ\text{F}$), the two quantities are NOT proportional, and you cannot convert by simple multiplication.

If the line DOES pass through $(0,0)$ (as for currency, or miles to kilometres), doubling one quantity doubles the other, so you CAN also convert by multiplying by the gradient.

theory_blocks.title: Checking a conversion
theory_blocks.body:
Check a conversion by looking at the SHAPE: on an increasing line, a bigger input must give a bigger output.

Also test a value you can compute exactly: for the Celsius-Fahrenheit line, $100^\circ\text{C}$ should give $212^\circ\text{F}$, matching the formula $F=1.8C+32$.

theory_blocks.title: Interpreting a straight-line graph
theory_blocks.body:
- GRADIENT $=\dfrac{\text{change up}}{\text{change across}}$, with the units "vertical unit per horizontal unit".
- INTERCEPT on the vertical axis $=$ the value when the horizontal quantity is $0$ (a starting value or fixed charge).
- To find the gradient, use a LARGE triangle with vertices on grid crossings of the line; the bigger the triangle, the smaller the reading error.

theory_blocks.title: Speed-time graphs
theory_blocks.body:
In a SPEED-TIME graph the horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is speed — the meaning of each feature changes from a distance-time graph.

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| horizontal line | constant speed (zero acceleration) |
| line sloping up | ACCELERATION (speed increasing) |
| line sloping down | DECELERATION (speed decreasing) |
| gradient | ACCELERATION $=\dfrac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{time taken}}$ (m/s$^2$) |
| area under the graph | DISTANCE TRAVELLED |

The area rule is the same as "distance $=$ speed $\times$ time": a rectangle of height $v$ and width $t$ has area $vt$. For a sloping line the area is a triangle or trapezium, so use $\tfrac12bh$ or $\tfrac12(a+b)h$.

In this course the areas involve straight-line sections only.

theory_blocks.title: Speed-time: three more mistakes
theory_blocks.body:
Speed-time and distance-time graphs LOOK alike but mean different things. A horizontal line on a speed-time graph is [[green:CONSTANT SPEED]], not "stopped": the object is stopped only when the line lies ON the time axis.

Always check the label on the vertical axis first.

- Calling a negative gradient "negative acceleration" without saying the object is slowing down; in exam answers give the SIZE and use the word DECELERATION.
- Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ when finding the area of a triangle, or using the slanted length instead of the VERTICAL height.
- Writing the unit of acceleration as m/s. It is m/s$^2$ (metres per second PER SECOND).

theory_blocks.title: Tangents and rates of change
theory_blocks.body:
Not every graph is made of straight lines. For a CURVE, the gradient changes from point to point. The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of its TANGENT: the straight line that just touches the curve there.

1. Place a ruler so it touches the curve at the required point and looks like it has the same direction as the curve there (balanced, with equal gaps on both sides).
2. Draw the line, extending it well beyond the point.
3. Choose two clear grid points on the tangent, far apart, and draw a right-angled triangle.
4. Gradient $=\dfrac{\text{vertical}}{\text{horizontal}}$, with units.

The answer is an ESTIMATE: examiners allow a range of values. On a distance-time curve, the gradient of the tangent is the SPEED at that instant; on a speed-time curve, it is the ACCELERATION at that instant.

A curve that gets steeper means the object is speeding up.

keywords.definition: A graph with time on the horizontal axis and distance from a starting point on the vertical axis; its gradient is speed.
A graph with time on the horizontal axis and speed on the vertical axis; its gradient is acceleration and its area is distance.
The change in the vertical quantity divided by the change in the horizontal quantity; represents a rate in a practical graph.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken, including any time spent stopped.
A straight-line graph used to change a value from one unit into another, read in either direction.
The rate of change of speed with time, found as the gradient of a speed-time graph; units m/s$^2$.
A decrease in speed over time; shown as a downward-sloping section of a speed-time graph, reported as a positive size.
A straight line that just touches a curve at one point, with the same direction as the curve there; its gradient estimates the curve's rate of change at that point.
How much one quantity changes for each unit change in another; shown by the gradient of a graph relating them.
On a speed-time graph, the area between the line and the time axis; represents the distance travelled.

worked_examples.statement:
A journey. A coach leaves a depot $O$, travels to a town ($P$), stops ($Q$), continues to a second town ($R$) and then returns directly to the depot ($S$), as shown.

(a) Find the speed from $O$ to $P$. (b) For how long was the coach stationary? (c) Find the speed from $R$ to $S$. (d) Find the average speed for the whole journey.
reasoning: (a) $O\to P$: read the change in distance and change in time from the graph.
(b) $PQ$ is horizontal: read the change in time only.
(c) $R\to S$: read the change in distance and change in time; the line slopes DOWN, so the coach is returning.
(d) Total distance is the FULL out-and-back distance (not the final distance from the depot, which is $0$); total time is the whole journey.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $40$ km in $1$ h, speed $=40$ km/h. (b) $0.5$ h $=30$ minutes. (c) $100$ km in $2$ h, speed $=50$ km/h. (d) Total distance $=100+100=200$ km, total time $=4.5$ h, average speed $=200\div4.5=44.4$ km/h (3 s.f.).
worked_examples.interpretation: The average speed ($44.4$ km/h) is NOT the average of the individual speeds ($40$, $60$ and $50$ km/h): the stop and the different speeds all count, so always divide the TOTAL distance by the TOTAL time.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (d), using the final distance from the depot (which is $0$, since the coach returns to $O$) instead of the total distance actually travelled ($200$ km).

assets.caption: The coach's distance-time graph: rising $O\to P$, flat (stopped) $P\to Q$, rising $Q\to R$, then falling back to the depot $R\to S$.
assets.purpose: Show all four distance-time features (moving, stopped, moving, returning) on one graph before reading speeds from it.

worked_examples.statement: Reading a conversion graph. The graph converts temperatures in degrees Celsius ($^\circ\text{C}$) to degrees Fahrenheit ($^\circ\text{F}$). Use it to convert (a) $25^\circ\text{C}$ to Fahrenheit, (b) $90^\circ\text{F}$ to Celsius.
reasoning: (a) Start at $25$ on the Celsius axis, go UP to the line, then ACROSS to the Fahrenheit axis.
(b) Start at $90$ on the Fahrenheit axis, go ACROSS to the line, then DOWN to the Celsius axis.
worked_examples.interpretation: The SAME ruled line is read in two different directions depending on which temperature scale the starting value is given in — up-then-across, or across-then-down.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Starting on the wrong axis (e.g. beginning at $25$ on the Fahrenheit axis instead of the Celsius axis), which reads off a completely different, unrelated value.

assets.caption: The conversion graph $^{\circ}\text{F}=1.8\times{}^{\circ}\text{C}+32$: (a) up from $25\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ to the line, then across to about $77\,^{\circ}\text{F}$; (b) across from $90\,^{\circ}\text{F}$ to the line, then down to about $32\,^{\circ}\text{C}$.
assets.purpose: Give the related idea the graph it tells the student to read, with both construction readings drawn: up-then-across and across-then-down.

worked_examples.statement:
A taxi fare. A taxi charges a fixed amount plus a price per kilometre. The fare $C$ pounds for a journey of $d$ km is given by the table: $d=0,2,4,6,8,10$ gives $C=3,7,11,15,19,23$.

Draw the graph and explain what the gradient and the point where the line meets the vertical axis represent.
reasoning: The points lie on a straight line, so join them with a ruler.
Draw a large triangle on the line to find the gradient: change up $12$, change across $6$.
Read the value where the line meets the vertical axis (at $d=0$).
worked_examples.solution: Gradient $=\dfrac{12}{6}=2$: the fare rises by £2 for every extra kilometre (the price per kilometre). The line meets the $C$-axis at $3$: the fixed charge is £3 (the fare for a $0$ km journey). The fare is $C=2d+3$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
The gradient of a real-world graph is always a RATE with units (here, pounds per kilometre),

and the vertical intercept is always the value of the vertical quantity when the horizontal one is zero (here, the fixed charge before any distance is travelled).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the gradient from a SMALL triangle spanning only $2$ km, where a small reading error in either coordinate has a much bigger effect on the computed gradient.

assets.caption: The taxi-fare data plotted and joined with a ruler, with a large gradient triangle (across $6$, up $12$) giving a gradient of $2$.
assets.purpose: Show how to turn a table of data into a graph, and how a large triangle on the resulting line gives a reliable gradient.

worked_examples.statement:
A car's journey. The speed-time graph of a car rises from $0$ to $20$ m/s over the first $10$ s ($A$), stays at $20$ m/s for the next $30$ s ($B$), then falls from $20$ m/s to $0$ over the final $10$ s ($C$), for a total of $50$ s.

(a) Find the acceleration in the first $10$ s. (b) Find the deceleration in the last $10$ s. (c) Find the distance travelled in the $50$ s. (d) Find the average speed.
reasoning: (a)/(b): acceleration (or deceleration) is the gradient, $\dfrac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{time taken}}$.
(c) Split the area under the graph into three pieces: triangle $A$, rectangle $B$, triangle $C$.
(d) Average speed $=$ total distance $\div$ total time.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $20\div10=2$ m/s$^2$. (b) $20\div10=2$ m/s$^2$. (c) $A=\tfrac12\times10\times20=100$, $B=30\times20=600$, $C=\tfrac12\times10\times20=100$; total $=800$ m (or, as one trapezium, $\tfrac12(50+30)\times20=800$). (d) $800\div50=16$ m/s.
worked_examples.interpretation: Splitting an irregular area into named shapes (triangle, rectangle, triangle) — or recognising the whole outline as a single trapezium — both give the same total, so either method is a valid check on the other.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Computing the triangular sections $A$ and $C$ as $10\times20=200$ each (forgetting the $\tfrac12$), which would roughly double the true total distance.

assets.caption: The car's speed-time graph: speed rises to $20$ m/s in the first $10$ s (triangle $A$), stays at $20$ m/s until $t=40$ s (rectangle $B$), then falls to $0$ by $t=50$ s (triangle $C$). The shaded area is the distance travelled.
assets.purpose: Show the three sections whose gradients give the acceleration and deceleration and whose areas add to the distance travelled.

worked_examples.statement: Speed at an instant. The graph shows the distance $s$ metres travelled by a cyclist after $t$ seconds, following a curve. Estimate the speed at $t=3$ s.
reasoning: Draw a tangent to the curve at the point where $t=3$.
Extend the tangent and read off two clear points on it, far apart.
Gradient of the tangent $=\dfrac{\text{change in }s}{\text{change in }t}$.
worked_examples.solution: The tangent touches the curve at $(3,9)$ and passes through $(1.5,0)$ and $(4.5,18)$. Gradient $=\dfrac{18}{4.5-1.5}=\dfrac{18}{3}=6$. The speed at $t=3$ s is about $6$ m/s.
worked_examples.interpretation: Because the curve's steepness changes continuously, 'the speed at $t=3$ s' only makes sense as the gradient of the tangent AT that one instant, not as an average over any stretch of time.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the gradient from the ORIGIN to the point $(3,9)$ (an average speed over the whole first $3$ seconds, $9\div3=3$ m/s) instead of the gradient of the tangent AT $t=3$.

assets.caption: The cyclist's distance-time curve $s=t^{2}$, with the tangent drawn at $(3,9)$. The tangent runs from $(1.5,0)$ to $(4.5,18)$, so its gradient is $18\div3=6$ and the speed at $t=3$ s is about $6$ m/s.
assets.purpose: Show what 'draw a tangent and find its gradient' looks like, with the gradient triangle the solution uses.

guided_exercises.statement: A runner sets off from home, covers $5$ km in the first $20$ minutes, rests for $10$ minutes, then runs the $5$ km back home in $10$ minutes. Find (a) her speed on the way out, (b) her speed on the way back, (c) her average speed for the whole trip.
hints: Convert each time to hours before dividing, e.g. $20$ minutes $=\tfrac13$ hour.
For the average speed, use the TOTAL distance (out and back) divided by the TOTAL time (including the rest).
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) $5\div\tfrac13=15$ km/h. (b) $5\div\tfrac16=30$ km/h. (c) Total distance $=10$ km, total time $=20+10+10=40$ min $=\tfrac23$ h, average speed $=10\div\tfrac23=15$ km/h.
common_errors: In (c), using the final distance from home (which is $0$) instead of the total distance covered (10 km).

guided_exercises.statement: A conversion graph for miles to kilometres is a straight line through the origin with gradient $1.6$. Use it to find (a) the number of kilometres in $20$ miles, (b) the number of miles in $40$ km.
hints: Since the line passes through the origin, you can convert directly by multiplying (or dividing) by the gradient.
To go from km back to miles, divide by the gradient instead of multiplying.
common_errors: In (b), multiplying by $1.6$ again instead of dividing by it, giving a far too large answer.

guided_exercises.statement: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to $12$ m/s in $4$ s, rides at $12$ m/s for $6$ s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in $3$ s. Find the total distance travelled.
hints: Split the area under the speed-time graph into three sections: an accelerating triangle, a constant-speed rectangle, and a decelerating triangle.
Alternatively, treat the whole shape as one trapezium with parallel sides equal to the total time and the constant-speed time.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Accelerating section: $\tfrac12\times4\times12=24$ m. Constant section: $6\times12=72$ m. Decelerating section: $\tfrac12\times3\times12=18$ m. Total $=24+72+18=114$ m. (Check: trapezium with parallel sides $13$ s and $6$ s, height $12$: $\tfrac12(13+6)\times12=114$ m.)
common_errors: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ on either triangular section, which would overstate the total distance.

exercises.statement: Sam cycles from home. He travels $15$ km in the first hour, rests for $30$ minutes, then cycles home at a steady speed and arrives $3$ hours after leaving. Find (a) his speed on the way out, (b) his speed on the way home, (c) his average speed for the whole trip.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $15\div1=15$ km/h. (b) Time home $=3-1-0.5=1.5$ h, speed $=15\div1.5=10$ km/h. (c) Total distance $=30$ km, total time $=3$ h, average $=10$ km/h.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract the rest time when finding the time spent cycling home.

exercises.statement: Mia cycles from $A$ to $B$, $60$ km apart, leaving at $10{:}00$ and arriving $3$ hours later. A car leaves $B$ at $11{:}00$ and drives to $A$, arriving $1$ hour later. Find (a) Mia's speed, (b) the car's speed, (c) the time and distance from $A$ at which they meet.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $60\div3=20$ km/h. (b) $60\div1=60$ km/h. (c) Mia's distance from $A$ is $20t$ (for $t$ hours after $10{:}00$); the car's is $120-60t$ (it starts at $A$-distance $60$ at $t=1$ and reaches $0$ at $t=2$). Setting equal: $20t=120-60t\Rightarrow t=1.5$, i.e. $11{:}30$, at distance $30$ km.
common_errors: Setting up the car's distance-from-$A$ equation as if it started moving at $t=0$ instead of $t=1$ (when the car actually leaves $B$).

exercises.statement: Ten miles is about $16$ km, and the conversion graph is a straight line through the origin. Find (a) the number of kilometres in $25$ miles, (b) the number of miles in $60$ km.
exercises.full_solution: Gradient $=16\div10=1.6$ km per mile. (a) $25\times1.6=40$ km. (b) $60\div1.6=37.5$ miles.
common_errors: Using the gradient the wrong way round in (b), multiplying by $1.6$ instead of dividing.

exercises.statement: The exchange rate is £1 $=$ 1.15 euros. Convert (a) £80 to euros, (b) 138 euros to pounds.
common_errors: In (b), multiplying by $1.15$ instead of dividing, since the conversion is being reversed.

exercises.statement: Water flows into a tank at a steady rate. The volume $V$ litres after $t$ minutes is $0,40,80,120$ for $t=0,2,4,6$. Draw the graph and find its gradient. What does it mean?
exercises.answer: Gradient $=20$: water flows in at $20$ litres per minute.
exercises.full_solution: Change in $V$ between consecutive data points is always $40$ over a change in $t$ of $2$: gradient $=40\div2=20$ litres per minute.
common_errors: Reading the gradient as $40$ (the change in $V$ alone), forgetting to divide by the corresponding change in $t$.

exercises.statement: A phone plan costs £5 per month plus 10p per minute of calls. (a) Complete a table of the monthly cost for $0,50,100,150,200$ minutes. (b) Draw the graph. (c) Explain what the gradient and the intercept mean. (d) Find the cost for $130$ minutes.
exercises.answer: (a) £5, £10, £15, £20, £25 (b) straight line from $(0,5)$ to $(200,25)$ (c) gradient $0.1=$ £0.10 per minute; intercept £5 $=$ fixed monthly charge (d) £18.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Cost $=5+0.1m$ for $m$ minutes. (c) Gradient $0.1$ is the price per minute; intercept £5 is the charge for $0$ minutes of calls. (d) $5+0.1(130)=5+13=18$.
common_errors: In (d), computing $0.1\times130$ as $130$ (misplacing the decimal point) instead of $13$.

exercises.statement: A train travels $150$ km in $1\tfrac23$ hours, stops for $20$ minutes and then travels a further $90$ km in $1$ hour. Find (a) its speed in the first part, (b) its average speed for the whole journey.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $150\div1\tfrac23=90$ km/h. (b) Total distance $=240$ km, total time $=1\tfrac23+\tfrac13+1=3$ h, average $=80$ km/h.
common_errors: Omitting the $20$-minute stop from the total time, giving an incorrect (too high) average speed.

exercises.statement: Use $F=1.8C+32$ to convert (a) $20^\circ\text{C}$ to Fahrenheit, (b) $50^\circ\text{F}$ to Celsius.
common_errors: In (b), dividing $50$ by $1.8$ directly without first subtracting $32$.

exercises.statement: A straight-line graph passes through $(0,4)$ and $(5,19)$. Find its gradient and its equation.
exercises.full_solution: Gradient $=\dfrac{19-4}{5-0}=\dfrac{15}{5}=3$. Intercept (at $x=0$) is $4$, so $y=3x+4$.
common_errors: Using $(0,4)$ as the intercept but then computing the gradient incorrectly as $19/5$, forgetting to subtract the $y$-value at $x=0$ first.

exercises.statement: On a distance-time graph, which of these is impossible for a real journey: a horizontal line, a line sloping down, a vertical line? Explain.
exercises.full_solution: A vertical line would mean travelling a non-zero distance in ZERO time, which requires infinite speed — impossible for a real journey. A horizontal line (stopped) and a line sloping down (returning) are both perfectly realistic.
common_errors: Choosing 'a line sloping down' as impossible, not recognising that a downward slope simply represents the return part of a journey.

exercises.statement: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to $15$ m/s in $6$ s, then travels at $15$ m/s for $10$ s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in $5$ s. Find (a) the acceleration, (b) the deceleration, (c) the total distance, (d) the average speed for the whole journey, to 3 s.f.
common_errors: In (c), forgetting the $\tfrac12$ on either of the two triangular sections, roughly doubling part of the total distance.

exercises.statement: The speed-time graph shows a cyclist's ride: speed rises from $4$ m/s to $14$ m/s over the first $5$ s, stays at $14$ m/s until $9$ s, then falls from $14$ m/s to $2$ m/s by $15$ s. Find (a) the acceleration, (b) the deceleration, (c) the total distance travelled.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $(14-4)\div5=2$ m/s$^2$. (b) $(14-2)\div(15-9)=12\div6=2$ m/s$^2$. (c) First section (trapezium): $\tfrac12(4+14)(5)=45$. Middle (rectangle): $4\times14=56$. Last section (trapezium): $\tfrac12(14+2)(6)=48$. Total $=45+56+48=149$ m.
common_errors: Treating the first and last sections as triangles (forgetting the speed does not start or end at $0$), instead of trapeziums.

exercises.statement: The distance $s$ metres of a particle from a point is given by $s=\tfrac14t^2$. Find the coordinates of the points for $t=0,1,\dots,8$, draw the graph, and estimate the speed at $t=4$ by drawing a tangent to the curve at $(4,4)$.
exercises.full_solution: Substituting $t=0,\ldots,8$ into $s=\tfrac14t^2$ gives the listed points. The tangent drawn at $(4,4)$ passes through about $(2,0)$ and $(6,8)$, so its gradient is $\dfrac{8-0}{6-2}=\dfrac84=2$, and the speed at $t=4$ is approximately $2$ m/s (accept $1.8$ to $2.2$). (The line joining $(2,1)$ and $(6,9)$ is a chord of the curve, not a tangent, although here it happens to be parallel to the tangent.)
common_errors: Using the gradient from the origin to $(4,4)$ (an average speed of $1$ m/s) instead of a tangent gradient estimated AT $t=4$.

exercises.statement: A car travelling at $30$ m/s brakes uniformly and stops in $6$ s. Find the deceleration and the braking distance.
exercises.full_solution: Deceleration $=30\div6=5$ m/s$^2$. Braking distance $=\tfrac12\times6\times30=90$ m.
common_errors: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ in the braking-distance formula, giving $180$ m instead of $90$ m.

exercises.statement: A train accelerates uniformly from rest for $20$ s to speed $V$ m/s, travels at $V$ m/s for $60$ s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in $40$ s. The total distance is $2\,700$ m. Find $V$, the acceleration and the deceleration.
exercises.full_solution: Total distance (trapezium) $=\tfrac12(20)V+60V+\tfrac12(40)V=90V=2700\Rightarrow V=30$ m/s. Acceleration $=30\div20=1.5$ m/s$^2$. Deceleration $=30\div40=0.75$ m/s$^2$.
common_errors: Setting up the total-distance equation as $20V+60V+40V$ (omitting both factors of $\tfrac12$), which gives an incorrect, much smaller value of $V$.

exercises.statement: (a) Convert $25$ m/s to km/h. (b) A car travels at $90$ km/h for $20$ s. How far does it go, in metres?
common_errors: In (b), using the speed in km/h directly with time in seconds, without first converting to consistent units (m/s and s, or km/h and hours).

exam_questions.statement:
A cyclist rides $24$ km in $2$ hours, stops for $45$ minutes, then rides a further $16$ km in $1.5$ hours back towards the start.
(a) Find her speed for the first part of the journey. [2]
(b) Find her average speed for the whole journey, including the stop, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $24\div2=12$ km/h. (b) Total distance $=24+16=40$ km (not the net distance from the start). Total time $=2+0.75+1.5=4.25$ h. Average speed $=40\div4.25=9.4117\ldots\approx9.41$ km/h.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correctly dividing $24$ by $2$; A1 for $12$ km/h

(b) M1 for using the TOTAL distance $40$ km (not the net distance from the start); M1 for using the correct total time $4.25$ h (including the $45$-minute stop); A1 for $9.41$ km/h (3 s.f.), following through correctly on the student's own total distance and time
common_errors: In (b), using the net distance from the start ($24-16=8$ km) instead of the total distance actually travelled ($40$ km).

exam_questions.statement:
A train accelerates uniformly from rest to $24$ m/s in $15$ s, maintains that speed for $40$ s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in $10$ s.
(a) Find the acceleration in the first $15$ s. [2]
(b) Find the total distance travelled. [3]
(c) Find the average speed for the whole journey, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for dividing $24$ by $15$; A1 for $1.6$ m/s$^2$

(b) M1 for a correct method splitting the area into three sections (two triangles and a rectangle, or an equivalent trapezium method); M1 for correctly including the $\tfrac12$ factor on both triangular sections; A1 for $1260$ m
(c) M1 for dividing the total distance by the correct total time ($65$ s); A1 for $19.4$ m/s (3 s.f.), following through on the student's own distance from (b)
common_errors: In (b), omitting the $\tfrac12$ on one or both triangular sections, which inflates the total distance well above the correct value.

exam_questions.statement: The depth of water $d$ cm in a container, $t$ minutes after a tap is opened, follows a curve. A tangent to the curve at $t=4$ touches it at $(4,8)$ and passes through the points $(2,0)$ and $(6,16)$. Estimate the rate at which the depth is increasing at $t=4$ minutes.
exam_questions.full_solution: Gradient of the tangent $=\dfrac{16-0}{6-2}=\dfrac{16}{4}=4$. The depth is increasing at approximately $4$ cm per minute at $t=4$ minutes.
mark_scheme: M1 for identifying the correct change in $d$ ($16-0=16$) between the two named points on the tangent
M1 for identifying the correct change in $t$ ($6-2=4$) between the same two points
A1 for the correct gradient $4$
B1 for stating the answer with the correct units, cm/min, and as a RATE (not just a bare number)
common_errors: Using the coordinates of the point of contact alone, $8\div4=2$ (the gradient of the line from the origin to $(4,8)$, i.e. the average rate over the first $4$ minutes), instead of the gradient of the tangent itself.

exam_questions.statement:
A conversion graph is to be drawn to change between kilometres and miles, using $8$ km $=5$ miles.

| Distance (km) | $0$ | $20$ | $40$ | $60$ | $80$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance (miles) | $0$ |  | $25$ |  | $50$ |

(a) Copy and complete the table. [2]
(b) Using a scale of $1$ cm to $10$ km and $1$ cm to $5$ miles, draw the conversion graph for distances from $0$ km to $80$ km. [2]
(c) Use your graph to convert $50$ km into miles. [1]
(d) Use your graph to convert $30$ miles into kilometres. [1]
(e) Write down what the gradient of your graph represents, and give its units. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $12.5$ and $37.5$. (b) A ruled straight line through $(0,0)$ and $(80,50)$. (c) About $31$ miles. (d) About $48$ km. (e) The number of miles in one kilometre, $0.625$ miles per kilometre.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $20\times\dfrac{5}{8}=12.5$ miles and $60\times\dfrac{5}{8}=37.5$ miles. (b) Plot $(0,0)$, $(20,12.5)$, $(40,25)$, $(60,37.5)$ and $(80,50)$; they lie on one straight line through the origin, so join them with a ruler. (c) Go UP from $50$ on the kilometre axis to the line, then ACROSS: $50\times\dfrac{5}{8}=31.25$, so about $31$ miles. (d) Go ACROSS from $30$ on the mile axis to the line, then DOWN: $30\times\dfrac{8}{5}=48$ km. (e) Gradient $=\dfrac{50}{80}=0.625$, so each kilometre is $0.625$ of a mile: the units are miles per kilometre.
mark_scheme: (b) B1 for all five points plotted correctly on the stated scales; B1 for one ruled straight line drawn through them from $(0,0)$ to $(80,50)$
(c) B1 for $31.25$, or any value from $30.5$ to $32$ miles read from the student's own correct line (construction lines shown)
(d) B1 for $48$, or any value from $47$ to $49$ km read from the student's own correct line (construction lines shown)
(e) B1 for stating that the gradient is the number of miles in one kilometre ($0.625$), with the units miles per kilometre
common_errors: In (d), starting at $30$ on the kilometre axis instead of the mile axis, which converts the wrong way round and gives $18.75$ instead of $48$.
Joining the plotted points with a freehand curve or with separate line segments instead of one ruled straight line, which makes every reading taken from the graph unreliable.

challenge_questions.statement: Train $A$ leaves a station at $09{:}00$ at $60$ km/h. Train $B$ leaves the same station along the same line at $09{:}30$ at $90$ km/h. Find when and where $B$ catches $A$, confirming with algebra.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $t$ be hours after $09{:}00$. Train $A$: $d=60t$. Train $B$ (starts $0.5$ h later): $d=90(t-0.5)$. Setting equal: $60t=90t-45\Rightarrow30t=45\Rightarrow t=1.5$, i.e. $10{:}30$, at distance $60(1.5)=90$ km.

challenge_questions.statement: A driver drives $60$ km at $30$ km/h and then a further $60$ km at $60$ km/h. Explain why the average speed is NOT $45$ km/h, and find it.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Time for the first leg $=60\div30=2$ h; time for the second leg $=60\div60=1$ h. Total distance $=120$ km, total time $=3$ h, so average speed $=120\div3=40$ km/h — not the simple mean of $30$ and $60$ (which is $45$), because MORE TIME is spent travelling at the slower speed, pulling the true average down.

challenge_questions.statement: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at $a$ m/s$^2$. Show that the distance covered in $t$ seconds is $\tfrac12at^2$. Deduce that doubling the time multiplies the distance by $4$, and find the distance in the first $10$ s when $a=2$.
challenge_questions.answer: Shown below; distance in the first $10$ s (with $a=2$) is $100$ m.
challenge_questions.full_solution: After $t$ seconds the speed is $v=at$, and the speed-time graph is a triangle with base $t$ and height $at$, so the area (distance) is $\tfrac12\times t\times at=\tfrac12at^2$. Since $(2t)^2=4t^2$, replacing $t$ with $2t$ multiplies the distance by $4$. For $a=2,t=10$: $\tfrac12\times2\times10^2=100$ m.

challenge_questions.statement: A driver travelling at $20$ m/s sees a hazard. There is a reaction time of $0.8$ s at constant speed before braking at a deceleration of $5$ m/s$^2$ until stopped. Find the total stopping distance. Find the stopping distance if the initial speed is $30$ m/s instead.
challenge_questions.answer: At $20$ m/s: $56$ m total. At $30$ m/s: $114$ m total.
challenge_questions.full_solution: At $20$ m/s: reaction distance $=20\times0.8=16$ m; braking time $=20\div5=4$ s, braking distance $=\tfrac12\times4\times20=40$ m; total $=16+40=56$ m. At $30$ m/s: reaction distance $=30\times0.8=24$ m; braking time $=30\div5=6$ s, braking distance $=\tfrac12\times6\times30=90$ m; total $=24+90=114$ m.

challenge_questions.statement: On the conversion graph for $F=1.8C+32$, the line $F=C$ is also drawn. Find where they cross and explain what this point means.
challenge_questions.answer: They cross at $-40$; $-40^\circ\text{C}=-40^\circ\text{F}$, the only temperature with the same value on both scales.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Setting $1.8C+32=C$: $0.8C=-32\Rightarrow C=-40$. So $F=C=-40$: the point $(-40,-40)$ is where the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales agree — the only temperature at which both readings are numerically equal.

mcq.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line represent?

options.text: The object is moving at a constant, steady speed.
options.why_wrong: This is the correct meaning of a horizontal line on a SPEED-time graph, not a distance-time graph; here, the distance is not changing at all, so there is no motion.
Acceleration is not shown directly on a distance-time graph at all, and a horizontal line specifically shows zero change in distance, not a changing speed.
Moving backward (returning) would be shown by a line sloping DOWNWARD, not a horizontal one.

mcq.explanation: On a distance-time graph, the vertical axis is distance; a horizontal line means distance is not changing, so the object is stationary.

mcq.stem: A cyclist rides $10$ km out from home and $10$ km back, taking $2$ hours in total. What is her average speed?

options.why_wrong: Uses the final distance FROM HOME (which is $0$, since she returns to the start) instead of the total distance actually ridden ($20$ km).
Uses only the outward distance ($10$ km) divided by the total time, ignoring the return leg's distance entirely.
Uses the correct total distance ($20$ km) but divides by only $1$ hour instead of the full $2$ hours taken.

mcq.explanation: Average speed $=$ total distance $\div$ total time $=20\div2=10$ km/h.

mcq.stem: On a SPEED-time graph, what does a horizontal line represent?

options.why_wrong: This is the correct meaning of a horizontal line on a DISTANCE-time graph, not a speed-time graph; here, the SPEED is unchanging but not necessarily zero.
Acceleration is shown by a SLOPING line (up for acceleration), not a horizontal one; a horizontal line means the gradient — the acceleration — is zero.
Deceleration is shown by a line sloping DOWN, not a horizontal one.

mcq.explanation: On a speed-time graph, the vertical axis is speed; a horizontal line means the speed is not changing, i.e. constant speed with zero acceleration — only a line ON the time axis itself means stopped.

mcq.stem: A speed-time graph shows a car accelerating uniformly from rest to $20$ m/s in $8$ seconds. What distance does it travel in this time?

options.why_wrong: Computes base $\times$ height ($8\times20$) as if the section were a RECTANGLE, forgetting the $\tfrac12$ needed for this TRIANGULAR section.
Adds the base and height ($8+20$) instead of using an area formula at all.
Computes $20\div8$, which gives the ACCELERATION (m/s$^2$), not the distance travelled.

mcq.explanation: This section is a triangle: distance $=\tfrac12\times8\times20=80$ m.

mcq.stem: A graph shows the total cost $C$ (pounds) of a plumber's visit against the number of hours $h$ worked, as a straight line from $(0,40)$ to $(3,100)$. What does the GRADIENT of this line represent?

options.text: The total cost for $1$ hour of work.
options.why_wrong: This would be read as the VALUE of the line at $h=1$ (which is £60), not the gradient, which measures the RATE of change, not a single value.

options.text: The rate charged per hour, £20 per hour.

options.why_wrong: The call-out fee is the vertical INTERCEPT (£40, the cost at $h=0$), not the gradient.

options.text: The total number of hours worked.
options.why_wrong: The gradient has units of pounds PER hour (a rate), not a plain number of hours.

mcq.explanation: Gradient $=\dfrac{100-40}{3-0}=\dfrac{60}{3}=20$: the cost rises by £20 for each extra hour worked, i.e. the hourly rate.

flashcards.front: On a distance-time graph, what does the gradient represent?
flashcards.back: The SPEED: $\text{speed}=\dfrac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}$.

flashcards.front: Horizontal line: distance-time graph vs. speed-time graph — what does each mean?
flashcards.back: Distance-time: the object is STATIONARY. Speed-time: the object moves at CONSTANT speed (it is NOT stopped).

flashcards.front: Average speed formula
flashcards.back: $\text{average speed}=\dfrac{\text{total distance travelled}}{\text{total time taken}}$ — including any time spent stopped.

flashcards.front: On a distance-time graph, is a horizontal line 'moving at constant speed'?
flashcards.back: No. It means the object is STATIONARY (distance is not changing, so speed is $0$).

flashcards.front: For a there-and-back journey, should average speed use the final distance from the start?
flashcards.back: No. It must use the TOTAL distance travelled (out and back added together), never the net distance from the start.

flashcards.front: On a speed-time graph, is a horizontal line 'stopped'?
flashcards.back: No. It means CONSTANT (steady) speed. The object is only stopped when the line lies ON the time axis.

flashcards.front: To find the distance for an accelerating section of a speed-time graph, do you just multiply base by height?
flashcards.back: No. An accelerating or decelerating section is a TRIANGLE (or trapezium), needing $\tfrac12bh$ or $\tfrac12(a+b)h$, not base $\times$ height alone.

flashcards.front: What are the units of acceleration?
flashcards.back: m/s$^2$ (metres per second PER SECOND) — never just m/s.

flashcards.front: On a speed-time graph, what does the AREA under the graph represent?
flashcards.back: The DISTANCE TRAVELLED, found with $\tfrac12bh$ (triangle) or $\tfrac12(a+b)h$ (trapezium) for sloping sections.

flashcards.front: A conversion graph's line passes through the origin. What does this tell you?
flashcards.back: The two quantities are DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL — doubling one doubles the other, so you can convert by multiplying (by the gradient) as well as by reading the graph.

flashcards.front: How do you find a reliable gradient from a graph?
flashcards.back: Use a LARGE triangle with both vertices on clear grid crossings of the line; a bigger triangle reduces the effect of any reading error.

flashcards.front: What does the gradient of a TANGENT to a curve represent?
flashcards.back: The rate of change AT THAT INSTANT — the speed at a point on a distance-time curve, or the acceleration at a point on a speed-time curve.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving at a constant speed.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'constant' is strongly associated with 'horizontal line' from speed-time and other graphs, so the specific meaning on a DISTANCE-time graph (no change in distance, so no movement at all) gets overridden by that more general association.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a flat section of a distance-time graph as the object 'travelling at a steady speed' rather than 'stationary'.
misconceptions.correct_model: On a DISTANCE-time graph, the vertical axis measures how far the object has travelled. A horizontal line means that distance is NOT changing, so the object is STATIONARY (speed $=0$) for that interval.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate the gradient of the horizontal section directly: change in distance $=0$, so speed $=0\div(\text{change in time})=0$ — zero speed, not a constant positive one.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Average speed for a journey is always the final distance from the start, divided by the total time.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: For an outward-only journey, final distance from the start and total distance travelled are the same number, so this shortcut works by coincidence until a RETURN journey breaks it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a there-and-back journey, the learner computes an average speed using the NET displacement (which can even be $0$ for a round trip back to the start), instead of the total distance actually covered.
misconceptions.correct_model: Average speed always uses the TOTAL DISTANCE TRAVELLED (every kilometre actually covered, in every direction) divided by the total time taken — never the final position relative to the start.
misconceptions.remediation: For a round trip back to the start, compute the final-distance-from-start version (always $0$) alongside the total-distance version, and discuss why only the second one is a sensible 'average speed'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A horizontal line on a speed-time graph means the object has stopped.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: This is exactly the correct interpretation for a DISTANCE-time graph, and distance-time and speed-time graphs look superficially identical, so the rule learned for one is applied to the other without checking the vertical axis label.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a flat section of a SPEED-time graph as the object being 'stopped' or 'stationary', when the graph is actually showing a period of constant, non-zero speed.
misconceptions.correct_model: On a SPEED-time graph, a horizontal line means the SPEED is not changing — the object moves at a steady, CONSTANT speed (zero acceleration). The object is only stopped when the line lies ON the time axis itself (speed $=0$).
misconceptions.remediation: Always read the label on the vertical axis FIRST, before interpreting any horizontal section — 'distance, unchanging' means stopped; 'speed, unchanging' means steady motion.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The distance travelled during an accelerating (or decelerating) section of a speed-time graph is found by multiplying the base and height directly, as if the shape were a rectangle.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The simplest case (constant speed) genuinely is a rectangle with area $=$ base $\times$ height, and that formula is applied directly to EVERY section of the graph, without checking whether the section is actually a triangle or trapezium instead.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's distance for an accelerating or decelerating section is exactly DOUBLE the correct value, because the factor of $\tfrac12$ for a triangular (or trapezium) area has been dropped.
misconceptions.correct_model: A sloping section of a speed-time graph forms a TRIANGLE or TRAPEZIUM, not a rectangle: its area needs $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$ or $\tfrac12(a+b)\times h$, never base $\times$ height alone.
misconceptions.remediation: Before computing any area, sketch and name the shape of that section (rectangle, triangle or trapezium) and write down which area formula applies to THAT shape before substituting any numbers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting each small square on a graph as worth $1$ unit, without checking the actual scale printed on the axis.
common_mistakes.why: Many simple diagrams really do use $1$ square $=1$ unit, so this becomes an unconscious default that is not re-checked for each new graph.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before reading any value from a graph, explicitly state what one small square is worth on EACH axis by checking two consecutive labelled values.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a negative gradient on a speed-time graph as 'negative acceleration' without naming it deceleration or reporting its SIZE.
common_mistakes.why: The algebraic sign from the gradient calculation (e.g. $-2$ m/s$^2$) feels like a complete, self-explanatory answer, so the word 'deceleration' and the positive magnitude can be skipped.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always translate a negative gradient on a speed-time graph into words: state the word 'deceleration' and give its SIZE as a positive number with units.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving a final numeric answer without its units (km/h, m/s, m/s$^2$, litres per minute, and so on).
common_mistakes.why: Once the correct number has been calculated, it can feel like the hard work is finished, so the unit label gets left off in the rush to move to the next part of the question.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit as part of the SAME line as the final number, every time, as a fixed habit rather than an afterthought.

exam_notes: Read scales carefully and state units in every answer (km/h, m/s, m/s$^2$).
If the question says "use the graph", you must show construction lines or triangles for method marks — a correct-looking final answer with no visible working on the graph can lose marks.
Give non-exact answers to 3 significant figures, and convert units before comparing two speeds given in different units ($1$ m/s $=3.6$ km/h).
For "estimate" questions involving a tangent, a tolerance of about $\pm10\%$ around the expected gradient is normally accepted.

summary.big_idea: A practical graph turns a changing situation into a picture where the gradient is always a rate (speed, acceleration, price per unit) and, on a speed-time graph specifically, the area is a distance — but the SAME shape (a horizontal line) means something different depending entirely on what the vertical axis measures, so always check the axis label first.
key_points: Distance-time graph: gradient $=$ speed; horizontal line $=$ stopped; average speed $=$ total distance $\div$ total time (including stops).
Conversion graphs are read across and down (or up and across); a line through the origin means direct proportion and allows converting by multiplication.
For any straight-line graph: gradient $=\dfrac{\text{change up}}{\text{change across}}$ (a rate), and the vertical intercept is the starting value; use a large triangle for an accurate gradient.
ADVANCED: speed-time graph: gradient $=$ acceleration (m/s$^2$); area under the graph $=$ distance, using $\tfrac12bh$ or $\tfrac12(a+b)h$ for sloping sections.
ADVANCED: the gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of its tangent there — an estimate, representing the instantaneous speed or acceleration.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Always check the vertical axis label before interpreting a flat or sloping line; on any graph the gradient is a rate (change up over change across), and on a speed-time graph specifically, the area underneath is the distance travelled.

17_Graphs_of_Functions.json.title: Graphs of Functions
17_Graphs_of_Functions.json.subject: Mathematics

objectives.statement: Complete a table of values for a given function and use it to draw a smooth, accurately scaled graph.
Recognise and sketch the shape of linear and quadratic graphs, including the symmetry and turning point of a parabola.
Recognise and sketch the shape of a reciprocal graph $y=a/x$, identifying its two branches and its asymptotes.
Solve an equation graphically by drawing the relevant graphs and reading the $x$-coordinates of their intersections, rearranging an equation where necessary.
Draw and interpret graphs of cubic functions and sums of powers of $x$ (including negative and fractional powers), identifying turning points and roots.
Draw and interpret exponential growth and decay graphs, identifying the horizontal asymptote and using the graph to solve $ab^x=k$.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a value into an algebraic expression, including negative numbers, to evaluate it correctly.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every table of values in this lesson is built one substitution at a time, and a sign slip in a single entry throws off the whole curve.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a quadratic equation by factorising, $x^2+bx+c=(x+p)(x+q)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Checking a graphical root against its exact algebraic value (and solving the intersection equations in the challenge problems) both need this skill.

prerequisites.statement: Plot coordinates accurately on a pair of axes and read values from a graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson is built entirely on plotting points, drawing curves through them, and reading values back off the finished graph.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the equation of a straight line $y=mx+c$ and identify its gradient $m$ and $y$-intercept $c$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several of this lesson's graphical solutions involve drawing a straight line alongside a curve, which requires finding and plotting that line correctly first.

diagnostic_items.question: What is special about the value $x=0$ in the graph of $y=6/x$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $x=0$ is not allowed: $6\div0$ is undefined, so the graph has no point at $x=0$. The $y$-axis is an asymptote that the curve approaches but never touches.

common_wrong_answers.answer: "The graph passes through the origin there" or leaving the point undefined without explanation.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has not yet connected the algebraic restriction (division by zero is undefined) to its graphical consequence (a gap in the curve, with the axis as an asymptote).

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner connects an algebraic restriction on a function to a specific visual feature of its graph.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Substitute $x=0$ directly into $y=6/x$ and show the calculator or working gives an error, then relate that error to the missing point on the graph.

diagnostic_items.question: How do you use the graph of $y=x^2-4x+1$ to solve $x^2-4x+1=3$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Draw the horizontal line $y=3$ on the same axes, and read the $x$-coordinates of the points where the line meets the curve.

common_wrong_answers.answer: "Read where the curve crosses the $x$-axis" (confusing this with solving $x^2-4x+1=0$).
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has memorised 'solve graphically $=$ find where the curve meets the $x$-axis' as the only case, rather than the general rule of drawing the line $y=k$ for the specific value on the right-hand side.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can adapt the general graphical method to a right-hand side other than $0$.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compare side by side: solving $=0$ needs the line $y=0$ (the $x$-axis itself); solving $=3$ needs the line $y=3$ drawn in separately.

diagnostic_items.question: What is the line of symmetry of a parabola that crosses the $x$-axis at $x=1$ and $x=5$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $x=3$ — the line of symmetry lies exactly halfway between the two roots: $(1+5)\div2=3$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Stating $x=1$ or $x=5$ (one of the roots itself), or adding the roots without halving ($x=6$).
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner recalls that the roots and the symmetry line are related but has not pinned down the exact relationship: the symmetry line is the AVERAGE (midpoint) of the two roots, not one of the roots or their sum.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the specific numerical relationship between a parabola's roots and its axis of symmetry, used throughout quadratic graph work.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch a simple symmetric U-shape with the two roots marked, and visually confirm the symmetry line sits exactly midway between them before computing the average.

diagnostic_items.question: Why does the graph of $y=2^x$ never reach the $x$-axis?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A positive number raised to any power is always positive, so $2^x>0$ for every value of $x$. As $x$ becomes very negative, $2^x$ gets extremely small (e.g. $2^{-10}\approx0.001$) but never reaches exactly $0$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: "Because the graph goes off the edge of the grid before it gets there" (a graphing/scale explanation rather than an algebraic one).
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is reasoning only from the limited picture drawn on paper, rather than from the algebraic fact that $2^x$ is a product of positive factors and can never equal zero for any real $x$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can justify an asymptote algebraically, not just describe what the picture looks like.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compute $2^x$ for a sequence of increasingly negative $x$ ($x=-1,-5,-10,-20$) and observe the values shrinking towards, but never reaching, $0$.

theory_blocks.title: A graph is a picture of solutions
theory_blocks.body:
A FUNCTION is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input, and its graph is a picture of every input-output pair. Every point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ is a solution of the equation $y=f(x)$.

So to solve an equation graphically, turn EACH SIDE into a graph and find where they meet: $x^2-2x-3=2$ is answered by the points where the curve $y=x^2-2x-3$ meets the line $y=2$.

The picture gives a number you can read off, to about half a small square.

theory_blocks.title: Drawing an accurate graph from a table
theory_blocks.body:
To draw the graph of a function:
1. Make a table of $x$-values (include negatives and zero when the function allows them).
2. Work out each $y$ carefully, one value at a time.
3. Choose a scale that uses the whole grid and label both axes.
4. Plot each point with a small cross $\times$.
5. Join the points with a SMOOTH CURVE (freehand for curves, ruler for lines).

A straight line $y=ax+b$ needs only a few points: for $y=2x-3$ the points $(-2,-7),(0,-3),(3,3)$ lie on one line, and a fourth point is a check. Its gradient is $a$ and it cuts the $y$-axis at $b$.

theory_blocks.title: Quadratic graphs
theory_blocks.body:
The graph of $y=ax^2+bx+c$ (with $a\ne0$) is a PARABOLA: a smooth U-shape if $a>0$, and an upside-down U (a cap) if $a<0$. It is symmetrical about a vertical line through its TURNING POINT.

If the parabola crosses the $x$-axis at two roots, the line of symmetry passes through the MIDPOINT of those two roots.

theory_blocks.title: Four quadratic-graph mistakes
theory_blocks.body:
- Joining points with straight segments, or drawing a pointed bottom. A quadratic curve is [[blue:SMOOTH and rounded]] at the turning point; a flat, ruled joint loses marks.
- Reading the $y$-value where the $x$-value is wanted. When solving $f(x)=k$, the answers are the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, not $k$.
- Stopping the curve at the first and last plotted points; if the domain is $-2\le x\le4$ the curve must reach exactly those ends.
- Sign slips when squaring negatives: $(-2)^2=4$, but $-2^2$ on a calculator without brackets gives $-4$.

theory_blocks.title: Solving an equation graphically
theory_blocks.body:
To solve $f(x)=g(x)$: draw $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$; the solutions are the $x$-coordinates of their intersections. Special cases:
- $f(x)=0$: where the curve meets the $x$-axis (a ROOT).
- $f(x)=k$: where the curve meets the horizontal line $y=k$.
- $f(x)=mx+c$: where the curve meets that straight line.

If the equation to solve is NOT already the function you have drawn, rearrange it so that one side matches your plotted curve exactly, then draw the other side as the second graph.

theory_blocks.title: Reciprocal graphs
theory_blocks.body:
The graph of $y=\dfrac ax$ has TWO SEPARATE BRANCHES. It never meets either axis: $x$ cannot be $0$ (division by zero), and $y$ can never be $0$. As $x$ gets very large, the curve gets very close to the $x$-axis;

as $x$ gets close to $0$, the curve shoots up or down (both axes are ASYMPTOTES). If $a>0$, the branches lie in the first and third quadrants; if $a<0$, they lie in the second and fourth.

theory_blocks.title: Drawing a reciprocal graph correctly
theory_blocks.body:
Do not join the two branches, and do not let a branch touch or cross the axes. Choose points close to $0$ (such as $\pm0.8$) so that the curve visibly bends steeply;

do NOT include $x=0$ in the table. The graph of $y=a/x$ is unchanged if you swap $x$ and $y$, so it is symmetrical about the line $y=x$.

theory_blocks.title: Cubics and sums of powers of x
theory_blocks.body:
The Extended course includes functions built from terms $ax^n$ with $n=-2,-1,-\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12,1,2,3$, and SUMS of up to three of them.

Make a table exactly as before, taking special care with negative and fractional powers: $x^{-1}=\dfrac1x$, $x^{-2}=\dfrac1{x^2}$, $x^{1/2}=\sqrt x$.

For a sum such as $y=2x+\dfrac3{x^2}$, work out each term SEPARATELY in the table (add rows for $2x$ and $\dfrac3{x^2}$) and then add — this avoids arithmetic slips and shows method for the marks.

A cubic graph can have up to TWO turning points and up to THREE roots. A graph combining $x$ and $1/x$ terms typically has two branches, approaching the line formed by the dominant term for large $|x|$,

and a curved "dip" or "peak" where the two parts balance.

theory_blocks.title: Exponential graphs: growth and decay
theory_blocks.body:
An EXPONENTIAL FUNCTION has the variable in the power: $y=ab^x+c$ with $b>0$. For $b>1$ the graph shows GROWTH (increasing faster and faster); for $0<b<1$ it shows DECAY.

The graph of $y=2^x$ is always above the $x$-axis and gets closer and closer to it on the left without touching: the $x$-axis is a HORIZONTAL ASYMPTOTE. Every exponential $y=ab^x$ passes through $(0,a)$.

After reading a value from an exponential graph, check it two ways: substitute it back into the equation,

and check that the MULTIPLIER between consecutive equally-spaced readings stays constant (e.g. for decay at $0.85$ per year, successive values should each be about $85\%$ of the one before).

keywords.definition: A rule that gives exactly one output for each input; its graph is a picture of every input-output pair.
The U-shaped (or cap-shaped) curve that is the graph of a quadratic function $y=ax^2+bx+c$.
The point on a curve where it changes from decreasing to increasing (or increasing to decreasing); the lowest or highest point of a local section of the curve.
A vertical line through a parabola's turning point, about which the curve is a mirror image of itself; it passes through the midpoint of any two roots.
The graph of $y=a/x$, formed of two separate branches that never touch either axis.
A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never actually touches or crosses.
A value of $x$ for which $f(x)=0$; graphically, where the curve $y=f(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.
Finding the solution of an equation by drawing the relevant graphs and reading the $x$-coordinates of their points of intersection.
A function of the form $y=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ (with $a\ne0$); its graph can have up to two turning points and up to three roots.
A function of the form $y=ab^x+c$ (with $b>0$) in which the variable appears in the power; shows growth if $b>1$ and decay if $0<b<1$.

worked_examples.statement: Drawing a quadratic and solving. (a) Complete the table for $y=x^2-2x-3$ and draw its graph for $-2\le x\le4$. (b) Solve $x^2-2x-3=0$. (c) Use the graph to solve $x^2-2x-3=2$.
reasoning: (a) Substitute each $x$-value in turn, plot the seven points with crosses, and join them with one smooth curve.
(b) Solving $=0$ means finding where the curve crosses the $x$-axis.
(c) Solving $=2$ means drawing the line $y=2$ and reading the $x$-coordinates of where it meets the curve.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $x=-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4$ gives $y=5,0,-3,-4,-3,0,5$. The lowest point (turning point) is $(1,-4)$, and the curve is symmetrical about $x=1$.

(b) The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=-1$ and $x=3$ (check by factorising: $(x+1)(x-3)=0$). (c) Draw the line $y=2$: it meets the curve at $x\approx-1.4$ and $x\approx3.4$ (exact values $1\pm\sqrt6$, that is $-1.45$ and $3.45$).
worked_examples.interpretation: The same curve answers several different equations, depending only on which horizontal line is drawn alongside it: $y=0$ for part (b), $y=2$ for part (c).
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (c), reading the answer as $x=2$ (the right-hand side of the equation) instead of the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the line $y=2$ actually meets the curve.

assets.purpose: Show a complete quadratic graph built from a table, together with the horizontal-line method for solving a shifted equation.

worked_examples.statement: A rearranged equation. Use the graph of $y=x^2-2x-3$ to solve $x^2-3x-4=0$.
reasoning: The equation to solve is NOT the plotted function, so rearrange it until one side matches $x^2-2x-3$ exactly.
Add $x+1$ to both sides of $x^2-3x-4=0$ to turn the left side into $x^2-2x-3$.
Draw the resulting straight line on the same axes and read the intersections.
worked_examples.solution: $x^2-3x-4=0$ becomes $x^2-2x-3=x+1$ (adding $x+1$ to both sides). Draw the line $y=x+1$, through $(-1,0)$ and $(4,5)$: it meets the curve at $x=-1$ and $x=4$.
worked_examples.interpretation: An equation does not have to already match a drawn graph to be solved from it — rearranging first to isolate the plotted function on one side lets the SAME graph answer many different equations.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to read $x^2-3x-4=0$ directly off the $y=x^2-2x-3$ graph (looking for where it crosses the $x$-axis) without first rearranging, which gives the wrong roots.

assets.tikz: \nbfuncplot{-2}{4}{-5}{6}{1}{2}{\addplot[NebulaNavyTwo,domain=-2:4,samples=120] {x^2-2*x-3};\addplot[NebulaError,domain=-2:4] {x+1};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt,NebulaCheck] coordinates {(-1,0) (4,5)};}
assets.caption: The same parabola with the line $y=x+1$ added, meeting it at $x=-1$ and $x=4$ — the solutions of the rearranged equation $x^2-3x-4=0$.
assets.purpose: Show how the same base curve can be reused for a different equation once it has been rearranged to match.

worked_examples.statement: Reciprocal and line. Draw $y=\dfrac6x$ for $-6\le x\le6$ and $y=x-1$ on the same axes. Hence solve $\dfrac6x=x-1$.
reasoning: Build the table for $y=6/x$ in two separate pieces, one for positive $x$ and one for negative $x$, avoiding $x=0$.
Draw the line $y=x-1$ on the same axes.
Read the $x$-coordinates of the points where the line crosses either branch of the curve.
worked_examples.solution: The line and the two branches meet at $(3,2)$ and $(-2,-3)$, so $x=3$ or $x=-2$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Solving an equation graphically works the same way whether the function being drawn is a straight line, a curve, or (as here) a reciprocal graph with two separate branches — only the SHAPE being drawn changes, not the method.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Searching for a third intersection point near $x=0$, forgetting that the reciprocal curve has no point there at all.

assets.tikz: \nbfuncplot{-6}{6}{-8}{8}{1}{2}{\addplot[NebulaNavyTwo,domain=0.8:6,samples=100] {6/x};\addplot[NebulaNavyTwo,domain=-6:-0.8,samples=100] {6/x};\addplot[NebulaError,domain=-6:6] {x-1};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt,NebulaCheck] coordinates {(3,2) (-2,-3)};}
assets.caption: The two branches of $y=6/x$ with the line $y=x-1$, meeting at $(3,2)$ and $(-2,-3)$.
assets.purpose: Show the graphical method applied to a reciprocal graph, with the two separate branches drawn correctly without joining them.

worked_examples.statement: A cubic. Draw $y=x^3+x-4$ for $-1\le x\le3$ and use it to solve $x^3+x-4=0$.
reasoning: Build the table, including some half-values near where the curve is expected to cross the axis, for a more accurate reading.
Plot the points and draw one smooth, continuously rising curve.
Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis.
worked_examples.solution: The table gives $y=-6,-4,-2,0.875,6,26$ for $x=-1,0,1,1.5,2,3$. The curve crosses the $x$-axis once, just before $x=1.5$: from the graph, $x\approx1.4$ (more precisely $x\approx1.38$).
worked_examples.interpretation: The curve rises all the way (it has no turning point for this function), so it can only cross the $x$-axis once: there is exactly one real root.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing down more than one root, by mistaking a steep but still-rising section of the curve for a second crossing of the axis.

assets.purpose: Show that a cubic curve can have exactly one root when it rises throughout its plotted domain.

worked_examples.statement: A sum with a reciprocal. Draw $y=x+\dfrac4x$ for $x\ne0$ and describe its shape.
reasoning: Build the table for positive $x$ first, then use the fact that the function is odd-symmetric to describe the negative branch.
Identify the lowest point of the positive branch directly from the table.
worked_examples.solution: For $x>0$: $x=0.6,1,2,3,4,6$ gives $y=7.27,5,4,4.33,5,6.67$. The curve falls to a lowest point $(2,4)$ and then rises. For $x<0$ it is the same shape turned upside down about the origin, with a highest point $(-2,-4)$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The $y$-axis is an asymptote (from the $4/x$ term), and for large $|x|$ the curve approaches the line $y=x$ (the $4/x$ term becomes negligible) — a curve can combine the behaviour of two simpler graphs at different scales.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the lowest point of the positive branch is where $x$ and $4/x$ are individually smallest, rather than reading it from the table as the point where their SUM is smallest.

assets.caption: The graph of $y=x+4/x$, with a lowest point at $(2,4)$ on the positive branch and a highest point at $(-2,-4)$ on the negative branch.
assets.purpose: Show the characteristic shape of a sum of a linear and a reciprocal term, including its point symmetry about the origin.

worked_examples.statement: Growth and decay. (a) Use the graph of $y=2^x$ to estimate the solution of $2^x=10$. (b) The value of a car is $V=20\,000\times0.85^n$ pounds after $n$ years. When is it worth £10\,000?
reasoning: (a) Draw the line $y=10$ and read down to the $x$-axis from where it meets the curve.
(b) Draw the decay curve and read across from $V=10$ (in thousands of pounds) to find $n$.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) The line $y=10$ meets the curve at $x\approx3.3$ (check: $2^{3.3}\approx9.85$, close to $10$). (b) On the decay curve, $V=10\,000$ occurs at $n\approx4.3$: the car is worth half its price after about $4.3$ years, a little over $4$ years.

Each year the value is multiplied by $0.85$ (a $15\%$ decrease).
worked_examples.interpretation: Growth and decay graphs both flatten towards a horizontal asymptote, but reading a SPECIFIC target value from either still uses exactly the same graphical method: draw the target line and read across or down to the matching axis.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (b), forgetting that the vertical scale is in THOUSANDS of pounds, and reading off $n$ at $V=10$ (ten pounds) rather than $V=10$ thousand pounds.
