exercises.statement: Rewrite the following in the form $a^{m/n}$: a $(\sqrt[5]{a})^3$, b $(\sqrt[6]{a})^2$, c $(\sqrt[4]{a})^4$, d $(\sqrt[7]{a})^3$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Rewrite the following in the form $(\sqrt[n]{b})^m$: a $b^{2/7}$, b $b^{8/3}$, c $b^{-2/5}$, d $b^{-4/3}$
exercises.full_solution: Write $b^{m/n}=(\sqrt[n]{b})^m$, so the denominator of the fractional index is the root and the numerator is the outer power. a $(\sqrt[7]{b})^2$. b $(\sqrt[3]{b})^8$. c $(\sqrt[5]{b})^{-2}$. d $(\sqrt[3]{b})^{-4}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify the following algebraic expressions, giving your answer in the form $a^{m/n}$: a $a^{1/2}\times a^{1/4}$, b $a^{2/5}\times a^{-1/4}$, c $\frac{\sqrt{a}}{a^{-2}}$, d $\frac{\sqrt[3]{a}}{a}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following linear equations: a $3x=2x-4$, b $5y=3y+10$, c $2y-5=3y$, d $p-8=3p$, e $3y-8=2y$, f $7x+11=5x$
exercises.full_solution: Collect the unknown terms on one side and the numbers on the other. a $x=-4$. b $2y=10\Rightarrow y=5$. c $-5=y\Rightarrow y=-5$. d $-8=2p\Rightarrow p=-4$. e $y=8$. f $11=-2x\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac{11}{2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following linear equations: a $3x-9=4$, b $4=3x-11$, c $6x-15=3x+3$, d $4y+5=3y-3$, e $8y-31=13-3y$, f $4m+2=5m-8$
exercises.full_solution: a $3x=13\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{13}{3}$. b $15=3x\Rightarrow x=5$. c $3x=18\Rightarrow x=6$. d $y=-8$. e $11y=44\Rightarrow y=4$. f $-m=-10\Rightarrow m=10$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following linear equations: a $7m-1=5m+1$, b $5p-3=3+3p$, c $12-2k=16+2k$, d $6x+9=3x-54$, e $8-3x=18-8x$, f $2-y=y-4$
exercises.full_solution: a $2m=2\Rightarrow m=1$. b $2p=6\Rightarrow p=3$. c $-4k=4\Rightarrow k=-1$. d $3x=-63\Rightarrow x=-21$. e $5x=10\Rightarrow x=2$. f $-2y=-6\Rightarrow y=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following linear equations: a $\frac{x}{2}=3$, b $\frac{1}{2}y=7$, c $\frac{x}{4}=1$, d $\frac{1}{4}m=3$, e $7=\frac{x}{5}$, f $4=\frac{1}{5}p$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply both sides by the denominator. a $x=6$. b $y=14$. c $x=4$. d $m=12$. e $x=35$. f $p=20$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following linear equations: a $\frac{x}{3}-1=4$, b $\frac{x}{5}+2=1$, c $\frac{2}{3}x=5$, d $\frac{3}{4}x=6$, e $\frac{1}{5}x=\frac{1}{2}$, f $\frac{2x}{5}=4$
exercises.full_solution: a $\tfrac{x}{3}=5\Rightarrow x=15$. b $\tfrac{x}{5}=-1\Rightarrow x=-5$. c Multiply by $\tfrac32$: $x=\tfrac{15}{2}$. d Multiply by $\tfrac43$: $x=8$. e Multiply by $5$: $x=\tfrac52$. f Multiply by $\tfrac52$: $x=10$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For each triangle, construct an equation in terms of $x$ using the angle sum of a triangle ($180^\circ$), solve it, and find each angle: a angles $x^\circ,\ (x+40)^\circ,\ (x+20)^\circ$; b angles $(x+20)^\circ,\ (x+20)^\circ,\ (x-40)^\circ$; c angles $(5x)^\circ,\ (11x)^\circ,\ (2x)^\circ$; d angles $x^\circ,\ (3x)^\circ,\ (2x)^\circ$; e angles $(x-20)^\circ,\ (4x+10)^\circ,\ (2x-20)^\circ$; f angles $(2x+5)^\circ,\ (4x)^\circ,\ (3x-50)^\circ$
exercises.answer: a $x=40$, angles $40^\circ,80^\circ,60^\circ$; b $x=60$, angles $80^\circ,80^\circ,20^\circ$; c $x=10$, angles $50^\circ,110^\circ,20^\circ$; d $x=30$, angles $30^\circ,90^\circ,60^\circ$; e $x=30$, angles $10^\circ,130^\circ,40^\circ$; f $x=25$, angles $55^\circ,100^\circ,25^\circ$
exercises.full_solution: The three angles of each triangle add to $180^\circ$. a $x+(x+40)+(x+20)=180\Rightarrow3x+60=180\Rightarrow x=40$; angles $40^\circ,80^\circ,60^\circ$ (sum $180^\circ$, check). b $3x=180\Rightarrow x=60$; angles $80^\circ,80^\circ,20^\circ$. c $18x=180\Rightarrow x=10$; angles $50^\circ,110^\circ,20^\circ$. d $6x=180\Rightarrow x=30$; angles $30^\circ,90^\circ,60^\circ$. e $7x-30=180\Rightarrow x=30$; angles $10^\circ,130^\circ,40^\circ$. f $9x-45=180\Rightarrow x=25$; angles $55^\circ,100^\circ,25^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The angles shown are grouped around a single point (sum $360^\circ$). Construct an equation in terms of $x$, solve it and find each angle: a $(3x)^\circ,\ (5x)^\circ,\ (4x)^\circ$; b $(3x)^\circ,\ (4x+15)^\circ,\ (4x+15)^\circ$; c $(6x+5)^\circ,\ (2x+40)^\circ,\ (x+10)^\circ,\ (3x+5)^\circ$; d $(3x+15)^\circ,\ x^\circ,\ (3x-5)^\circ,\ (3x+20)^\circ$
exercises.answer: a $x=30$, angles $90^\circ,150^\circ,120^\circ$; b $x=30$, angles $90^\circ,135^\circ,135^\circ$; c $x=25$, angles $155^\circ,90^\circ,35^\circ,80^\circ$; d $x=33$, angles $114^\circ,33^\circ,94^\circ,119^\circ$
exercises.full_solution: Angles at a point add to $360^\circ$. a $12x=360\Rightarrow x=30$; angles $90^\circ,150^\circ,120^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$). b $11x+30=360\Rightarrow x=30$; angles $90^\circ,135^\circ,135^\circ$. c $12x+60=360\Rightarrow x=25$; angles $155^\circ,90^\circ,35^\circ,80^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$). d $10x+30=360\Rightarrow x=33$; angles $114^\circ,33^\circ,94^\circ,119^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the value of $x$ from the rectangle dimensions given (width $\times$ height $=$ area): a width $(x+1)$, height $4$, area $24$; b width $7$, height $(x+9)$, area $77$; c width $4.5$, height $(x+3)$, area $45$; d width $(x+0.4)$, height $3.8$, area $5.7$; e width $(x+0.5)$, height $0.2$, area $5.1$; f width $2x$, height $x$, area $450$
exercises.full_solution: Form the equation width $\times$ height $=$ area and solve for $x$. a $4(x+1)=24\Rightarrow x+1=6\Rightarrow x=5$. b $7(x+9)=77\Rightarrow x+9=11\Rightarrow x=2$. c $4.5(x+3)=45\Rightarrow x+3=10\Rightarrow x=7$. d $3.8(x+0.4)=5.7\Rightarrow x+0.4=1.5\Rightarrow x=1.1$. e $0.2(x+0.5)=5.1\Rightarrow x+0.5=25.5\Rightarrow x=25$. f $2x\cdot x=450\Rightarrow x^2=225\Rightarrow x=15$ (rejecting $x=-15$ since a length must be positive).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations: a $2x+y=7,\ 3x+2y=12$; b $5x+4y=21,\ x+2y=9$; c $x+y=7,\ 3x+4y=23$; d $2x-3y=-3,\ 3x+2y=15$; e $4x=4y+8,\ x+3y=10$; f $x+5y=11,\ 2x-2y=10$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $2x+y=7$ (1) and $3x+2y=12$ (2). Multiplying (1) by $2$ gives $4x+2y=14$ (3). Then (3)$-$(2): $x=2$. Substituting into (1): $4+y=7$, so $y=3$.

The same method gives: b $x=1,\ y=4$; c $x=5,\ y=2$; d $x=3,\ y=3$; e $x=4,\ y=2$; f $x=6,\ y=1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations: a $x+y=5,\ 3x-2y+5=0$; b $2x-2y=6,\ x-5y=-5$; c $2x+3y=15,\ 2y=15-3x$; d $x-6y=0,\ 3x-3y=15$; e $2x-5y=-11,\ 3x+4y=18$; f $x+y=5,\ 2x-2y=-2$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $x+y=5$ (1) and $3x-2y+5=0$, i.e. $3x-2y=-5$ (2). Multiplying (1) by $2$ gives $2x+2y=10$ (3). Then (3)$+$(2): $5x=5$, so $x=1$. Substituting into (1): $1+y=5$, so $y=4$.

The same method gives: b $x=5,\ y=2$; c $x=3,\ y=3$; d $x=6,\ y=1$; e $x=2,\ y=3$; f $x=2,\ y=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations: a $3y=9+2x,\ 3x+2y=6$; b $x+4y=13,\ 3x-3y=9$; c $2x=3y-19,\ 3x+2y=17$; d $2x-5y=-8,\ -3x-2y=-26$; e $5x-2y=0,\ 2x+5y=29$; f $8y=3-x,\ 3x-2y=9$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $3y=9+2x$, i.e. $-2x+3y=9$ (1), and $3x+2y=6$ (2). Multiplying (1) by $2$ gives $-4x+6y=18$ (3); multiplying (2) by $3$ gives $9x+6y=18$ (4). Then (4)$-$(3): $13x=0$, so $x=0$. Substituting into (1): $3y=9$, so $y=3$.

The same method gives: b $x=5,\ y=2$; c $x=1,\ y=7$; d $x=6,\ y=4$; e $x=2,\ y=5$; f $x=3,\ y=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations: a $4x+2y=5,\ 3x+6y=6$; b $4x+y=14,\ 6x-3y=3$; c $10x-y=-2,\ -15x+3y=9$; d $-2y=0.5-2x,\ 6x+3y=6$; e $x+3y=6,\ 2x-9y=7$; f $5x-3y=-0.5,\ 3x+2y=3.5$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $4x+2y=5$ (1) and $3x+6y=6$ (2). Multiplying (1) by $3$ gives $12x+6y=15$ (3). Then (3)$-$(2): $9x=9$, so $x=1$. Substituting into (1): $4+2y=5$, so $y=\tfrac12$.

The same method gives: b $x=\tfrac52,\ y=4$; c $x=\tfrac15,\ y=4$; d $x=0.75,\ y=0.5$; e $x=5,\ y=\tfrac13$; f $x=0.5,\ y=1$. Parts a to f have fractional or decimal solutions, so leave the answers as exact fractions rather than rounding.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The sum of two numbers is $17$ and their difference is $3$. Find the two numbers by forming two equations and solving them simultaneously.
exercises.full_solution: Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$: $x+y=17$ and $x-y=3$. Adding: $2x=20\Rightarrow x=10$, then $y=7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The difference between two numbers is $7$. If their sum is $25$, find the two numbers by forming two equations and solving them simultaneously.
exercises.full_solution: Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$: $x-y=7$ and $x+y=25$. Adding: $2x=32\Rightarrow x=16$, then $y=9$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A rectangle has top side $(x+3y)$, left side $(3x+y)$, bottom side $13$ and right side $7$. Find the values of $x$ and $y$.
exercises.full_solution: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so $x+3y=13$ and $3x+y=7$. Solving simultaneously: from the second equation $y=7-3x$; substituting, $x+3(7-3x)=13\Rightarrow x+21-9x=13\Rightarrow -8x=-8\Rightarrow x=1$, then $y=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A rectangle has top side $(3x-2y)$, left side $(2x-3y)$, bottom side $11$ and right side $4$. Find the values of $x$ and $y$.
exercises.full_solution: Opposite sides equal: $3x-2y=11$ and $2x-3y=4$. Eliminate: multiply the first by $3$ and the second by $2$: $9x-6y=33$ and $4x-6y=8$; subtracting gives $5x=25\Rightarrow x=5$, then $2(5)-3y=4\Rightarrow y=2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A man's age is three times his son's age. Ten years ago he was five times his son's age. By forming two equations and solving them simultaneously, find both of their ages.
exercises.full_solution: Let the man's age be $m$ and the son's age $s$: $m=3s$ and $m-10=5(s-10)$. Substituting: $3s-10=5s-50\Rightarrow40=2s\Rightarrow s=20$, so $m=60$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A grandfather is ten times older than his granddaughter. He is also 54 years older than her. How old is each of them?
exercises.full_solution: Let the grandfather's age be $g$ and the granddaughter's age $d$: $g=10d$ and $g=d+54$. Substituting: $10d=d+54\Rightarrow9d=54\Rightarrow d=6$, so $g=60$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $x^2+7x+12=0$, b $x^2+8x+12=0$, c $x^2+13x+12=0$, d $x^2-7x+10=0$, e $x^2-5x+6=0$, f $x^2-6x+8=0$
exercises.full_solution: Factorise each quadratic and set each bracket to zero. a $(x+3)(x+4)=0\Rightarrow x=-3,-4$. b $(x+2)(x+6)=0\Rightarrow x=-2,-6$. c $(x+1)(x+12)=0\Rightarrow x=-1,-12$. d $(x-2)(x-5)=0\Rightarrow x=2,5$. e $(x-2)(x-3)=0\Rightarrow x=2,3$. f $(x-2)(x-4)=0\Rightarrow x=2,4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $x^2+3x-10=0$, b $x^2-3x-10=0$, c $x^2+5x-14=0$, d $x^2-5x-14=0$, e $x^2+2x-15=0$, f $x^2-2x-15=0$
exercises.full_solution: a $(x-2)(x+5)=0\Rightarrow x=2,-5$. b $(x-5)(x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=5,-2$. c $(x-2)(x+7)=0\Rightarrow x=2,-7$. d $(x-7)(x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=7,-2$. e $(x-3)(x+5)=0\Rightarrow x=3,-5$. f $(x-5)(x+3)=0\Rightarrow x=5,-3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $x^2+5x=-6$, b $x^2+6x=-9$, c $x^2+11x=-24$, d $x^2-10x=-24$, e $x^2+x=12$, f $x^2-4x=12$
exercises.full_solution: First rearrange to $=0$, then factorise. a $x^2+5x+6=0\Rightarrow(x+2)(x+3)=0\Rightarrow x=-2,-3$. b $x^2+6x+9=0\Rightarrow(x+3)^2=0\Rightarrow x=-3$ (a repeated root). c $x^2+11x+24=0\Rightarrow(x+3)(x+8)=0\Rightarrow x=-3,-8$. d $x^2-10x+24=0\Rightarrow(x-4)(x-6)=0\Rightarrow x=4,6$. e $x^2+x-12=0\Rightarrow(x-3)(x+4)=0\Rightarrow x=3,-4$. f $x^2-4x-12=0\Rightarrow(x-6)(x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=6,-2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $x^2-2x=8$, b $x^2-x=20$, c $x^2+x=30$, d $x^2-x=42$, e $x^2-2x=63$, f $x^2+3x=54$
exercises.full_solution: a $x^2-2x-8=0\Rightarrow(x-4)(x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=4,-2$. b $x^2-x-20=0\Rightarrow(x-5)(x+4)=0\Rightarrow x=5,-4$. c $x^2+x-30=0\Rightarrow(x-5)(x+6)=0\Rightarrow x=5,-6$. d $x^2-x-42=0\Rightarrow(x-7)(x+6)=0\Rightarrow x=7,-6$. e $x^2-2x-63=0\Rightarrow(x-9)(x+7)=0\Rightarrow x=9,-7$. f $x^2+3x-54=0\Rightarrow(x-6)(x+9)=0\Rightarrow x=6,-9$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $x^2-9=0$, b $x^2-16=0$, c $x^2=25$, d $x^2=121$, e $x^2-144=0$, f $x^2-220=5$
exercises.full_solution: Each is solved by isolating $x^2$ and taking the square root (two roots, $\pm$). a $x=\pm3$. b $x=\pm4$. c $x=\pm5$. d $x=\pm11$. e $x=\pm12$. f $x^2=225\Rightarrow x=\pm15$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $4x^2-25=0$, b $9x^2-36=0$, c $25x^2=64$, d $x^2=\frac{1}{4}$, e $x^2-\frac{1}{9}=0$, f $16x^2-\frac{1}{25}=0$
exercises.answer: a $x=\pm\frac{5}{2}$; b $x=\pm2$; c $x=\pm\frac{8}{5}$; d $x=\pm\frac{1}{2}$; e $x=\pm\frac{1}{3}$; f $x=\pm\frac{1}{20}$
exercises.full_solution: a $x^2=\tfrac{25}{4}\Rightarrow x=\pm\tfrac52$. b $x^2=4\Rightarrow x=\pm2$. c $x^2=\tfrac{64}{25}\Rightarrow x=\pm\tfrac85$. d $x=\pm\tfrac12$. e $x=\pm\tfrac13$. f $x^2=\tfrac{1}{400}\Rightarrow x=\pm\tfrac{1}{20}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $x^2+5x+4=0$, b $x^2+7x+10=0$, c $x^2+6x+8=0$, d $x^2-6x+8=0$, e $x^2-7x+10=0$, f $x^2+2x-8=0$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $x^2-3x-10=0$, b $x^2+3x-10=0$, c $x^2-3x-18=0$, d $x^2+3x-18=0$, e $x^2-2x-24=0$, f $x^2-2x-48=0$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $x^2+x=12$, b $x^2+8x=-12$, c $x^2+5x=36$, d $x^2+2x=-1$, e $x^2+4x=-4$, f $x^2+17x=-72$
exercises.full_solution: Rearrange to $=0$ then factorise. a $x^2+x-12=0\Rightarrow(x-3)(x+4)=0$. b $x^2+8x+12=0\Rightarrow(x+2)(x+6)=0$. c $x^2+5x-36=0\Rightarrow(x-4)(x+9)=0$. d $x^2+2x+1=0\Rightarrow(x+1)^2=0\Rightarrow x=-1$. e $x^2+4x+4=0\Rightarrow(x+2)^2=0\Rightarrow x=-2$. f $x^2+17x+72=0\Rightarrow(x+8)(x+9)=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations: a $x^2-8x=0$, b $x^2-7x=0$, c $x^2+3x=0$, d $x^2+4x=0$, e $x^2-9x=0$, f $4x^2-16x=0$
exercises.full_solution: Each factorises by taking out $x$ (no constant term). a $x(x-8)=0$. b $x(x-7)=0$. c $x(x+3)=0$. d $x(x+4)=0$. e $x(x-9)=0$. f $4x(x-4)=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=4$ and $y=(x-3)^2+4$.
exercises.full_solution: Setting the expressions equal: $4=(x-3)^2+4\Rightarrow(x-3)^2=0\Rightarrow x=3$ (a repeated root), giving $y=4$. Graphically, the horizontal line $y=4$ touches the parabola $y=(x-3)^2+4$ exactly once, at its vertex $(3,4)$ — the line is a tangent to the curve there.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=-2x-3$ and $y=x^2+5x+3$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $x^2+5x+3=-2x-3\Rightarrow x^2+7x+6=0\Rightarrow(x+1)(x+6)=0\Rightarrow x=-1,-6$. For $x=-1$: $y=-2(-1)-3=-1$. For $x=-6$: $y=-2(-6)-3=9$. These are the two points where the line crosses the parabola.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=2x^2+4x+1$ and $y=3x+11$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $2x^2+4x+1=3x+11\Rightarrow2x^2+x-10=0\Rightarrow(2x+5)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac52,2$. For $x=-\tfrac52$: $y=3(-\tfrac52)+11=\tfrac72$. For $x=2$: $y=3(2)+11=17$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=6x^2-5x+2$ and $y=5x+6$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $6x^2-5x+2=5x+6\Rightarrow6x^2-10x-4=0\Rightarrow3x^2-5x-2=0\Rightarrow(3x+1)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac13,2$. For $x=-\tfrac13$: $y=5(-\tfrac13)+6=\tfrac{13}{3}$. For $x=2$: $y=5(2)+6=16$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=-2x+2$ and $y=2(x-3)^2-16$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $-2x+2=2(x-3)^2-16\Rightarrow2(x-3)^2=18-2x\Rightarrow(x-3)^2=9-x\Rightarrow x^2-6x+9=9-x\Rightarrow x^2-5x=0\Rightarrow x(x-5)=0\Rightarrow x=0,5$. For $x=0$: $y=2$. For $x=5$: $y=-2(5)+2=-8$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=-5x^2-5x+10$ and $y=6x-2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=11-x$ and $y=\frac{30}{x}$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $11-x=\dfrac{30}{x}\Rightarrow11x-x^2=30\Rightarrow x^2-11x+30=0\Rightarrow(x-5)(x-6)=0\Rightarrow x=5,6$. For $x=5$: $y=6$. For $x=6$: $y=5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=2x-7-\frac{3}{x}$ and $y=\frac{2}{x}$.
exercises.full_solution: Set equal: $2x-7-\dfrac{3}{x}=\dfrac{2}{x}\Rightarrow2x-7=\dfrac{5}{x}\Rightarrow2x^2-7x-5=0$. Discriminant $=49+40=89$ (not a perfect square), so $x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{89}}{4}$. Numerically $x\approx4.1085$ (giving $y=2/x\approx0.4868$) or $x\approx-0.6085$ (giving $y\approx-3.2868$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two rectangles are shown: rectangle A has sides $(3x-1)$ and $(2x+1)$; rectangle B has sides $(2x+1)$ and $\left(x+\frac12\right)$. Calculate the value of $x$ if the area of rectangle A and the perimeter of rectangle B have the same numerical value.
exercises.full_solution: Area of A $=(3x-1)(2x+1)=6x^2+x-1$. Perimeter of B $=2\left[(2x+1)+\left(x+\tfrac12\right)\right]=2(3x+\tfrac32)=6x+3$. Setting these equal: $6x^2+x-1=6x+3\Rightarrow6x^2-5x-4=0$. Discriminant $=25+96=121=11^2$, so $x=\dfrac{5\pm11}{12}$, giving $x=\tfrac{4}{3}$ or $x=-\tfrac12$. Since a side length $3x-1$ must be positive ($x>\tfrac13$), the valid solution is $x=\tfrac{4}{3}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two circles are shown: circle A has radius $(3p-1)$ and circle B has radius $(p+2)$. Calculate the value of $p$ if the area of circle A has the same numerical value as the perimeter (circumference) of circle B. Give your answer correct to 2 d.p.
exercises.full_solution: Area of A $=\pi(3p-1)^2$. Circumference of B $=2\pi(p+2)$. Setting these equal and cancelling $\pi$: $(3p-1)^2=2(p+2)\Rightarrow9p^2-6p+1=2p+4\Rightarrow9p^2-8p-3=0$. Discriminant $=64+108=172$, so $p=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{172}}{18}$. Taking the positive root (a radius must be positive): $p\approx\dfrac{8+13.115}{18}\approx1.1730\approx1.17$ (2 d.p.). (The other root $p\approx-0.28$ is rejected since it would make $3p-1$ negative.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $x+y=6$, $x-y=2$; b $x+y=11$, $x-y-1=0$; c $x+y=5$, $x-y=7$; d $2x+y=12$, $2x-y=8$; e $3x+y=17$, $3x-y=13$; f $5x+y=29$, $5x-y=11$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $x+y=6$ (1) and $x-y=2$ (2). Adding (1)$+$(2) removes $y$: $2x=8$, so $x=4$. Substituting into (1): $4+y=6$, so $y=2$.

The same method gives: b $x=6,\ y=5$; c $x=6,\ y=-1$; d $x=5,\ y=2$; e $x=5,\ y=2$; f $x=4,\ y=9$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $3x+2y=13$, $4x=2y+8$; b $6x+5y=62$, $4x-5y=8$; c $x+2y=3$, $8x-2y=6$; d $9x+3y=24$, $x-3y=-14$; e $7x-y=-3$, $4x+y=14$; f $3x=5y+14$, $6x+5y=58$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $3x+2y=13$ (1) and $4x=2y+8$, i.e. $4x-2y=8$ (2). Adding (1)$+$(2) removes $y$: $7x=21$, so $x=3$. Substituting into (1): $9+2y=13$, so $y=2$.

The same method gives: b $x=7,\ y=4$; c $x=1,\ y=1$; d $x=1,\ y=5$; e $x=1,\ y=10$; f $x=8,\ y=2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $2x+y=14$, $x+y=9$; b $5x+3y=29$, $x+3y=13$; c $4x+2y=50$, $x+2y=20$; d $x+y=10$, $3x=-y+22$; e $2x+5y=28$, $4x+5y=36$; f $x+6y=-2$, $3x+6y=18$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $2x+y=14$ (1) and $x+y=9$ (2). Subtracting (1)$-$(2) removes $y$: $x=5$. Substituting into (2): $5+y=9$, so $y=4$.

The same method gives: b $x=4,\ y=3$; c $x=10,\ y=5$; d $x=6,\ y=4$; e $x=4,\ y=4$; f $x=10,\ y=-2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $x-y=1$, $2x-y=6$; b $3x-2y=8$, $2x-2y=4$; c $7x-3y=26$, $2x-3y=1$; d $x=y+7$, $3x-y=17$; e $8x-2y=-2$, $3x-2y=-7$; f $4x-y=-9$, $7x-y=-18$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $x-y=1$ (1) and $2x-y=6$ (2). Subtracting (2)$-$(1) removes $y$: $x=5$. Substituting into (1): $5-y=1$, so $y=4$.

The same method gives: b $x=4,\ y=2$; c $x=5,\ y=3$; d $x=5,\ y=-2$; e $x=1,\ y=5$; f $x=-3,\ y=-3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $x+y=-7$, $x-y=-3$; b $2x+3y=-18$, $2x=3y+6$; c $5x-3y=9$, $2x+3y=19$; d $7x+4y=42$, $9x-4y=-10$; e $4x-4y=0$, $8x+4y=12$; f $x-3y=-25$, $5x-3y=-17$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $x+y=-7$ (1) and $x-y=-3$ (2). Adding (1)$+$(2) removes $y$: $2x=-10$, so $x=-5$. Substituting into (1): $-5+y=-7$, so $y=-2$.

The same method gives: b $x=-3,\ y=-4$; c $x=4,\ y=\tfrac{11}{3}$; d $x=2,\ y=7$; e $x=1,\ y=1$; f $x=2,\ y=9$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $2x+3y=13$, $2x-4y+8=0$; b $2x+4y=50$, $2x+y=20$; c $x+y=10$, $3y=22-x$; d $5x+2y=28$, $5x+4y=36$; e $2x-8y=2$, $2x-3y=7$; f $x-4y=9$, $x-7y=18$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $2x+3y=13$ (1) and $2x-4y+8=0$, i.e. $2x-4y=-8$ (2). Subtracting (1)$-$(2) removes $x$: $7y=21$, so $y=3$. Substituting into (1): $2x+9=13$, so $x=2$.

The same method gives: b $x=5,\ y=10$; c $x=4,\ y=6$; d $x=4,\ y=4$; e $x=5,\ y=1$; f $x=-3,\ y=-3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following simultaneous equations either by elimination or by substitution: a $-4x=4y$, $4x-8y=12$; b $3x=19+2y$, $-3x+5y=5$; c $3x+2y=12$, $-3x+9y=-12$; d $3x+5y=29$, $3x+y=13$; e $-5x+3y=14$, $5x+6y=58$; f $-2x+8y=6$, $2x=3-y$
exercises.full_solution:
Label the two equations (1) and (2). Eliminate one letter by adding or subtracting a suitable multiple of one equation from the other (or substitute one equation into the other), then back-substitute to find the second letter.

**a** $-4x=4y$ gives $y=-x$ (1), and $4x-8y=12$ (2). Substituting $y=-x$ into (2): $4x+8x=12$, so $12x=12$ and $x=1$; then $y=-1$.

The same method gives: b $x=\tfrac{35}{3},\ y=8$; c $x=4,\ y=0$; d $x=3,\ y=4$; e $x=2,\ y=8$; f $x=1,\ y=1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
Calculate the value of $x$ in each of the following figures (all lengths in the same units):
a An L-shaped figure with a square notch cut from one corner of a bounding rectangle of width $x+3$ and height $x+5$; perimeter $=44$.
b A staircase figure (two steps) whose overall bounding width is $(2x+5)+2x$ and overall bounding height is $8+3x$ (side labels $8$, $2x+5$, $3x$, $2x$ going round the boundary); perimeter $=68$.
c An L-shaped figure with a square notch of side $x$ cut from the top-right corner of a bounding rectangle of width $5x$ and height $4x$ (labels $x$, $x$, $3x$, $5x$); perimeter $=108$.
d An L-shaped figure with a small square notch of side $x$ cut from the bottom-left corner of a bounding rectangle of width $5x-10$ and height $6x+3$; perimeter $=140$.
e An L-shaped figure: left side $7x$, bottom $12$, with a notch of width $3x$ and height $3x$ cut from the bottom-right corner (so the overall bounding width, along the top, is $12+3x$); perimeter $=224$.
f A quadrilateral with three equal sides of length $2x$ (the top side and two slanted sides, marked with matching tick marks) and a fourth (longest) side of length $4x$, with two interior angles of $60°$; perimeter $=150$.
exercises.full_solution: For a rectilinear 'staircase' figure obtained by cutting one or more rectangular notches from the corner(s) of a bounding $W\times H$ rectangle, the perimeter is always $2(W+H)$, since the inward/outward detour segments sum to exactly $W$ horizontally and $H$ vertically. a $W=x+3$, $H=x+5$: $2((x+3)+(x+5))=44 \Rightarrow 4x+16=44 \Rightarrow x=7$. b $W=(2x+5)+2x=4x+5$, $H=8+3x$: $2((4x+5)+(8+3x))=68 \Rightarrow 14x+26=68 \Rightarrow x=3$. c $W=5x$, $H=4x$: $2(5x+4x)=108 \Rightarrow 18x=108 \Rightarrow x=6$. d $W=5x-10$, $H=6x+3$: $2((5x-10)+(6x+3))=140 \Rightarrow 22x-14=140 \Rightarrow x=7$. e Here the bottom (12) is shorter than the top because the notch is cut from the bottom-right corner, so the overall bounding width is $12+3x$ and the height is $7x$: $2((12+3x)+7x)=224 \Rightarrow 24+20x=224 \Rightarrow x=10$. f This figure is a simple quadrilateral (the perimeter does not depend on the $60°$ angles): $2x+2x+2x+4x=10x=150 \Rightarrow x=15$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For each statement below, form an equation and solve it to find the unknown number. a A number is trebled and then 7 is added to it. If the total is 28, find the number. b Multiply a number by 4 and then add 5 to it. If the total is 29, find the number. c If 31 is the result of adding 1 to 5 times a number, find the number. d Double a number and then subtract 9. If the answer is 11, what is the number? e If 9 is the result of subtracting 12 from 7 times a number, find the number.
exercises.full_solution: a equation $3 x + 7 = 28$ $\Rightarrow x=7$; b equation $4 x + 5 = 29$ $\Rightarrow x=6$; c equation $5 x + 1 = 31$ $\Rightarrow x=6$; d equation $2 x - 9 = 11$ $\Rightarrow x=10$; e equation $7 x - 12 = 9$ $\Rightarrow x=3$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For each statement below, form an equation and solve it to find the unknown number. a Add 3 to a number and then double the result. If the total is 22, find the number. b 27 is the answer when you add 4 to a number and then treble it. What is the number? c Subtract 1 from a number and multiply the result by 5. If the answer is 35, what is the number?
exercises.full_solution: a equation $2 x + 6 = 22$ $\Rightarrow x=8$; b equation $3 x + 12 = 27$ $\Rightarrow x=5$; c equation $5 x - 5 = 35$ $\Rightarrow x=8$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $2x^2+5x+3=0$ b $2x^2-3x-5=0$ c $3x^2+2x-1=0$ d $2x^2+11x+5=0$ e $2x^2-13x+15=0$ f $12x^2+10x-8=0$
exercises.full_solution: a factorises as $\left(x + 1\right) \left(2 x + 3\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-3/2, -1$; b factorises as $\left(x + 1\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-1, 5/2$; c factorises as $\left(x + 1\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-1, 1/3$; d factorises as $\left(x + 5\right) \left(2 x + 1\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-5, -1/2$; e factorises as $\left(x - 5\right) \left(2 x - 3\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=3/2, 5$; f factorises as $2 \left(2 x - 1\right) \left(3 x + 4\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-4/3, 1/2$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations by factorising: a $x^2+12x=0$ b $x^2+12x+27=0$ c $x^2+4x=32$ d $x^2+5x=14$ e $2x^2=72$ f $3x^2-12=288$
exercises.full_solution: a factorises as $x \left(x + 12\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-12, 0$; b factorises as $\left(x + 3\right) \left(x + 9\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-9, -3$; c factorises as $\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 8\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-8, 4$; d factorises as $\left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 7\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-7, 2$; e factorises as $2 \left(x - 6\right) \left(x + 6\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-6, 6$; f factorises as $3 \left(x - 10\right) \left(x + 10\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=-10, 10$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: When a number $x$ is added to its square, the total is 12. Find two possible values for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: $x+x^2=12 \Rightarrow x^2+x-12=0 \Rightarrow (x+4)(x-3)=0 \Rightarrow x=-4$ or $x=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A number $x$ is equal to its own square minus 42. Find two possible values for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: $x=x^2-42 \Rightarrow x^2-x-42=0 \Rightarrow (x-7)(x+6)=0 \Rightarrow x=7$ or $x=-6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If the area of a rectangle with sides $x$ cm and $(x+3)$ cm is $10\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the only possible (positive) value for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: $x(x+3)=10 \Rightarrow x^2+3x-10=0 \Rightarrow (x+5)(x-2)=0 \Rightarrow x=-5$ or $x=2$. Since $x$ is a length, $x=2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If the area of a rectangle with sides $x$ cm and $(x+9)$ cm is $52\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the only possible (positive) value for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: $x(x+9)=52 \Rightarrow x^2+9x-52=0 \Rightarrow (x+13)(x-4)=0 \Rightarrow x=-13$ or $x=4$. Since $x$ is a length, $x=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A triangle has a base length of $2x$ cm and a height of $(x-3)$ cm. If its area is $18\text{ cm}^2$, calculate its height and base length.
exercises.full_solution: Area $=\frac{1}{2}(2x)(x-3)=x(x-3)=18 \Rightarrow x^2-3x-18=0 \Rightarrow (x-6)(x+3)=0 \Rightarrow x=6$ (rejecting $x=-3$ since lengths must be positive). Base $=2x=12$ cm, height $=x-3=3$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A triangle has a base length of $(x-8)$ cm and a height of $2x$ cm. If its area is $20\text{ cm}^2$, calculate its height and base length.
exercises.full_solution: Area $=\frac{1}{2}(x-8)(2x)=x(x-8)=20 \Rightarrow x^2-8x-20=0 \Rightarrow (x-10)(x+2)=0 \Rightarrow x=10$ (rejecting $x=-2$, and also rejecting the case where base $x-8$ would be negative). Base $=x-8=2$ cm, height $=2x=20$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A right-angled triangle has a base length of $x$ cm and a height of $(x-1)$ cm. If its area is $15\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the base length and height.
exercises.full_solution: Area $=\frac{1}{2}x(x-1)=15 \Rightarrow x^2-x-30=0 \Rightarrow (x-6)(x+5)=0 \Rightarrow x=6$ (rejecting $x=-5$). Base $=6$ cm, height $=x-1=5$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A rectangular garden has a square flower bed of side length $x$ m in one of its corners. The garden is $(7+x)$ m long (made up of a $7$ m section plus the $x$ m flower-bed width) and $(x+2)$ m wide (the flower bed of height $x$ m plus a further $2$ m strip), and the remainder of the garden (the lawn) has a total area of $50\text{ m}^2$. a Form an equation in terms of $x$. b Solve the equation. c Calculate the length and width of the whole garden.
exercises.full_solution: a Total garden area $=(7+x)(x+2)$; subtracting the flower bed $x^2$ gives the lawn area: $(7+x)(x+2)-x^2=50$. b Expanding: $x^{2} + 9 x + 14-x^2=50 \Rightarrow 9x+14=50 \Rightarrow 9x=36 \Rightarrow x=4$. c Garden length $=7+x=11$ m, width $=x+2=6$ m (check: lawn $=11\times 6-4^2=66-16=50$ ✓).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations using the quadratic formula (give answers to 2 d.p.): a $x^2-x-13=0$ b $x^2+4x-11=0$ c $x^2+5x-7=0$ d $x^2+6x+6=0$ e $x^2+5x-13=0$ f $x^2-9x+19=0$
exercises.full_solution: Using the quadratic formula $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ for each part: a: $a=1,b=-1,c=-13$, discriminant $=53$, $x=\frac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{53}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -3.14$ or $4.14$; b: $a=1,b=4,c=-11$, discriminant $=60$, $x=\frac{-(4)\pm\sqrt{60}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -5.87$ or $1.87$; c: $a=1,b=5,c=-7$, discriminant $=53$, $x=\frac{-(5)\pm\sqrt{53}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -6.14$ or $1.14$; d: $a=1,b=6,c=6$, discriminant $=12$, $x=\frac{-(6)\pm\sqrt{12}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -4.73$ or $-1.27$; e: $a=1,b=5,c=-13$, discriminant $=77$, $x=\frac{-(5)\pm\sqrt{77}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -6.89$ or $1.89$; f: $a=1,b=-9,c=19$, discriminant $=5$, $x=\frac{-(-9)\pm\sqrt{5}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx 3.38$ or $5.62$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations using the quadratic formula (give answers to 2 d.p.): a $x^2+7x+9=0$ b $x^2-35=0$ c $x^2+3x-3=0$ d $x^2-5x-7=0$ e $x^2+x-18=0$ f $x^2-8=0$
exercises.full_solution: Using the quadratic formula $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ for each part: a: $a=1,b=7,c=9$, discriminant $=13$, $x=\frac{-(7)\pm\sqrt{13}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -5.30$ or $-1.70$; b: $a=1,b=0,c=-35$, discriminant $=140$, $x=\frac{-(0)\pm\sqrt{140}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -5.92$ or $5.92$; c: $a=1,b=3,c=-3$, discriminant $=21$, $x=\frac{-(3)\pm\sqrt{21}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -3.79$ or $0.79$; d: $a=1,b=-5,c=-7$, discriminant $=53$, $x=\frac{-(-5)\pm\sqrt{53}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -1.14$ or $6.14$; e: $a=1,b=1,c=-18$, discriminant $=73$, $x=\frac{-(1)\pm\sqrt{73}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -4.77$ or $3.77$; f: $a=1,b=0,c=-8$, discriminant $=32$, $x=\frac{-(0)\pm\sqrt{32}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -2.83$ or $2.83$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations using the quadratic formula (give answers to 2 d.p.): a $x^2-2x-2=0$ b $x^2-4x-11=0$ c $x^2-x-5=0$ d $x^2+2x-7=0$ e $x^2-3x+1=0$ f $x^2-8x+3=0$
exercises.full_solution: Using the quadratic formula $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ for each part: a: $a=1,b=-2,c=-2$, discriminant $=12$, $x=\frac{-(-2)\pm\sqrt{12}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -0.73$ or $2.73$; b: $a=1,b=-4,c=-11$, discriminant $=60$, $x=\frac{-(-4)\pm\sqrt{60}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -1.87$ or $5.87$; c: $a=1,b=-1,c=-5$, discriminant $=21$, $x=\frac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{21}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -1.79$ or $2.79$; d: $a=1,b=2,c=-7$, discriminant $=32$, $x=\frac{-(2)\pm\sqrt{32}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx -3.83$ or $1.83$; e: $a=1,b=-3,c=1$, discriminant $=5$, $x=\frac{-(-3)\pm\sqrt{5}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx 0.38$ or $2.62$; f: $a=1,b=-8,c=3$, discriminant $=52$, $x=\frac{-(-8)\pm\sqrt{52}}{2(1)}$ giving $x\approx 0.39$ or $7.61$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following quadratic equations using the quadratic formula (give answers to 2 d.p.): a $2x^2-3x-4=0$ b $4x^2+2x-5=0$ c $5x^2-8x+1=0$ d $-2x^2-5x-2=0$ e $3x^2-4x-2=0$ f $-7x^2-x+15=0$
exercises.full_solution: Using the quadratic formula $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ for each part: a: $a=2,b=-3,c=-4$, discriminant $=41$, $x=\frac{-(-3)\pm\sqrt{41}}{2(2)}$ giving $x\approx -0.85$ or $2.35$; b: $a=4,b=2,c=-5$, discriminant $=84$, $x=\frac{-(2)\pm\sqrt{84}}{2(4)}$ giving $x\approx -1.40$ or $0.90$; c: $a=5,b=-8,c=1$, discriminant $=44$, $x=\frac{-(-8)\pm\sqrt{44}}{2(5)}$ giving $x\approx 0.14$ or $1.46$; d: $a=-2,b=-5,c=-2$, discriminant $=9$, $x=\frac{-(-5)\pm\sqrt{9}}{2(-2)}$ giving $x=-2$ or $-0.5$ exactly, i.e. $-2.00$ or $-0.50$; e: $a=3,b=-4,c=-2$, discriminant $=40$, $x=\frac{-(-4)\pm\sqrt{40}}{2(3)}$ giving $x\approx -0.39$ or $1.72$; f: $a=-7,b=-1,c=15$, discriminant $=421$, $x=\frac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{421}}{2(-7)}$ giving $x\approx -1.54$ or $1.39$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following inequalities and illustrate your solution on a number line: a $x+3<7$ b $5+x>6$ c $4+2x\leq 10$ d $8\leq x+1$ e $5>3+x$ f $7<3+2x$
exercises.full_solution: Solve like an equation, doing the same to both sides. a $x+3<7\Rightarrow x<4$. b $5+x>6\Rightarrow x>1$. c $4+2x\leq10\Rightarrow2x\leq6\Rightarrow x\leq3$. d $8\leq x+1\Rightarrow7\leq x$, i.e. $x\geq7$. e $5>3+x\Rightarrow2>x$, i.e. $x<2$. f $7<3+2x\Rightarrow4<2x\Rightarrow x>2$. On the number line, draw an open circle for $<$ or $>$ and a filled circle for $\leq$ or $\geq$, then shade in the direction of the solution.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following inequalities and illustrate your solution on a number line: a $x-3<4$ b $x-6\geq -8$ c $8+3x>-1$ d $5\geq -x-7$ e $12>-x-12$ f $4\leq 2x+10$
exercises.full_solution: a $x-3<4\Rightarrow x<7$. b $x-6\geq-8\Rightarrow x\geq-2$. c $8+3x>-1\Rightarrow3x>-9\Rightarrow x>-3$. d $5\geq-x-7\Rightarrow x+5\geq-7\Rightarrow x\geq-12$ (adding $x$ to both sides avoids dividing by a negative). e $12>-x-12\Rightarrow x+12>-12\Rightarrow x>-24$. f $4\leq2x+10\Rightarrow-6\leq2x\Rightarrow x\geq-3$. On the number line, draw an open circle for $<$ or $>$ and a filled circle for $\leq$ or $\geq$, then shade in the direction of the solution.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the following inequalities and illustrate your solution on a number line: a $\frac{x}{2}<1$ b $4\geq\frac{x}{3}$ c $1\leq\frac{x}{2}$ d $9x\geq -18$ e $-4x+1<3$ f $1\geq -3x+7$
exercises.answer: a $x<2$; b $x\leq12$; c $x\geq2$; d $x\geq-2$; e $x>-\frac{1}{2}$; f $x\geq2$
exercises.full_solution: a $\frac{x}{2}<1\Rightarrow x<2$. b $4\geq\frac{x}{3}\Rightarrow12\geq x$, i.e. $x\leq12$. c $1\leq\frac{x}{2}\Rightarrow2\leq x$, i.e. $x\geq2$. d $9x\geq-18\Rightarrow x\geq-2$. e $-4x+1<3\Rightarrow-4x<2\Rightarrow x>-\frac12$ (dividing by $-4$ reverses the inequality sign). f $1\geq-3x+7\Rightarrow3x\geq6\Rightarrow x\geq2$. On the number line, draw an open circle for $<$ or $>$ and a filled circle for $\leq$ or $\geq$, then shade in the direction of the solution.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the range of values of $x$ for which the following inequalities are satisfied, and illustrate each solution on a number line: a $4<2x\leq 8$ b $3\leq 3x<15$ c $7\leq 2x<10$ d $10\leq 5x<21$
exercises.full_solution: Divide every part of the inequality by the coefficient of $x$. a $4<2x\leq8\Rightarrow2<x\leq4$. b $3\leq3x<15\Rightarrow1\leq x<5$. c $7\leq2x<10\Rightarrow3.5\leq x<5$. d $10\leq5x<21\Rightarrow2\leq x<4.2$. On a number line, mark both end values (open circle for $<$, filled circle for $\leq$) and shade the segment between them.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the range of values of $x$ for which the following inequalities are satisfied, and illustrate each solution on a number line: a $5<3x+2\leq 17$ b $3\leq 2x+5<7$ c $12<8x-4<20$ d $9\leq 3(x-2)<15$
exercises.full_solution: Apply the same operation to all three parts of each inequality. a $5<3x+2\leq17\Rightarrow3<3x\leq15\Rightarrow1<x\leq5$. b $3\leq2x+5<7\Rightarrow-2\leq2x<2\Rightarrow-1\leq x<1$. c $12<8x-4<20\Rightarrow16<8x<24\Rightarrow2<x<3$. d $9\leq3(x-2)<15\Rightarrow3\leq x-2<5\Rightarrow5\leq x<7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve each of the following inequalities: a $15+3x<21$ b $18\leq 7y+4$ c $19-4x\geq 27$ d $2\geq \dfrac{y}{3}$ e $-4t+1<1$ f $1\geq 3p+10$
exercises.answer: a $x<2$; b $y\geq 2$; c $x\leq -2$; d $y\leq 6$; e $t>0$; f $p\leq -3$
exercises.full_solution: a $15+3x<21 \Rightarrow 3x<6 \Rightarrow x<2$. b $18\leq 7y+4 \Rightarrow 14\leq 7y \Rightarrow y\geq 2$. c $19-4x\geq 27 \Rightarrow -4x\geq 8 \Rightarrow x\leq -2$ (dividing by $-4$ reverses the inequality). d $2\geq \frac{y}{3} \Rightarrow 6\geq y$, i.e. $y\leq 6$. e $-4t+1<1 \Rightarrow -4t<0 \Rightarrow t>0$ (dividing by $-4$ reverses the inequality). f $1\geq 3p+10 \Rightarrow -9\geq 3p \Rightarrow p\leq -3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve each of the following inequalities: a $7<3y+1\leq 13$ b $3\leq 3p<15$ c $9\leq 3(m-2)<15$ d $20<8x-4<28$
exercises.full_solution: a $7<3y+1\leq 13 \Rightarrow 6<3y\leq 12 \Rightarrow 2<y\leq 4$. b $3\leq 3p<15 \Rightarrow 1\leq p<5$. c $9\leq 3(m-2)<15 \Rightarrow 3\leq m-2<5 \Rightarrow 5\leq m<7$. d $20<8x-4<28 \Rightarrow 24<8x<32 \Rightarrow 3<x<4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: By drawing appropriate axes, shade the region which satisfies each of the following inequalities: a $y>2$ b $x<3$ c $y\leq 4$ d $x\geq -1$ e $y>2x+1$ f $y\leq x-3$
exercises.answer: a Shade above the dashed horizontal line $y=2$. b Shade to the left of the dashed vertical line $x=3$. c Shade on/below the solid horizontal line $y=4$. d Shade on/to the right of the solid vertical line $x=-1$. e Shade above the dashed line $y=2x+1$ (gradient 2, $y$-intercept 1). f Shade on/below the solid line $y=x-3$ (gradient 1, $y$-intercept $-3$).
exercises.full_solution: For each inequality, draw the boundary line (solid for $\leq,\geq$, dashed for $<,>$) and test a point not on the line, e.g. the origin $(0,0)$ where possible, to see which side satisfies the inequality. a Boundary $y=2$ (dashed, since strict); test $(0,0)$: $0>2$ false, so shade the side NOT containing the origin, i.e. above the line. b Boundary $x=3$ (dashed); test $(0,0)$: $0<3$ true, so shade the side containing the origin, i.e. left of the line. c Boundary $y=4$ (solid); test $(0,0)$: $0\leq 4$ true, so shade below/on the line. d Boundary $x=-1$ (solid); test $(0,0)$: $0\geq -1$ true, so shade right of/on the line. e Boundary $y=2x+1$ (dashed); test $(0,0)$: $0>2(0)+1=1$ false, so shade the side not containing the origin, i.e. above the line. f Boundary $y=x-3$ (solid); test $(0,0)$: $0\leq 0-3=-3$ false, so shade the side not containing the origin, i.e. below the line.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: By drawing appropriate axes, leave unshaded the region which satisfies each of the following inequalities (i.e. shade the region that does NOT satisfy it): a $y\geq -x$ b $y\leq 2-x$ c $x\leq y-3$ d $x+y\geq 4$ e $2x-y\geq 3$ f $2y-x<4$
exercises.answer: a Leave unshaded on/above the solid line $y=-x$. b Leave unshaded on/below the solid line $y=2-x$. c Leave unshaded on/above the solid line $y=x+3$ (i.e. where $x\leq y-3$). d Leave unshaded on/above the solid line $x+y=4$ (the side away from the origin). e Leave unshaded on/below the solid line $y=2x-3$ (i.e. where $2x-y\geq 3$, the side away from the origin). f Leave unshaded below the dashed line $y=\frac{x+4}{2}$ (i.e. where $2y-x<4$).
exercises.full_solution: For each, draw the boundary line by replacing the inequality sign with '=' (solid for $\leq,\geq$, dashed for $<,>$). Then test a point not on the line to find which side satisfies the inequality; shade out the other side. a Boundary $y=-x$ passes through the origin, so test $(1,1)$: $1\geq-1$ true $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side containing $(1,1)$, i.e. on/above $y=-x$. b $y=2-x$; test $(0,0)$: $0\leq2$ true $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side containing the origin (on/below the line). c Rearranged $y\geq x+3$; test $(0,0)$: $0\geq3$ false $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side not containing the origin (on/above $y=x+3$). d $x+y=4$; test $(0,0)$: $0\geq4$ false $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side not containing the origin (on/above the line). e Rearranged $y\leq2x-3$; test $(0,0)$: $0\geq3$ false $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side not containing the origin (on/below $y=2x-3$). f Rearranged $y<\frac{x+4}{2}$ (dashed boundary); test $(0,0)$: $0<4$ true $\Rightarrow$ leave unshaded the side containing the origin.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same pair of axes, plot the following inequalities and leave unshaded the region which satisfies all of them simultaneously: $y\leq x$, $y>1$, $x\leq 5$.
exercises.answer: The unshaded (feasible) region is the triangle with vertices $(1,1)$ (open, excluded), $(5,1)$ and $(5,5)$ (both included), bounded by the solid lines $y=x$ and $x=5$ and the dashed line $y=1$.
exercises.full_solution: Draw $y=x$ (solid, since $\leq$), $y=1$ (dashed, since $>$) and $x=5$ (solid, since $\leq$). Testing a point such as $(4,2)$: $2\leq 4$ ✓, $2>1$ ✓, $4\leq 5$ ✓, so this point lies in the region. The three boundary lines pairwise intersect at $(1,1)$ [on $y=x$ and $y=1$, excluded since $y>1$ is strict], $(5,5)$ [on $y=x$ and $x=5$] and $(5,1)$ [on $y=1$ and $x=5$]. The unshaded feasible region is therefore the (half-open) triangle with these three vertices.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same pair of axes, plot the following inequalities and leave unshaded the region which satisfies all of them simultaneously: $x+y\leq 6$, $y<x$, $y\geq 1$.
exercises.answer: The unshaded (feasible) region is the triangle with vertices $(1,1)$ (open, excluded), $(5,1)$ and $(3,3)$ (open, excluded), bounded by the solid lines $x+y=6$ and $y=1$ and the dashed line $y=x$.
exercises.full_solution: Draw $x+y=6$ (solid), $y=x$ (dashed, since strict $<$) and $y=1$ (solid). Testing $(3,1)$: $3+1=4\leq 6$ ✓, $1<3$ ✓, $1\geq 1$ ✓. The boundary lines intersect pairwise at $(1,1)$ [on $y=x$ and $y=1$, excluded since $y<x$ is strict], $(3,3)$ [on $y=x$ and $x+y=6$, excluded for the same reason] and $(5,1)$ [on $y=1$ and $x+y=6$, included]. The unshaded feasible region is the (half-open) triangle with these three vertices.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same pair of axes, plot the following inequalities and leave unshaded the region which satisfies all of them simultaneously: $y\geq 3x$, $y\leq 5$, $x+y>4$.
exercises.answer: The unshaded (feasible) region is the triangle with vertices $(1,3)$ (open, excluded), $\left(\frac{5}{3},5\right)$ and $(-1,5)$ (open, excluded), bounded by the solid lines $y=3x$ and $y=5$ and the dashed line $x+y=4$.
exercises.full_solution: Draw $y=3x$ (solid), $y=5$ (solid) and $x+y=4$ (dashed, since strict $>$). Testing $(0.5,4.5)$: $4.5\geq 1.5$ ✓, $4.5\leq 5$ ✓, $5>4$ ✓. The boundary lines intersect pairwise at $(1,3)$ [on $y=3x$ and $x+y=4$, excluded], $\left(\frac{5}{3},5\right)$ [on $y=3x$ and $y=5$, included] and $(-1,5)$ [on $y=5$ and $x+y=4$, excluded]. The unshaded feasible region is the (half-open) triangle with these three vertices.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same pair of axes, plot the following inequalities and leave unshaded the region which satisfies all of them simultaneously: $2y\geq x+4$, $y\leq 2x+2$, $y<4$, $x\leq 3$.
exercises.answer: The unshaded (feasible) region is the quadrilateral with vertices $(0,2)$, $(1,4)$, $(3,4)$ and $(3,3.5)$. It lies on/above the solid line $y=\frac{x}{2}+2$, on/below the solid line $y=2x+2$, below the dashed line $y=4$ and on/left of the solid line $x=3$; the points $(1,4)$ and $(3,4)$ lie on the dashed line, so they are not included.
exercises.full_solution: Rearranging: $2y\geq x+4 \Rightarrow y\geq \frac{x}{2}+2$ (solid line, region above it); $y\leq 2x+2$ (solid line, region below it); $y<4$ (dashed line, region below it); $x\leq 3$ (solid vertical line, region to its left). Find where the boundary lines meet: $\frac{x}{2}+2=2x+2 \Rightarrow x=0$, giving $(0,2)$; $2x+2=4 \Rightarrow x=1$, giving $(1,4)$; $y=4$ meets $x=3$ at $(3,4)$; $y=\frac{x}{2}+2$ meets $x=3$ at $(3,3.5)$. Check with a point inside, e.g. $(2,3.5)$: $7\geq 6$ ✓, $3.5\leq 6$ ✓, $3.5<4$ ✓, $2\leq 3$ ✓. So the unshaded region is the quadrilateral with vertices $(0,2)$, $(1,4)$, $(3,4)$ and $(3,3.5)$, with the edge along $y=4$ (dashed) not included.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A taxi firm has at its disposal one morning a car and a minibus for hire. During the morning, it makes $x$ car trips and $y$ minibus trips. It makes at least five car trips; between two and eight minibus trips; the total number of car and minibus trips does not exceed 12. a Write an inequality for each statement. b Graph the inequalities, leaving the region which satisfies them unshaded. c Using your graph, state one solution which satisfies all the inequalities simultaneously.
exercises.answer: a $x\geq 5$, $2\leq y\leq 8$, $x+y\leq 12$. c One possible solution: $x=5$ car trips and $y=2$ minibus trips (check: $5\geq5$ ✓, $2\leq2\leq8$ ✓, $5+2=7\leq12$ ✓).
exercises.full_solution: a Each English statement converts directly: 'at least five car trips' $\Rightarrow x\geq5$; 'between two and eight minibus trips' $\Rightarrow 2\leq y\leq8$; 'total does not exceed 12' $\Rightarrow x+y\leq12$. b Draw the solid lines $x=5$, $y=2$, $y=8$ and $x+y=12$ on axes numbered 0 to 12, and leave unshaded the region satisfying $x\geq5$ (right of $x=5$), $2\leq y\leq8$ (the horizontal band between $y=2$ and $y=8$) and $x+y\leq12$ (below/on the line $x+y=12$); this is the triangle with vertices $(5,2)$, $(10,2)$ and $(5,7)$ (the condition $y\leq8$ is automatically met, since $x\geq5$ and $x+y\leq12$ force $y\leq7$). c For example, $(x,y)=(5,2)$ lies in this region, since all three conditions hold; other valid solutions exist, e.g. $(8,4)$ or $(6,6)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A woman is baking bread and cakes. She makes $p$ loaves and $q$ cakes. She bakes at least five loaves and at least two cakes but no more than ten loaves and cakes altogether. a Write an inequality for each statement. b Graph the inequalities, leaving the region which satisfies them unshaded. c Using your graph, state one solution which satisfies all the inequalities simultaneously.
exercises.answer: a $p\geq5$, $q\geq2$, $p+q\leq10$. c One possible solution: $p=5$ loaves and $q=2$ cakes (check: $5\geq5$ ✓, $2\geq2$ ✓, $5+2=7\leq10$ ✓).
exercises.full_solution: a 'At least five loaves' $\Rightarrow p\geq5$; 'at least two cakes' $\Rightarrow q\geq2$; 'no more than ten loaves and cakes altogether' $\Rightarrow p+q\leq10$. b Draw the solid lines $p=5$, $q=2$ and $p+q=10$, and leave unshaded the region to the right of $p=5$, above $q=2$ and below/on $p+q=10$: a small triangular region with vertices $(5,2)$, $(8,2)$ and $(5,5)$. c For example, $(p,q)=(5,2)$ satisfies all three inequalities; other valid solutions include $(6,2)$ or $(5,4)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A couple are buying curtains for their house. They buy $m$ long curtains and $n$ short curtains. They buy at least two long curtains. They also buy at least twice as many short curtains as long curtains. A maximum of 11 curtains are bought altogether. a Write an inequality for each statement. b Graph the inequalities, leaving the region which satisfies them unshaded. c Using your graph, state one solution which satisfies all the inequalities simultaneously.
exercises.answer: a $m\geq2$, $n\geq2m$, $m+n\leq11$. c One possible solution: $m=2$ long curtains and $n=4$ short curtains (check: $2\geq2$ ✓, $4\geq2(2)=4$ ✓, $2+4=6\leq11$ ✓).
exercises.full_solution: a 'At least two long curtains' $\Rightarrow m\geq2$; 'at least twice as many short as long' $\Rightarrow n\geq2m$; 'a maximum of 11 curtains altogether' $\Rightarrow m+n\leq11$. b Draw the solid lines $m=2$, $n=2m$ and $m+n=11$, and leave unshaded the region to the right of $m=2$, on/above the line $n=2m$ and below/on $m+n=11$; the boundary lines meet at $(2,4)$ [$m=2$ and $n=2m$], and $n=2m$ meets $m+n=11$ where $m+2m=11\Rightarrow m=\frac{11}{3}$, i.e. $\left(\frac{11}{3},\frac{22}{3}\right)$, and $m=2$ meets $m+n=11$ at $(2,9)$ — a triangular feasible region with these three vertices. c For example, $(m,n)=(2,4)$ satisfies all three inequalities.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A shop sells large and small oranges. A girl buys $L$ large oranges and $S$ small oranges. She buys at least three but fewer than nine large oranges. She also buys fewer than six small oranges. The maximum number of oranges she needs to buy is 10. a Write an inequality for each statement. b Graph the inequalities, leaving the region which satisfies them unshaded. c Using your graph, state one solution which satisfies all the inequalities simultaneously.
exercises.answer: a $3\leq L<9$, $S<6$, $L+S\leq10$. c One possible solution: $L=3$ large oranges and $S=5$ small oranges (check: $3\leq3<9$ ✓, $5<6$ ✓, $3+5=8\leq10$ ✓).
exercises.full_solution: a 'At least three but fewer than nine large' $\Rightarrow 3\leq L<9$; 'fewer than six small' $\Rightarrow S<6$; 'maximum number to buy is 10' $\Rightarrow L+S\leq10$. b Draw the solid line $L=3$, the dashed lines $L=9$ and $S=6$, and the solid line $L+S=10$; leave unshaded the region satisfying all four conditions simultaneously (right of/on $L=3$, left of $L=9$, below $S=6$, and below/on $L+S=10$). c For example, $(L,S)=(3,5)$ satisfies all the inequalities; other valid solutions include $(4,5)$ or $(3,0)$.

exercises.statement: For each of the following sequences, the term-to-term rule and one of the terms are given. Calculate the terms required and state whether the sequence generated is arithmetic or not. a $u_{n+1}=u_n+5$, where $u_1=2$. Calculate $u_2,u_3,u_4$. b $u_{n+1}=u_n-3$, where $u_1=4$. Calculate $u_2,u_3,u_4$. c $u_{n+1}=u_n-4$, where $u_3=2$. Calculate $u_1,u_2,u_4$. d $u_{n+1}=2u_n-1$, where $u_2=0$. Calculate $u_1,u_3,u_4$. e $u_{n+1}=\dfrac{u_n}{2}+3$, where $u_1=2$. Calculate $u_2,u_3,u_4$. f $u_{n+1}=\dfrac{u_n}{2}-1$, where $u_3=10$. Calculate $u_1,u_2,u_4$.
exercises.full_solution: a Apply the rule forwards from $u_1=2$: $u_2=2+5=7$, $u_3=7+5=12$, $u_4=12+5=17$; consecutive differences are all $5$, so arithmetic. b From $u_1=4$: $u_2=4-3=1$, $u_3=1-3=-2$, $u_4=-2-3=-5$; constant difference $-3$, arithmetic. c Since $u_3=2$ is given (not $u_1$), work backwards using $u_n=u_{n+1}+4$: $u_2=u_3+4=6$, $u_1=u_2+4=10$; and forwards $u_4=u_3-4=-2$. Differences are all $-4$, arithmetic. d From $u_2=0$: solving $u_2=2u_1-1=0$ gives $u_1=0.5$. Forwards: $u_3=2u_2-1=-1$, $u_4=2u_3-1=-3$. Differences are $-0.5,-1,-2$ — not constant, so not arithmetic. e From $u_1=2$: $u_2=\frac{2}{2}+3=4$, $u_3=\frac{4}{2}+3=5$, $u_4=\frac{5}{2}+3=5.5$. Differences $2,1,0.5$ — not constant, not arithmetic. f Since $u_3=10$ is given, work backwards using $u_n=2(u_{n+1}+1)$: $u_2=2(10+1)=22$, $u_1=2(22+1)=46$; forwards $u_4=\frac{10}{2}-1=4$. Differences $-24,-12,-6$ — not constant, not arithmetic.

exercises.full_solution: For each table, use the given $n$th-term formula to fill in missing terms (substitute the known position), or set the formula equal to a known term and solve for the missing position; where no formula is given (d, e, f), first find the common difference $d$ from two known consecutive-ish terms and derive $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$. a $4n-3$: $n=1\to1$, $n=2\to5$, $n=5\to17$, $n=50\to197$; and $4n-3=45\Rightarrow n=12$. b $6n-1$: $n=1\to5$, $n=2\to11$, $n=5\to29$; $6n-1=59\Rightarrow n=10$; $6n-1=449\Rightarrow n=75$. c $-n+3$: $n=1\to2$; $-n+3=0\Rightarrow n=3$; $-n+3=-5\Rightarrow n=8$; $-n+3=-47\Rightarrow n=50$; $n=100\to-97$. d $d=0-3=-3$, so $u_n=3-3(n-1)=6-3n$; check $u_3=-3$ ✓. $6-3n=-24\Rightarrow n=10$; $6-3n=-294\Rightarrow n=100$. e From position 5 (term 10) to position 7 (term 16): $d=\frac{16-10}{7-5}=3$, so $u_n=10+3(n-5)=3n-5$; check $u_7=16$ ✓. $3n-5=1\Rightarrow n=2$; $3n-5=25\Rightarrow n=10$; $3n-5=145\Rightarrow n=50$. f $d=-7-(-5.5)=-1.5$, so $u_n=-5.5-1.5(n-1)=-1.5n-4$; check $u_2=-7$ ✓. $u_5=-1.5(5)-4=-11.5$; $-1.5n-4=-34\Rightarrow n=20$; $u_{50}=-1.5(50)-4=-79$.

exercises.statement: By using a table of differences if necessary, find the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence $2,5,10,17,26$.
exercises.full_solution:
1st differences: $3, 5, 7, 9$; 2nd differences: $2, 2, 2$. The 2nd differences are constant, so the sequence is quadratic: $u_n=an^2+bn+c$, with $2a=2$, giving $a=1$.

Substituting $n=1,2,3$ into $u_n=n^2+bn+c$ gives three equations:
- (1) $1+b+c=2$
- (2) $4+2b+c=5$
- (3) $9+3b+c=10$

(2)$-$(1) removes $c$: $3+b=3$, so $b=0$. (3)$-$(2) gives $5+b=5$, the same value of $b$, which is a useful check. Substituting $a=1$ and $b=0$ into (1) gives $c=1$.

So $u_n=n^2+1$. Checking the fifth term, $n=5$: $25+1=26$, as given.
