exercises.statement: Evaluate $fg(2)$ in each of the following: a $f(x)=x-4$, $g(x)=x+3$; b $f(x)=2x$, $g(x)=-x+6$; c $f(x)=3x$, $g(x)=6x+1$; d $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{2}$, $g(x)=-2x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $gh(-4)$ in each of the following: a $g(x)=3x+2$, $h(x)=-4x$; b $g(x)=\tfrac12(3x-1)$, $h(x)=\dfrac{2x}{5}$; c $g(x)=4(-x+2)$, $h(x)=\dfrac{2x+6}{4}$; d $g(x)=\dfrac{4x+4}{5}$, $h(x)=-\tfrac13(-x+5)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $3(x+4)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $3$: $3(x+4)=3\times x+3\times 4=3x+12$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $5x(2y+3)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $5x$: $5x(2y+3)=5x\times 2y+5x\times 3=10xy+15x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $2a(3a+2b-3c)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $2a$: $2a\times 3a+2a\times 2b+2a\times(-3c)=6a^2+4ab-6ac$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $-4p(2p-q+r^2)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $-4p$: $-4p\times 2p=-8p^2$, $-4p\times(-q)=4pq$, $-4p\times r^2=-4pr^2$. So the result is $-8p^2+4pq-4pr^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $-2x^2\left(1x+3y-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $-2x^2$: $-2x^2\times x=-2x^3$, $-2x^2\times 3y=-6x^2y$, $-2x^2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=2x$. So the result is $-2x^3-6x^2y+2x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $\dfrac{-2}{x}\left(-2x+4y+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply every term inside the bracket by $\dfrac{-2}{x}$: $\dfrac{-2}{x}\times(-2x)=4$, $\dfrac{-2}{x}\times 4y=-\dfrac{8y}{x}$, $\dfrac{-2}{x}\times\dfrac{1}{x}=-\dfrac{2}{x^2}$. So the result is $4-\dfrac{8y}{x}-\dfrac{2}{x^2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $(x+3)(x+5)$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the grid (area) method with rows $x, +5$ and columns $x, +3$: the four products are $x^2$, $3x$, $5x$ and $15$. So $(x+3)(x+5)=x^2+5x+3x+15=x^2+8x+15$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Expand $(x+2)(x+1)$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the grid (area) method with rows $x, +2$ and columns $x, +1$: the four products are $x^2$, $x$, $2x$ and $2$. So $(x+2)(x+1)=x^2+x+2x+2=x^2+3x+2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $10x+15$.
exercises.full_solution: The highest common factor of $10x$ and $15$ is $5$. Taking it outside the bracket: $10x+15=5(2x+3)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $8p-6q+10r$.
exercises.full_solution: The highest common factor of $8p$, $6q$ and $10r$ is $2$. Taking it outside the bracket: $8p-6q+10r=2(4p-3q+5r)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $-2q-6p+12$.
exercises.full_solution: The highest common factor of $2q$, $6p$ and $12$ is $2$. Taking it outside the bracket: $-2q-6p+12=2(-q-3p+6)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $2a^2+3ab-5ac$.
exercises.full_solution: Every term contains a factor of $a$. Taking it outside the bracket: $2a^2+3ab-5ac=a(2a+3b-5c)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $6ax-12ay-18a^2$.
exercises.full_solution: The highest common factor of $6ax$, $12ay$ and $18a^2$ is $6a$. Taking it outside the bracket: $6ax-12ay-18a^2=6a(x-2y-3a)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $3b+9ba-6bd$.
exercises.full_solution: The highest common factor of $3b$, $9ba$ and $6bd$ is $3b$. Taking it outside the bracket: $3b+9ba-6bd=3b(1+3a-2d)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $2a+3b-c$ if $a=3$, $b=4$, $c=-5$.
exercises.full_solution: Substitute the values: $2(3)+3(4)-(-5)=6+12+5=23$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $3a-4b+2c$ if $a=3$, $b=4$, $c=-5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $-2a+2b-3c$ if $a=3$, $b=4$, $c=-5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $3a(2b-3c)$ if $a=3$, $b=4$, $c=-5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Substitute the values: $-2(-5)(-3+2(4))=10(-3+8)=10\times 5=50$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Rearrange the formula $a=2b+c$ to make $c$ the subject.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $2b$ from both sides: $a-2b=c$, i.e. $c=a-2b$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Rearrange the formula $2r+p=q$ to make $p$ the subject.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $2r$ from both sides: $p=q-2r$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Rearrange the formula $ab=cd$ to make $c$ the subject.
exercises.full_solution: Divide both sides by $d$: $\dfrac{ab}{d}=c$, i.e. $c=\dfrac{ab}{d}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Rearrange the formula $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{c}{d}$ to make $d$ the subject.
exercises.full_solution: Cross-multiply: $ad=cb$. Divide both sides by $a$: $d=\dfrac{cb}{a}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Using the grid method with rows $3x, -6$ and columns $2x, -3$: the four products are $6x^2$, $-9x$, $-12x$ and $18$. So $(2x-3)(3x-6)=6x^2-9x-12x+18=6x^2-21x+18$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: First expand the pair of linear brackets: $(x-1)(x+2)=x^2-x+2x-2=x^2+x-2$. Then multiply this by the remaining bracket using the grid method with rows $2x,-5$ and columns $x^2,+x,-2$: $2x\times x^2=2x^3$, $2x\times x=2x^2$, $2x\times(-2)=-4x$, $-5\times x^2=-5x^2$, $-5\times x=-5x$, $-5\times(-2)=10$. Adding these: $2x^3+2x^2-4x-5x^2-5x+10=2x^3-3x^2-9x+10$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $6x+3+2xy+y$.
exercises.full_solution: Group terms with a common factor: $6x+3=3(2x+1)$ and $2xy+y=y(2x+1)$. So $6x+3+2xy+y=3(2x+1)+y(2x+1)=(3+y)(2x+1)$, since $(2x+1)$ is a common factor of both groups.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $ax+ay-bx-by$.
exercises.full_solution: Group terms: $ax+ay=a(x+y)$ and $-bx-by=-b(x+y)$. So $ax+ay-bx-by=a(x+y)-b(x+y)=(a-b)(x+y)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $2x^2-3x+2xy-3y$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $p^2-q^2$.
exercises.full_solution: This is a difference of two squares, so $p^2-q^2=(p+q)(p-q)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $4a^2-9b^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Write each term as a square: $4a^2=(2a)^2$ and $9b^2=(3b)^2$. So $4a^2-9b^2=(2a)^2-(3b)^2=(2a+3b)(2a-3b)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $(mn)^2-25k^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Write each term as a square: $(mn)^2$ and $25k^2=(5k)^2$. So $(mn)^2-25k^2=(mn+5k)(mn-5k)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Factorise $4x^2-(9y)^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $13^2-7^2$ by factorising.
exercises.full_solution: Using the difference of two squares: $13^2-7^2=(13+7)(13-7)=20\times 6=120$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate $6.25^2-3.75^2$ by factorising.
exercises.full_solution: Using the difference of two squares: $6.25^2-3.75^2=(6.25+3.75)(6.25-3.75)=10\times 2.5=25$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $r$ the subject of the formula $C=2\pi r$.
exercises.full_solution: Divide both sides by $2\pi$: $\dfrac{C}{2\pi}=r$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $r$ the subject of the formula $A=\pi r^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Divide both sides by $\pi$: $\dfrac{A}{\pi}=r^2$. Take the square root of both sides (keeping both roots): $r=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$. If $r$ is the radius of a circle it must be positive, so in that context $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $y$ the subject of the formula $x^2+y^2=h^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $x^2$ from both sides: $y^2=h^2-x^2$. Take the square root of both sides: $y=\pm\sqrt{h^2-x^2}$. Note that this is NOT the same as $y=h-x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $x$ the subject of the formula $f=\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{k}}$.
exercises.full_solution: Square both sides: $f^2=\dfrac{x}{k}$. Multiply both sides by $k$: $f^2k=x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $x$ the subject of the formula $m=3a\sqrt{\dfrac{p}{x}}$.
exercises.full_solution: Square both sides: $m^2=\dfrac{9a^2p}{x}$. Multiply both sides by $x$: $m^2x=9a^2p$. Divide both sides by $m^2$: $x=\dfrac{9a^2p}{m^2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Make $q$ the subject of the formula $A=\dfrac{y+x}{p+q^2}$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply both sides by $(p+q^2)$: $A(p+q^2)=y+x$. Divide both sides by $A$: $p+q^2=\dfrac{y+x}{A}$. Subtract $p$: $q^2=\dfrac{y+x}{A}-p$. Take the square root: $q=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{y+x}{A}-p}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{5}{7}$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together: $\dfrac{3\times5}{4\times7}=\dfrac{15}{28}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{a}{c}\times\dfrac{b}{d}$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together: $\dfrac{a}{c}\times\dfrac{b}{d}=\dfrac{ab}{cd}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{5}{6}$.
exercises.full_solution: Before multiplying, cancel the common factor of $3$ between the numerator $3$ and the denominator $6$: $3\to1$, $6\to2$. This gives $\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{5}{8}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{a}{c}\times\dfrac{b}{2a}$.
exercises.full_solution: Cancel the common factor of $a$ between the numerator of the first fraction and the denominator of the second: $\dfrac{a}{c}\times\dfrac{b}{2a}=\dfrac{1}{c}\times\dfrac{b}{2}=\dfrac{b}{2c}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{ab}{ce}\times\dfrac{cd}{af}$.
exercises.full_solution: Cancel the common factor of $a$ (numerator of the first fraction with denominator of the second) and the common factor of $c$ (denominator of the first fraction with numerator of the second): $\dfrac{ab}{ce}\times\dfrac{cd}{af}=\dfrac{b}{e}\times\dfrac{d}{f}=\dfrac{bd}{ef}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{x^5}{x^3}$.
exercises.full_solution: Writing out the powers: $\dfrac{x\times x\times x\times x\times x}{x\times x\times x}$. Cancel three factors of $x$ from top and bottom, leaving $x\times x=x^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{2b}{5}\div\dfrac{b}{7}$.
exercises.full_solution: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal: $\dfrac{2b}{5}\div\dfrac{b}{7}=\dfrac{2b}{5}\times\dfrac{7}{b}=\dfrac{14b}{5b}=\dfrac{14}{5}=2.8$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{4}{11}+\dfrac{3}{11}$.
exercises.full_solution: Since the denominators are the same, add the numerators: $\dfrac{4+3}{11}=\dfrac{7}{11}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{a}{11}+\dfrac{b}{11}$.
exercises.full_solution: Since the denominators are the same, add the numerators: $\dfrac{a+b}{11}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{4}{x}+\dfrac{3}{x}$.
exercises.full_solution: Since the denominators are the same, add the numerators: $\dfrac{4+3}{x}=\dfrac{7}{x}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{2}{9}+\dfrac{1}{3}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{1}{3}$ with denominator $9$: $\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{3}{9}$. So $\dfrac{2}{9}+\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{5}{9}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{a}{9}+\dfrac{b}{3}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{b}{3}$ with denominator $9$: $\dfrac{b}{3}=\dfrac{3b}{9}$. So $\dfrac{a}{9}+\dfrac{3b}{9}=\dfrac{a+3b}{9}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{4}{5a}+\dfrac{7}{10a}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{4}{5a}$ with denominator $10a$: $\dfrac{4}{5a}=\dfrac{8}{10a}$. So $\dfrac{8}{10a}+\dfrac{7}{10a}=\dfrac{15}{10a}=\dfrac{3}{2a}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{7}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2a}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{7}{a}$ with denominator $2a$: $\dfrac{7}{a}=\dfrac{14}{2a}$. So $\dfrac{14}{2a}-\dfrac{1}{2a}=\dfrac{13}{2a}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{p}{3}-\dfrac{q}{15}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{p}{3}$ with denominator $15$: $\dfrac{p}{3}=\dfrac{5p}{15}$. So $\dfrac{5p}{15}-\dfrac{q}{15}=\dfrac{5p-q}{15}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{5}{3b}-\dfrac{8}{9b}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\dfrac{5}{3b}$ with denominator $9b$: $\dfrac{5}{3b}=\dfrac{15}{9b}$. So $\dfrac{15}{9b}-\dfrac{8}{9b}=\dfrac{7}{9b}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}$.
exercises.full_solution: The lowest common multiple of $4$ and $3$ is $12$. Rewrite each fraction with denominator $12$: $\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{12}$, $\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{4}{12}$. So $\dfrac{3}{12}+\dfrac{4}{12}=\dfrac{7}{12}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{2}{3}$.
exercises.full_solution: The lowest common multiple of $5$ and $3$ is $15$. Rewrite each fraction with denominator $15$: $\dfrac{1}{5}=\dfrac{3}{15}$, $\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{10}{15}$. So $\dfrac{3}{15}+\dfrac{10}{15}=\dfrac{13}{15}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{a}{3}+\dfrac{b}{4}$.
exercises.full_solution: The lowest common multiple of $3$ and $4$ is $12$. Rewrite each fraction with denominator $12$: $\dfrac{a}{3}=\dfrac{4a}{12}$, $\dfrac{b}{4}=\dfrac{3b}{12}$. So $\dfrac{4a}{12}+\dfrac{3b}{12}=\dfrac{4a+3b}{12}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{2a}{3}+\dfrac{3b}{5}$.
exercises.full_solution: The lowest common multiple of $3$ and $5$ is $15$. Rewrite each fraction with denominator $15$: $\dfrac{2a}{3}=\dfrac{10a}{15}$, $\dfrac{3b}{5}=\dfrac{9b}{15}$. So $\dfrac{10a}{15}+\dfrac{9b}{15}=\dfrac{10a+9b}{15}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{2}{x+1}+\dfrac{3}{x+2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{5}{p+3}-\dfrac{3}{p-5}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{x^2-2x}{x^2+x-6}$.
exercises.full_solution: Factorise numerator and denominator: $x^2-2x=x(x-2)$ and $x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)$. So $\dfrac{x(x-2)}{(x+3)(x-2)}=\dfrac{x}{x+3}$ after cancelling the common factor $(x-2)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{x^2-3x}{x^2+2x-15}$.
exercises.full_solution: Factorise numerator and denominator: $x^2-3x=x(x-3)$ and $x^2+2x-15=(x-3)(x+5)$. So $\dfrac{x(x-3)}{(x-3)(x+5)}=\dfrac{x}{x+5}$ after cancelling the common factor $(x-3)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $d^3\times d^4$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the law $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$: $d^3\times d^4=d^{3+4}=d^7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{(p^2)^4}{p^2\times p^4}$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the law $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$, the numerator becomes $(p^2)^4=p^{2\times4}=p^8$. Using the law $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$, the denominator becomes $p^{2+4}=p^6$. So $\dfrac{p^8}{p^6}=p^{8-6}=p^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express $(\sqrt[3]{a})^4$ in the form $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$.
exercises.full_solution: Since $\sqrt[3]{a}=a^{\frac{1}{3}}$, raising to the power $4$ gives $(\sqrt[3]{a})^4=\left(a^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^4=a^{\frac{4}{3}}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express $b^{\frac{2}{5}}$ in the form $(\sqrt[n]{b})^m$.
exercises.full_solution: Write $b^{\frac{2}{5}}$ as $\left(b^{\frac{1}{5}}\right)^2$. Since $b^{\frac{1}{5}}=\sqrt[5]{b}$, this gives $b^{\frac{2}{5}}=(\sqrt[5]{b})^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify $\dfrac{p^{\frac{1}{2}}\times p^{\frac{1}{3}}}{p}$, giving your answer in the form $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the laws of indices, the numerator simplifies to $p^{\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)}=p^{\frac{5}{6}}$. So the expression becomes $\dfrac{p^{\frac{5}{6}}}{p}=p^{\frac{5}{6}}\times p^{-1}=p^{\left(\frac{5}{6}-1\right)}=p^{-\frac{1}{6}}$. (Equivalent forms: $(\sqrt[6]{p})^{-1}$ or $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[6]{p}}$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the linear equation $3x+8=14$.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $8$ from both sides: $3x=6$. Divide both sides by $3$: $x=2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the linear equation $12=20+2x$.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $20$ from both sides: $-8=2x$. Divide both sides by $2$: $-4=x$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the linear equation $3(p+4)=21$.
exercises.full_solution: Expand the bracket: $3p+12=21$. Subtract $12$ from both sides: $3p=9$. Divide both sides by $3$: $p=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the linear equation $4(x-5)=7(2x-5)$.
exercises.full_solution: Expand both brackets: $4x-20=14x-35$. Add $35$ to both sides: $4x+15=14x$. Subtract $4x$ from both sides: $15=10x$. Divide both sides by $10$: $x=1.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A right-angled triangle has angles $(x+30)^{\circ}$, $(x-30)^{\circ}$ and a right angle ($90^{\circ}$). Construct an equation and solve it to find the value of $x$, then state the size of each angle.
exercises.full_solution: The angles of a triangle sum to $180^{\circ}$: $(x+30)+(x-30)+90=180$. Simplifying: $2x+90=180$, so $2x=90$, giving $x=45$. The three angles are therefore $90^{\circ}$, $x+30=75^{\circ}$ and $x-30=15^{\circ}$. Check: $90+75+15=180^{\circ}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A quadrilateral has interior angles $(4x+30)^{\circ}$, $(3x+10)^{\circ}$, $(3x)^{\circ}$ and $(2x+20)^{\circ}$. Construct an equation and solve it to find the value of $x$, then state the size of each angle.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $3x+y=9$ (1) and $5x-y=7$ (2) by elimination.
exercises.full_solution: Adding equations (1) and (2) eliminates $y$: $8x=16$, so $x=2$. Substituting $x=2$ into equation (1): $6+y=9$, so $y=3$. Check in equation (2): $5(2)-3=10-3=7$, which matches the right-hand side.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $4x+y=23$ (1) and $x+y=8$ (2) by elimination.
exercises.full_solution: Subtracting equation (2) from equation (1) eliminates $y$: $3x=15$, so $x=5$. Substituting $x=5$ into equation (2): $5+y=8$, so $y=3$. Check in equation (1): $4(5)+3=20+3=23$, which matches.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $3x+y=9$ (1) and $5x-y=7$ (2) by substitution.
exercises.full_solution: Rearrange equation (2) to give $y=5x-7$. Substitute into equation (1): $3x+(5x-7)=9$, i.e. $8x-7=9$, so $8x=16$ and $x=2$. Substituting $x=2$ into either original equation gives $y=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $4x+y=23$ (1) and $x+y=8$ (2) by substitution.
exercises.full_solution: Rearrange equation (2) to give $y=8-x$. Substitute into equation (1): $4x+(8-x)=23$, i.e. $3x+8=23$, so $3x=15$ and $x=5$. Substituting back, $y=8-5=3$, which matches the result already found by elimination earlier on this page.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 22b (p.131, completed using the same system solved earlier on this page by elimination)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $3x+2y=22$ (1) and $x+y=9$ (2).
exercises.full_solution: To eliminate $y$, multiply equation (2) by $2$: $2x+2y=18$ (3). Subtracting (3) from (1): $x=4$. Substituting $x=4$ into equation (2): $4+y=9$, so $y=5$. Check in equation (1): $3(4)+2(5)=12+10=22$, which matches.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $5x-3y=1$ (1) and $3x+4y=18$ (2).
exercises.full_solution: To eliminate $y$, multiply equation (1) by $4$ and equation (2) by $3$: $20x-12y=4$ (3) and $9x+12y=54$ (4). Adding (3) and (4): $29x=58$, so $x=2$. Substituting $x=2$ into equation (2): $6+4y=18$, so $4y=12$ and $y=3$. Check in equation (1): $5(2)-3(3)=10-9=1$, which matches.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: An L-shaped figure (a rectangle with a rectangular notch cut from one corner) has a perimeter of $54\,\text{cm}$. Going around the shape, its six sides have lengths $x+3$, $x$, $x-5$, $8$, $8$ and $x+8$. Construct an equation for the perimeter in terms of $x$ and solve it to find the value of $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Summing all six side-lengths and setting the total equal to the perimeter: $(x+3)+x+(x-5)+8+8+(x+8)=54$. Simplifying: $4x+22=54$, so $4x=32$, giving $x=8$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A number is doubled, then $5$ is subtracted from it, and the total is $17$. Find the number.
exercises.full_solution: Let $x$ be the unknown number. Doubling and subtracting $5$ gives the equation $2x-5=17$. Adding $5$ to both sides: $2x=22$. Dividing by $2$: $x=11$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $3$ is added to a number. The result is multiplied by $8$. If the answer is $64$, calculate the value of the original number.
exercises.full_solution: Let $x$ be the unknown number. The description gives the equation $8(x+3)=64$. Expanding: $8x+24=64$, so $8x=40$, giving $x=5$. (Equivalently, dividing both sides of $8(x+3)=64$ by $8$ first gives $x+3=8$, so $x=5$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the equation $x^2-x-12=0$ to give two solutions for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Factorise: $x^2-x-12=(x-4)(x+3)$, so the equation becomes $(x-4)(x+3)=0$. Either $x-4=0$, giving $x=4$, or $x+3=0$, giving $x=-3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the equation $x^2+2x=24$ to give two solutions for $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Rearrange so that one side is zero: $x^2+2x-24=0$. Factorise: $(x+6)(x-4)=0$. Either $x+6=0$, giving $x=-6$, or $x-4=0$, giving $x=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the quadratic equation $x^2+7x+3=0$ using the quadratic formula, giving answers to 3 significant figures.
exercises.full_solution: Here $a=1$, $b=7$, $c=3$. Substituting into $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$: $x=\dfrac{-7\pm\sqrt{7^2-4(1)(3)}}{2(1)}=\dfrac{-7\pm\sqrt{49-12}}{2}=\dfrac{-7\pm\sqrt{37}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{37}\approx6.083$, $x=\dfrac{-7+6.083}{2}\approx-0.459$ or $x=\dfrac{-7-6.083}{2}\approx-6.54$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the quadratic equation $x^2-4x-2=0$ using the quadratic formula, giving answers to 3 significant figures.
exercises.full_solution: Here $a=1$, $b=-4$, $c=-2$. Substituting into the quadratic formula: $x=\dfrac{-(-4)\pm\sqrt{(-4)^2-4(1)(-2)}}{2(1)}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16+8}}{2}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{24}}{2}$. Since $\sqrt{24}\approx4.899$, $x=\dfrac{4+4.899}{2}\approx4.45$ or $x=\dfrac{4-4.899}{2}\approx-0.449$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the quadratic equation $x^2-4x-2=0$ by completing the square, giving answers to 3 significant figures.
exercises.full_solution: The perfect square $(x-2)^2$ expands to $x^2-4x+4$, which has the same $x^2$ and $x$ terms as the original quadratic. So $(x-2)^2-6=x^2-4x-2$, and the equation becomes $(x-2)^2-6=0$, i.e. $(x-2)^2=6$. Taking the square root of both sides: $x-2=\pm\sqrt{6}$, so $x=2\pm\sqrt{6}$. This gives $x\approx4.45$ or $x\approx-0.449$ (3 s.f.), matching the quadratic-formula result for the same equation.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $y=2x+3$ and $y=x^2+x-9$.
exercises.full_solution: Since both expressions equal $y$, set them equal to each other: $2x+3=x^2+x-9$. Rearranging to collect all terms on one side: $x^2-x-12=0$. Factorising: $(x-4)(x+3)=0$, so $x=4$ or $x=-3$. Substituting into the linear equation $y=2x+3$: when $x=4$, $y=2(4)+3=11$; when $x=-3$, $y=2(-3)+3=-3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the inequality $15+3x<6$ and represent the solution on a number line.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $15$ from both sides: $3x<-9$. Divide both sides by $3$: $x<-3$. On a number line this is shown with an open circle at $-3$ and an arrow pointing left (since $-3$ itself is not included).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the inequality $17\le7x+3$ and represent the solution on a number line.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $3$ from both sides: $14\le7x$. Divide both sides by $7$: $2\le x$, that is $x\ge2$. On a number line this is shown with a closed (filled) circle at $2$ and an arrow pointing right (since $2$ is included).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Solve the inequality $9-4x\ge17$ and represent the solution on a number line.
exercises.full_solution: Subtract $9$ from both sides: $-4x\ge8$. Divide both sides by $-4$; since we are dividing by a negative number, the inequality sign must be reversed: $x\le-2$. On a number line this is shown with a closed circle at $-2$ and an arrow pointing left.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the range of values for which $7<3x+1\le13$ and illustrate the solution on a number line.
exercises.full_solution: This is in fact two inequalities which can be solved separately. From $7<3x+1$: subtract $1$ to get $6<3x$, then divide by $3$ to get $2<x$, i.e. $x>2$. From $3x+1\le13$: subtract $1$ to get $3x\le12$, then divide by $3$ to get $x\le4$. Combining both conditions gives $2<x\le4$. On a number line this is shown with an open circle at $2$, a closed circle at $4$, and the line segment between them shaded.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On a pair of axes, shade the region which satisfies the inequality $x\ge3$.
exercises.answer: The region on and to the right of the vertical line $x=3$ is shaded.
exercises.full_solution: Draw the line $x=3$ (a solid vertical line, since the inequality is $\ge$ rather than strict). The region satisfying $x\ge3$ is everything to the right of this line (including the line itself), so this region is shaded.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same pair of axes, leave unshaded the regions which satisfy the following inequalities simultaneously: $x\le2$, $y>-1$, $y\le3$, $y\le x+2$. Hence find the region which satisfies all four inequalities.
exercises.answer: The unshaded (feasible) region is the quadrilateral with vertices $(-3,-1)$, $(2,-1)$, $(2,3)$ and $(1,3)$ (the edge along $y=-1$ is not included, since $y>-1$ is a strict inequality; the other three edges, along $x=2$, $y=3$ and $y=x+2$, are included).
exercises.full_solution: Graph each inequality in turn: $x\le2$ shades everything to the right of the vertical line $x=2$ (so the allowed region is to the left of/on it); $y>-1$ shades everything on or below the horizontal line $y=-1$ (so the allowed region is strictly above it); $y\le3$ shades everything above the horizontal line $y=3$ (so the allowed region is on or below it); $y\le x+2$ shades everything above the line $y=x+2$ (so the allowed region is on or below it). Superimposing all four shaded regions on one pair of axes, the region left unshaded is the area satisfying all four inequalities simultaneously: a quadrilateral bounded below by $y=-1$ (from $x=-3$ to $x=2$, where $y=x+2$ meets $y=-1$ at $(-3,-1)$), on the right by $x=2$ (from $y=-1$ to $y=3$), on top by $y=3$ (from $x=2$ to $x=1$, where $y=3$ meets $y=x+2$ at $(1,3)$), and on the lower-left by the line $y=x+2$ (from $(1,3)$ back to $(-3,-1)$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer plants $w$ fields of wheat and $c$ fields of corn, subject to: there must be at least two fields of corn; there must be at least two fields of wheat; not more than 10 fields in total are to be sown with wheat or corn. (a) Construct three inequalities from this information. (b) Graph the three inequalities, leaving unshaded the region satisfying all three simultaneously. (c) Give one possible arrangement for how the farmer should plant his fields.
exercises.answer: (a) $c\ge2$, $w\ge2$, $c+w\le10$. (c) One possible arrangement: four fields of corn and four fields of wheat.
exercises.full_solution: (a) 'At least two fields of corn' gives $c\ge2$; 'at least two fields of wheat' gives $w\ge2$; 'not more than 10 fields in total' gives $c+w\le10$. (b) Graphing $c\ge2$ (region to the right of/on the vertical line $c=2$), $w\ge2$ (region above/on the horizontal line $w=2$) and $c+w\le10$ (region below/on the line $w=10-c$) and leaving unshaded the overlap gives a triangular region with vertices $(2,2)$, $(8,2)$ and $(2,8)$ (using $(c,w)$ coordinates). (c) Any integer point $(c,w)$ inside or on the boundary of this triangle is a valid arrangement; for example $c=4$, $w=4$ satisfies $c\ge2$, $w\ge2$ and $c+w=8\le10$, giving four fields of corn and four fields of wheat.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A sequence is given by the term-to-term rule $u_{n+1}=u_n+3$, where $u_1=0$. Generate the terms $u_2$, $u_3$ and $u_4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the rule for the $n$th term of the sequence $12, 7, 2, -3, -8, \ldots$
exercises.full_solution: The sequence decreases by $5$ each time (the common difference is $-5$), so the rule has the form $u_n=-5n+b$. Since $u_1=12$: $-5(1)+b=12$, so $b=17$. Therefore $u_n=-5n+17$. Check: $u_2=-10+17=7$ ✓, $u_3=-15+17=2$ ✓, $u_4=-20+17=-3$ ✓, $u_5=-25+17=-8$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Deduce the rule for the $n$th term of the sequence $4, 7, 10, 13, 16, \ldots$
exercises.full_solution: The first differences (consecutive term gaps) are all $3$, so the rule is linear: $u_n=an+b$. Substituting the position values: the terms can be written as $a+b, 2a+b, 3a+b, \ldots$, whose first differences all equal $a$. Comparing with the actual first difference of $3$ gives $a=3$. Since $u_1=a+b=4$ and $a=3$, we get $b=1$. So $u_n=3n+1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Deduce the rule for the $n$th term of the sequence $0, 7, 18, 33, 52, \ldots$
exercises.full_solution: The first differences are $7, 11, 15, 19$, which are not constant, so the rule is not linear. The second differences are $4, 4, 4$, which are constant, so the rule is quadratic of the form $u_n=an^2+bn+c$. For a quadratic sequence, the second difference equals $2a$, so $2a=4$ gives $a=2$. Using $u_1=a+b+c=0$ and $u_2=4a+2b+c=7$: subtracting gives $3a+b=7$, so with $a=2$, $b=1$. Then from $a+b+c=0$: $2+1+c=0$, so $c=-3$. The rule is $u_n=2n^2+n-3$. Check: $u_1=2+1-3=0$ ✓, $u_2=8+2-3=7$ ✓, $u_3=18+3-3=18$ ✓, $u_4=32+4-3=33$ ✓, $u_5=50+5-3=52$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Alex deposits \$1500 in his savings account. The interest rate offered is $6\%$ compound interest each year for a 10-year period. Assuming Alex leaves the money in the account, calculate how much interest he has gained after the 10 years.
exercises.full_solution: An interest rate of $6\%$ implies a common ratio of $1.06$. Therefore $u_{10}=1500\times1.06^{10}=2686.27$ (to 2 d.p.). The amount of interest gained is $2686.27-1500=\$1186.27$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Adrienne deposits \$2000 in her savings account. The interest rate offered by the bank is $8\%$ compound interest per year. Calculate the number of years Adrienne needs to leave the money in her account for it to double in value.
exercises.full_solution: An interest rate of $8\%$ implies a common ratio of $1.08$, so after $n$ years the amount is $2000\times1.08^n$. We need the smallest whole number of years $n$ for which $2000\times1.08^n\ge4000$, i.e. $1.08^n\ge2$. Trying values: $1.08^5\approx1.47$ (too small), $1.08^9\approx1.999$, so $2000\times1.08^9\approx\$3998.01$ (not yet doubled); $1.08^{10}\approx2.159$, so $2000\times1.08^{10}\approx\$4317.85$ (more than doubled). Interest is added only at the end of each whole year, so Adrienne needs to leave the money in the account for $10$ years.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 36b (p.161) - completed and verified independently, since the book's continuation of the solution is on printed p.162, not in this agent's assigned page list

exercises.statement: For the sequence $2, 8, 18, 32, \ldots$: (i) by inspection, write the rule for the $n$th term; (ii) write down the next two terms.
exercises.full_solution: The terms of the sequence are double those of the well-known sequence of square numbers $1,4,9,16,25,\ldots$ (whose $n$th term is $n^2$), so $u_n=2n^2$. The next two terms (for $n=5,6$) are $2(5^2)=50$ and $2(6^2)=72$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For the sequence $1, 3, 7, 15, 31, \ldots$, by inspection write down the rule for the $n$th term and the next two terms.
exercises.full_solution: The terms of the sequence are each one less than the terms of the well-known sequence of powers of two $2,4,8,16,32,\ldots$ (whose $n$th term is $2^n$), so $u_n=2^n-1$. The next two terms (for $n=6,7$) are $2^6-1=63$ and $2^7-1=127$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $y$ is directly proportional to $x$ (i.e. $y\propto x$). If $y=7$ when $x=2$, find $y$ when $x=5$.
exercises.full_solution: Since $y\propto x$, write $y=kx$. Substituting $y=7$, $x=2$: $7=2k$, so $k=3.5$. When $x=5$: $y=3.5\times5=17.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$ (i.e. $y\propto\dfrac{1}{x}$). If $y=5$ when $x=3$, find $y$ when $x=30$.
exercises.full_solution: Since $y\propto\dfrac{1}{x}$, write $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$. Substituting $y=5$, $x=3$: $5=\dfrac{k}{3}$, so $k=15$. When $x=30$: $y=\dfrac{15}{30}=0.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A conversion graph converts South African rand into euros, based on an exchange rate of €1 = 8.80 rand. Using the graph, estimate the number of rand equivalent to €5.
exercises.full_solution: Reading a line up from €5 on the horizontal axis until it meets the plotted line, then across to the vertical axis, gives approximately $44$ rand. (This agrees with the exact calculation $5\times8.80=44$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the same rand-to-euro conversion graph (€1 = 8.80 rand), what would be the cost in euros of a drink costing 25 rand?
exercises.full_solution: Reading a line across from 25 rand on the vertical axis until it meets the plotted line, then down to the horizontal axis, gives a cost of approximately €2.80. (The exact value is $25\div8.80\approx\text{€}2.84$; the graph reading of €2.80 is a reasonable estimate given the scale of the grid.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the same rand-to-euro conversion graph, if a meal costs 200 rand, estimate its cost in euros (noting the graph only goes up to 10 euros / 88 rand).
exercises.full_solution: Since the graph does not extend to 200 rand, use a convenient factor: 200 rand $=4\times50$ rand. From the graph, 50 rand $\approx$ €5.70. So 200 rand $\approx4\times5.70=$ €22.80. (The exact value is $200\div8.80\approx\text{€}22.73$, close to the graph-based estimate.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A distance-time graph represents an object travelling at constant speed. (a) From the graph, calculate how long it took to cover a distance of $30\,\text{m}$. (b) Calculate the gradient of the graph (using a rise of $40\,\text{m}$ over a run of $4\,\text{s}$ read from the graph). (c) Calculate the speed at which the object was travelling.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Reading from the graph, a distance of $30\,\text{m}$ is reached at $t=3$ seconds. (b) Taking two points on the line, gradient $=\dfrac{40}{4}=10$. (c) For a distance–time graph, the gradient represents the speed, so the object is travelling at $10\,\text{m/s}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The journeys of two cars, X and Y, travelling between points A and B (100 km apart) are represented on a distance–time graph; both cars reach B at 1100. Car X travels from A, reaching 60 km by 0800, stays stationary until 0900, then continues to B by 1100. Car Y starts its journey from A at 0900 and reaches B (100 km) by 1100. (a) Calculate the speed of Car X between 0700 and 0800. (b) Calculate the speed of Car Y between 0900 and 1100. (c) Explain what is happening to Car X between 0800 and 0900.
exercises.answer: (a) $60\,\text{km/h}$; (b) $50\,\text{km/h}$; (c) Car X is stationary (no distance travelled)
exercises.full_solution: (a) Speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}=\dfrac{60\,\text{km}}{1\,\text{h}}=60\,\text{km/h}$. (b) Speed $=\dfrac{100\,\text{km}}{2\,\text{h}}=50\,\text{km/h}$. (c) Since the distance–time graph is flat (horizontal) for Car X between 0800 and 0900, no distance is travelled in that hour, so Car X is stationary during that time.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A speed–time graph shows the speed of a car over 16 seconds: the speed increases uniformly from $0$ to $16\,\text{m/s}$ over the first $8$ seconds, stays constant at $16\,\text{m/s}$ from $8$ to $14$ seconds, then decreases uniformly to $0$ between $14$ and $16$ seconds. Explain the shape of the graph.
exercises.answer: The car accelerates at a constant rate for the first 8 seconds, travels at a constant speed of $16\,\text{m/s}$ from 8 to 14 seconds, then decelerates at a constant rate from 14 to 16 seconds.
exercises.full_solution: For the first 8 seconds the speed increases uniformly with time, meaning the car is accelerating at a constant rate. Between 8 and 14 seconds, the speed is unchanged at $16\,\text{m/s}$, meaning the car travels at constant speed. Between 14 and 16 seconds, the speed decreases uniformly, meaning the car is decelerating at a constant rate.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the same speed–time graph (speed rises from $0$ to $16\,\text{m/s}$ over the first 8 seconds), calculate the rate of acceleration during the first 8 seconds.
exercises.full_solution: On a speed–time graph, the acceleration is the gradient of the line. During the first 8 seconds: acceleration $=\dfrac{16}{8}=2\,\text{m/s}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the same speed–time graph (speed falls from $16\,\text{m/s}$ to $0$ between 14 and 16 seconds), calculate the rate of deceleration between 14 and 16 seconds.
exercises.full_solution: Deceleration is the magnitude of the (negative) gradient over that interval: deceleration $=\dfrac{16}{2}=8\,\text{m/s}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cyclist starts cycling from rest. For the first 10 seconds, her distance from the start is given by $D=0.6t^2$, where $D$ is the distance travelled in metres and $t$ is the time in seconds. (a) Complete a distance–time table of results for $t=0$ to $10$ seconds. (b) Describe/plot the graph of the cyclist's motion on a distance–time graph.
exercises.full_solution: Substituting each value of $t$ into $D=0.6t^2$: e.g. $D(3)=0.6\times3^2=0.6\times9=5.4$, $D(7)=0.6\times49=29.4$, $D(10)=0.6\times100=60$, and so on for the other values. Plotting $D$ against $t$ gives a curve (not a straight line) that starts at the origin and becomes steeper as $t$ increases, since $D$ is proportional to $t^2$ rather than to $t$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Plot a graph of the function $y=x^2-5x+6$ for $0\le x\le5$ (construct a table of values first).
exercises.answer: Table: $x=0,1,2,3,4,5$ gives $y=6,2,0,0,2,6$. Plotting these points gives a U-shaped parabola with its minimum between $x=2$ and $x=3$.
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=x^2-5x+6$: e.g. at $x=0$: $y=0-0+6=6$; at $x=2$: $y=4-10+6=0$; at $x=3$: $y=9-15+6=0$; at $x=5$: $y=25-25+6=6$. Plotting the points $(0,6),(1,2),(2,0),(3,0),(4,2),(5,6)$ and joining them with a smooth curve gives an upward-opening parabola.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Plot a graph of the function $y=-x^2+x+2$ for $-3\le x\le4$ (construct a table of values first).
exercises.answer: Table: $x=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4$ gives $y=-10,-4,0,2,2,0,-4,-10$. Plotting these points gives a downward-opening (∩-shaped) parabola with its maximum between $x=0$ and $x=1$.
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=-x^2+x+2$: e.g. at $x=-3$: $y=-9-3+2=-10$; at $x=0$: $y=0+0+2=2$; at $x=1$: $y=-1+1+2=2$; at $x=4$: $y=-16+4+2=-10$. Plotting the points and joining them with a smooth curve gives a downward-opening parabola, symmetric about $x=0.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Draw a graph of $y=x^2-4x+3$ for $-2\le x\le5$ (construct a table of values first).
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=x^2-4x+3$: e.g. at $x=-2$: $y=4+8+3=15$; at $x=1$: $y=1-4+3=0$; at $x=2$: $y=4-8+3=-1$; at $x=5$: $y=25-20+3=8$. Plotting these points and joining them with a smooth curve gives an upward-opening parabola with minimum at $(2,-1)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the graph of $y=x^2-4x+3$, solve the equation $x^2-4x+3=0$.
exercises.full_solution: To solve the equation, find the values of $x$ where $y=0$, i.e. where the graph crosses the $x$-axis. From the table/graph, this occurs at $x=1$ and $x=3$ (since $1^2-4(1)+3=0$ and $3^2-4(3)+3=0$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the graph of $y=x^2-4x+3$ to solve the equation $x^2-4x+1=0$.
exercises.full_solution: Rearrange $x^2-4x+1=0$ by adding $2$ to both sides: $x^2-4x+3=2$. So the solutions are the $x$-values where the graph of $y=x^2-4x+3$ meets the horizontal line $y=2$. Plotting $y=2$ on the same axes and reading off the two intersection points with the curve gives $x\approx0.3$ and $x\approx3.7$ (the exact values are $x=2\pm\sqrt{3}$, i.e. $x\approx0.27$ and $x\approx3.73$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Plot the graph of the function $y=(x-4)^2+2$ for $0\le x\le6$ (construct a table of values first).
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=(x-4)^2+2$: e.g. at $x=0$: $y=16+2=18$; at $x=3$: $y=1+2=3$; at $x=4$: $y=0+2=2$; at $x=6$: $y=4+2=6$. Plotting these points gives an upward-opening parabola symmetric about $x=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the coordinates of the turning point of the graph of $y=(x-4)^2+2$.
exercises.full_solution: Since $(x-4)^2\ge0$ for all $x$, with equality when $x=4$, the smallest value of $y$ is $2$, occurring at $x=4$. So the turning point is the minimum point $(4,2)$. (In general, for $y=a(x-b)^2+c$ with $a>0$, the turning point is the minimum $(b,c)$; the graph is a '∪'-shaped parabola, so this is a minimum rather than a maximum.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Draw the graph of $y=\dfrac{2}{x}$ for $-4\le x\le4$.
exercises.answer: Table: $x=-4,-3,-2,-1,1,2,3,4$ gives $y=-0.5,-0.7,-1,-2,2,1,0.7,0.5$ ($x=0$ is excluded, since the function is undefined there).
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=\dfrac{2}{x}$: e.g. at $x=-4$: $y=-0.5$; at $x=-1$: $y=-2$; at $x=1$: $y=2$; at $x=4$: $y=0.5$. Note that $x=0$ must be excluded, since division by zero is undefined. Plotting these points gives two separate branches of a curve (one in the region $x<0$, one in $x>0$), each approaching but never touching the axes. This is an example of a reciprocal function, and its graph is called a hyperbola.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Draw a graph of the function $y=2x^2$ for $-3\le x\le3$.
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=2x^2$: e.g. at $x=-3$: $y=2(9)=18$; at $x=-1$: $y=2(1)=2$; at $x=0$: $y=0$; at $x=3$: $y=18$. Plotting these points gives a symmetric, upward-opening parabola with minimum at the origin $(0,0)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Plot the graph of the function $y=2^x$ for $-3\le x\le3$.
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=2^x$: e.g. at $x=-3$: $y=2^{-3}=0.125$; at $x=-1$: $y=2^{-1}=0.5$; at $x=0$: $y=2^0=1$; at $x=3$: $y=2^3=8$. Plotting these points gives an increasing curve that rises slowly at first, then much more steeply — characteristic of an exponential function.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the gradient of the straight line passing through the points $(0,2)$ and $(4,4)$.
exercises.full_solution: Using gradient $=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$ with $(x_1,y_1)=(0,2)$ and $(x_2,y_2)=(4,4)$: gradient $=\dfrac{4-2}{4-0}=\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 51 (p.201) - Gradient of a straight line

exercises.statement: For the function $y=2x^2$, calculate the gradient of the curve at the point where $x=1$.
exercises.full_solution: Identify the point on the curve $y=2x^2$ where $x=1$ (the point $(1,2)$) and draw a tangent to the curve at that point. Reading off two points that lie on this tangent line — $(0,-2)$ and $(3,10)$ — the gradient of the tangent (and hence the gradient of the curve at $x=1$) is $\dfrac{10-(-2)}{3-0}=\dfrac{12}{3}=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Plot a graph of $y=3x^2-x-2$ for $-3\le x\le3$ (construct a table of values first).
exercises.full_solution: Substitute each value of $x$ into $y=3x^2-x-2$: e.g. at $x=-3$: $y=27+3-2=28$; at $x=0$: $y=-2$; at $x=1$: $y=3-1-2=0$; at $x=3$: $y=27-3-2=22$. Plotting these points gives an upward-opening parabola with minimum between $x=0$ and $x=1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the graph of $y=3x^2-x-2$ to solve the equation $3x^2-x-2=0$.
exercises.full_solution: To solve the equation, find the values of $x$ where $y=0$, i.e. where the curve crosses the $x$-axis. Reading from the graph/table, this occurs at $x\approx-0.7$ and at $x=1$ (checking $x=1$: $3(1)-1-2=0$ exactly; the exact second root is $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}\approx-0.667$, consistent with the graph-reading value of $-0.7$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sketch the graph of $y=-3x+5$.
exercises.full_solution: The graph intersects the $y$-axis when $x=0$: substituting gives $y=-3(0)+5=5$. The graph intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0$: substituting gives $0=-3x+5$, so $3x=5$, i.e. $x=\dfrac{5}{3}\approx1.67$. The sketch is a straight line through $(0,5)$ and $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},0\right)$ with negative gradient.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sketch the graph of $y=x^2-8x+15$.
exercises.answer: $y$-intercept at $(0,15)$; $x$-intercepts at $x=3$ and $x=5$; minimum (turning) point at $(4,-1)$
exercises.full_solution: The graph meets the $y$-axis when $x=0$: $y=15$. The graph meets the $x$-axis when $y=0$: $x^2-8x+15=0$ factorises as $(x-5)(x-3)=0$, so $x=5$ or $x=3$. Since the $x^2$ term is positive, the graph is U-shaped. By symmetry, the minimum occurs midway between the roots, at $x=4$; substituting gives $y=4^2-8(4)+15=16-32+15=-1$, so the minimum point is $(4,-1)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sketch the graph of the quadratic $y=-x^2-4x-9$.
exercises.answer: $y$-intercept at $(0,-9)$; the graph does not cross the $x$-axis; maximum (turning) point at $(-2,-5)$
exercises.full_solution: The graph meets the $y$-axis when $x=0$: $y=-9$. Setting $y=0$ gives $-x^2-4x-9=0$, which does not factorise; the discriminant is $(-4)^2-4(-1)(-9)=16-36=-20<0$, so there are no real roots and the graph never crosses the $x$-axis. Since there is no $x$-axis intersection, the turning point must be found using the completed square form: $y=-x^2-4x-9=-(x+2)^2-5$. This gives the maximum (turning) point as $(-2,-5)$ (a maximum since the $x^2$ term is negative, giving an inverted-U shape).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sketch the function $y=(x-2)(x-3)(x-5)$.
exercises.full_solution: Since the function is already factorised, the $x$-intercepts (roots) can be read off directly: $x=2$, $x=3$ and $x=5$ (the values that make each bracket zero). The graph meets the $y$-axis when $x=0$: substituting gives $y=(0-2)(0-3)(0-5)=(-2)(-3)(-5)=-30$. (Since the $x^3$ coefficient is positive, the overall shape rises from bottom-left to top-right, crossing the $x$-axis three times at $x=2,3,5$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 56a (p.209) - y-intercept, with x-intercepts read directly from the factored form

exercises.statement: Sketch on the same axes the graphs of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$, labelling each graph clearly.
exercises.answer: Both are reciprocal-function hyperbolas in the same two quadrants; $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$ lies further from the axes than $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ for the same $x$.
exercises.full_solution: As the numerator increases from $1$ to $3$, the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ is stretched in the direction parallel to the $y$-axis (each $y$-value is tripled for a given $x$), giving the appearance of the curve moving away from both axes while keeping the same general hyperbola shape and the same asymptotes (the $x$- and $y$-axes).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}+2$, stating clearly the equations of any asymptotes.
exercises.full_solution: Compared with the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}$, every $y$-value for $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}+2$ has $2$ added to it. This translates the whole graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ up by $2$ units. Since $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ has asymptotes $y=0$ and $x=0$, the translated graph has asymptotes $y=2$ (the horizontal asymptote shifted up by 2) and $x=0$ (the vertical asymptote, unchanged).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On the same axes, plot the graphs of $y=2^x$, $y=3^x$ and $y=4^x$, and comment on any similarities between the three graphs.
exercises.answer: All three graphs pass through the point $(0,1)$, and in each case the $x$-axis is an asymptote.
exercises.full_solution: All graphs of the form $y=a^x$ pass through $(0,1)$, because when $x=0$ the equation becomes $y=a^0=1$ for any base $a$ (any nonzero number raised to the power zero equals one). The $x$-axis is an asymptote in each case because, for negative $x$, writing $x=-k$ with $k>0$ gives $a^x=a^{-k}=\dfrac{1}{a^k}$; as $x$ becomes more negative, $k$ gets larger, so $a^k$ grows and $\dfrac{1}{a^k}$ gets closer and closer to zero (but stays positive), meaning the curve approaches but never reaches the $x$-axis.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
**Extension — not examined.** Differentiation from first principles, and the limit notation $\lim_{h\to0}$, are not in the 0580 syllabus: E2.12 asks only for gradients ESTIMATED by drawing tangents, for the derivatives of functions of the form $ax^n$, and for applying them to gradients and stationary points. Work through this to see where that rule comes from, not because the exam will ask for it.

For the curve $f(x)=x^2$ and the fixed point $P(1,1)$, calculate the gradient of the chord $PQ$ for points $Q_2(2,2^2)$, $Q_3(1.5,1.5^2)$, $Q_4(1.25,1.25^2)$ and $Q_5(1.1,1.1^2)$ as $Q$ gets closer to $P$, and comment on the pattern.
exercises.answer: Gradient of $PQ_2=3$, $PQ_3=2.5$, $PQ_4=2.25$, $PQ_5=2.1$; as $Q$ approaches $P$, the gradient approaches $2$.
exercises.full_solution: The gradient of chord $PQ$ is $\dfrac{x_Q^2-1}{x_Q-1}$. For $Q_2$: $\dfrac{2^2-1}{2-1}=\dfrac{3}{1}=3$. For $Q_3$: $\dfrac{1.5^2-1}{1.5-1}=\dfrac{1.25}{0.5}=2.5$. For $Q_4$: $\dfrac{1.25^2-1}{1.25-1}=\dfrac{0.5625}{0.25}=2.25$. For $Q_5$: $\dfrac{1.1^2-1}{1.1-1}=\dfrac{0.21}{0.1}=2.1$. As $Q$ gets closer to $P$ (i.e. $x_Q\to1$), the gradient of $PQ$ gets closer and closer to $2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 59 (p.221) - Numerical approximations to the gradient at P(1,1) on y=x^2

exercises.statement:
**Extension — not examined.** Differentiation from first principles, and the limit notation $\lim_{h\to0}$, are not in the 0580 syllabus: E2.12 asks only for gradients ESTIMATED by drawing tangents, for the derivatives of functions of the form $ax^n$, and for applying them to gradients and stationary points. Work through this to see where that rule comes from, not because the exam will ask for it.

Prove that the gradient of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is $2$ when $x=1$.
exercises.full_solution: Let $P=(1,1)$ and let $Q$ be the point $h$ units from $P$ in the $x$-direction, so $Q=(1+h,(1+h)^2)$. The gradient of the line segment $PQ$ is $\dfrac{(1+h)^2-1}{(1+h)-1}=\dfrac{1+2h+h^2-1}{h}=\dfrac{2h+h^2}{h}=\dfrac{h(2+h)}{h}=2+h$ (for $h\ne0$). As $Q$ gets closer to $P$, $h$ tends to $0$, and the gradient $2+h$ tends to $2$. This can be written as $\lim_{h\to0}(2+h)=2$, so the gradient of the curve at $P(1,1)$ is $2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 60 (p.221) - Gradient of y=x^2 at x=1, from first principles

exercises.statement:
**Extension — not examined.** Differentiation from first principles, and the limit notation $\lim_{h\to0}$, are not in the 0580 syllabus: E2.12 asks only for gradients ESTIMATED by drawing tangents, for the derivatives of functions of the form $ax^n$, and for applying them to gradients and stationary points. Work through this to see where that rule comes from, not because the exam will ask for it.

Find, from first principles, the gradient function of $f(x)=x^2+x$.
exercises.full_solution: By definition, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$. Here $f(x+h)-f(x)=\big((x+h)^2+(x+h)\big)-(x^2+x)$. Expanding: $(x^2+2xh+h^2+x+h)-x^2-x=2xh+h^2+h$. Dividing by $h$: $\dfrac{2xh+h^2+h}{h}=2x+h+1$ (for $h\ne0$). Taking the limit as $h\to0$: $\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h+1)=2x+1$. So the gradient at any point $P(x,y)$ on the curve $y=x^2+x$ is given by $2x+1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the gradient function of $f(x)=2x^3$. (b) Calculate the gradient function of $y=5x^4$.
exercises.full_solution: Using the rule that for $y=ax^n$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=an\,x^{n-1}$: (a) for $f(x)=2x^3$, $f'(x)=3\times2\,x^{(3-1)}=6x^2$. (b) for $y=5x^4$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4\times5\,x^{(4-1)}=20x^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Differentiate the function $f(x)=3$ with respect to $x$.
exercises.full_solution: The graph of $f(x)=3$ is a horizontal line (it never rises or falls as $x$ changes). A horizontal line has a gradient of $0$ everywhere. Therefore, for $f(x)=3$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. (In general, the derivative of any constant is zero.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A stone is thrown vertically upwards from the ground with a speed of $10\,\text{m/s}$. Its distance $s$ from its point of release is given by $s=10t-4.9t^2$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after release. Find the velocity $v$ of the stone at any time $t$.
exercises.full_solution: The velocity is the rate of change of distance with respect to time, i.e. $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}$. Differentiating $s=10t-4.9t^2$ term by term: $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=10-2\times4.9t=10-9.8t$. So $v=10-9.8t$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 64 (p.227) - velocity of a stone thrown upwards

exercises.statement: Calculate $\dfrac{ds}{dt}$ for the function $s=6t^2-4t+1$.
exercises.full_solution: Differentiating term by term with respect to $t$: the derivative of $6t^2$ is $12t$, the derivative of $-4t$ is $-4$, and the derivative of the constant $1$ is $0$. So $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=12t-4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ when $y=x^3-2x^2$.
exercises.full_solution: First differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-4x$. Differentiating again (term by term) gives the second derivative: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Work out $\dfrac{d^2s}{dt^2}$ for $s=3t+\dfrac{1}{2}t^2$.
exercises.full_solution: First differentiate: $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=3+t$ (since $\dfrac{d}{dt}(3t)=3$ and $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12t^2\right)=t$). Differentiating again: $\dfrac{d^2s}{dt^2}=1$ (the derivative of $t$ with respect to $t$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2-2x+4$, find the gradient function and use it to calculate the gradient of the curve when $x=4$.
exercises.full_solution: Differentiating $f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-2x+4$ gives the gradient function $f'(x)=x-2$. Substituting $x=4$: $f'(4)=4-2=2$. Therefore the gradient of the curve $f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-2x+4$ is $2$ when $x=4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 67 (p.229) - gradient of a curve at a given point

exercises.statement: Calculate the gradient of the curve $f(x)=x^3+x-6$ when $x=-1$.
exercises.full_solution: The gradient function is $f'(x)=3x^2+1$. Substituting $x=-1$: $f'(-1)=3(-1)^2+1=3(1)+1=4$. Therefore the gradient of the curve at $x=-1$ is $4$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The function $f(x)=x^3-x^2-5$ has a gradient of $8$ at a point $P$ on the curve. Calculate the possible coordinates of point $P$.
exercises.full_solution: The gradient function is $f'(x)=3x^2-2x$. At $P$, $3x^2-2x=8$, i.e. $3x^2-2x-8=0$. Factorising: $(3x+4)(x-2)=0$ (check: $(3x+4)(x-2)=3x^2-6x+4x-8=3x^2-2x-8$, correct). So $3x+4=0\Rightarrow x=-\dfrac{4}{3}$, or $x-2=0\Rightarrow x=2$. Substituting into $f(x)$: $f\left(-\tfrac43\right)=\left(-\tfrac43\right)^3-\left(-\tfrac43\right)^2-5=-\tfrac{64}{27}-\tfrac{16}{9}-5=-\tfrac{247}{27}=-9\tfrac{4}{27}$; $f(2)=2^3-2^2-5=8-4-5=-1$. Therefore the possible coordinates of $P$ are $\left(-1\tfrac13,\,-9\tfrac{4}{27}\right)$ and $(2,-1)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the equation of the tangent to $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2+3x+1$ at the point $P$, where $x=1$.
exercises.full_solution: The gradient function is $f'(x)=x+3$. At $P$, where $x=1$, the gradient of the curve (and hence of the tangent) is $f'(1)=1+3=4$. The tangent is a straight line of the form $y=mx+c$ with $m=4$, so $y=4x+c$. Since $f(1)=\tfrac12(1)^2+3(1)+1=4.5$, the tangent passes through $P(1,4.5)$. Substituting: $4.5=4(1)+c\Rightarrow c=0.5$. So the equation of the tangent is $y=4x+\dfrac{1}{2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A graph has equation $y=\dfrac{1}{3}x^3-4x+5$. Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the graph.
exercises.full_solution: At a stationary point, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Here $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^2-4$, so $x^2-4=0\Rightarrow x^2=4\Rightarrow x=\pm2$. Substituting $x=2$: $y=\tfrac13(2)^3-4(2)+5=\tfrac83-8+5=\tfrac83-3=-\tfrac13$. Substituting $x=-2$: $y=\tfrac13(-2)^3-4(-2)+5=-\tfrac83+8+5=-\tfrac83+13=\tfrac{31}{3}=10\tfrac13$. So the stationary points are $(2,-\tfrac13)$ and $(-2,10\tfrac13)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example 71a (p.235) - note: the book's classification of these stationary points (part b) continues using a graphical-deduction argument that is not completed on this page and continues onto an unassigned page, so only the (fully self-contained) location of the stationary points is included here

exercises.statement: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=x+2$.
exercises.full_solution: Write $y=x+2$. Interchange $x$ and $y$: $x=y+2$. Rearrange to make $y$ the subject: $y=x-2$. So $f^{-1}(x)=x-2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the inverse of the function $g(x)=2x-3$.
exercises.full_solution: Write $y=2x-3$. Interchange $x$ and $y$: $x=2y-3$. Rearrange to make $y$ the subject: $x+3=2y$, so $y=\dfrac{x+3}{2}$. So $g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x+3}{2}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=x+3$, find $fg(x)$.
exercises.full_solution: $fg(x)=f(g(x))=f(x+3)$. Substituting $x+3$ into $f$: $f(x+3)=(x+3)+2=x+5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If $f(x)=2x-1$ and $g(x)=x-2$, find $fg(x)$.

exercises.statement: If $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=2x$, evaluate $fg(3)$.
exercises.full_solution: First find $fg(x)=f(g(x))=f(2x)=2(2x)+3=4x+3$. Then $fg(3)=4\times3+3=12+3=15$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Expand the following and simplify where possible:
a $5(2a-6b+3c)$
b $3x(5x-9)$
c $-5y(3xy+y^2)$
d $3x^2(5xy+3y^2-x^3)$
e $5p-3(2p-4)$
f $4m(2m-3)+2(3m^2-m)$
g $\frac{1}{3}(6x-9)+\frac{1}{4}(8x+24)$
h $\frac{m}{4}(6m-8)+\frac{m}{2}(10m-2)$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Multiply out each bracket term by term and collect like terms.
a $5\times 2a-5\times 6b+5\times 3c=10a-30b+15c$.
b $3x\times5x-3x\times9=15x^2-27x$.
c $-5y\times3xy-5y\times y^2=-15xy^2-5y^3$.
d $3x^2\times5xy+3x^2\times3y^2-3x^2\times x^3=15x^3y+9x^2y^2-3x^5$.
e $5p-6p+12=-p+12$.
f $8m^2-12m+6m^2-2m=14m^2-14m$.
g $2x-3+2x+6=4x+3$.
h $\frac{6m^2-8m}{4}+\frac{10m^2-2m}{2}=1.5m^2-2m+5m^2-m=\frac{13}{2}m^2-3m$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct, fully simplified expansion: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h) (8 × B1 = 8 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Factorise the following:
a $12a-4b$
b $x^2-4xy$
c $8p^3-4p^2q$
d $24xy-16x^2y+8xy^2$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Take out the highest common factor of each term.
a HCF is $4$: $12a-4b=4(3a-b)$.
b HCF is $x$: $x^2-4xy=x(x-4y)$.
c HCF is $4p^2$: $8p^3-4p^2q=4p^2(2p-q)$.
d HCF is $8xy$: $24xy-16x^2y+8xy^2=8xy(3-2x+y)$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each fully factorised form: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Rearrange the following formulae to make the letter in brackets the subject:
a $x=3p+q$ (subject $q$)
b $3m-5n=8r$ (subject $n$)
c $2m=\frac{3y}{t}$ (subject $y$)
d $x(w+y)=2y$ (subject $y$)
e $\frac{xy}{2p}=\frac{rs}{t}$ (subject $p$)
f $\frac{x+y}{w}=m+n$ (subject $w$)
exam_questions.answer: a $q=x-3p$  b $n=\frac{3m-8r}{5}$  c $y=\frac{2mt}{3}$  d $y=\frac{xw}{2-x}$  e $p=\frac{xyt}{2rs}$  f $w=\frac{x+y}{m+n}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Subtract $3p$: $q=x-3p$.
b Subtract $3m$: $-5n=8r-3m$, divide by $-5$: $n=\frac{3m-8r}{5}$.
c Multiply by $t$: $2mt=3y$, divide by 3: $y=\frac{2mt}{3}$.
d Expand: $xw+xy=2y\Rightarrow xw=2y-xy=y(2-x)\Rightarrow y=\frac{xw}{2-x}$.
e Cross-multiply: $xyt=2prs\Rightarrow p=\frac{xyt}{2rs}$.
f Multiply by $w$: $x+y=w(m+n)\Rightarrow w=\frac{x+y}{m+n}$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct rearrangement in (a), (b), (c), (f) (4 × B1 = 4 marks); (d) M1 multiply out the bracket and collect the $y$ terms on one side, M1 factorise out $y$, A1 $y=\frac{xw}{2-x}$ (3 marks); (e) M1 cross-multiply, A1 $p=\frac{xyt}{2rs}$ (2 marks). Total 9 marks.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Expand the following and simplify where possible:
a $3(2x-3y+5z)$
b $4p(2m-7)$
c $-4m(2mn-n^2)$
d $4p^2(5pq-2q^2-2p)$
e $4x-2(3x+1)$
f $4x(3x-2)+2(5x^2-3x)$
g $\frac{1}{5}(15x-10)-\frac{1}{3}(9x-12)$
h $\frac{x}{2}(4x-6)+\frac{x}{4}(2x+8)$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Expand each bracket and collect like terms, following the same method as the first assessment.
a $6x-9y+15z$.
b $8mp-28p$.
c $-8m^2n+4mn^2$.
d $20p^3q-8p^2q^2-8p^3$.
e $4x-6x-2=-2x-2$.
f $12x^2-8x+10x^2-6x=22x^2-14x$.
g $3x-2-3x+4=2$.
h $(2x^2-3x)+(0.5x^2+2x)=2.5x^2-x$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct, fully simplified expansion: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h) (8 × B1 = 8 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Factorise the following:
a $16p-8q$
b $p^2-6pq$
c $5p^2q-10pq^2$
d $9pq-6p^2q+12q^2p$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Take out the HCF of each term.
a $16p-8q=8(2p-q)$.
b $p^2-6pq=p(p-6q)$.
c $5p^2q-10pq^2=5pq(p-2q)$.
d HCF is $3pq$: $9pq-6p^2q+12pq^2=3pq(3-2p+4q)$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each fully factorised form: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
If $a=4$, $b=3$ and $c=-2$, evaluate the following:
a $3a-2b+3c$
b $5a-3b^2$
c $a^2+b^2+c^2$
d $(a+b)(a-b)$
e $a^2-b^2$
f $b^3-c^3$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Substitute $a=4,\ b=3,\ c=-2$.
a $12-6-6=0$.
b $20-27=-7$.
c $16+9+4=29$.
d $(7)(1)=7$.
e $16-9=7$ (consistent with d, difference of two squares).
f $27-(-8)=35$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct value: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Rearrange the following formulae to make the letter in brackets the subject:
a $p=4m+n$ (subject $n$)
b $4x-3y=5z$ (subject $y$)
c $2x=\frac{3y}{5p}$ (subject $y$)
d $m(x+y)=3w$ (subject $y$)
e $\frac{pq}{4r}=\frac{mn}{t}$ (subject $p$)
f $\frac{p+q}{r}=m-n$ (subject $r$)
exam_questions.answer: a $n=p-4m$  b $y=\frac{4x-5z}{3}$  c $y=\dfrac{10xp}{3}$  d $y=\frac{3w-mx}{m}=\frac{3w}{m}-x$  e $p=\frac{4rmn}{qt}$  f $r=\frac{p+q}{m-n}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $n=p-4m$.
b $-3y=5z-4x\Rightarrow y=\frac{4x-5z}{3}$.
c Multiply both sides by $5p$: $10xp=3y\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{10xp}{3}$.
d $mx+my=3w\Rightarrow my=3w-mx\Rightarrow y=\frac{3w-mx}{m}=\frac{3w}{m}-x$.
e Cross-multiply: $pqt=4rmn\Rightarrow p=\frac{4rmn}{qt}$.
f $p+q=r(m-n)\Rightarrow r=\frac{p+q}{m-n}$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct rearrangement in (a), (b), (c), (f) (4 × B1 = 4 marks); (d) M1 multiply out the bracket, M1 isolate $my$, A1 $y=\frac{3w-mx}{m}$ (3 marks); (e) M1 cross-multiply, A1 $p=\frac{4rmn}{qt}$ (2 marks). Total 9 marks.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Expand the following and simplify where possible:
a $(x-4)(x+2)$
b $(x-8)^2$
c $(x+y)^2$
d $(x-11)(x+11)$
e $(3x-2)(2x-3)$
f $(5-3x)^2$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Use the FOIL method (or $(a\pm b)^2$ identities) on each bracket.
a $x^2+2x-4x-8=x^2-2x-8$.
b $x^2-16x+64$.
c $x^2+2xy+y^2$.
d Difference of two squares: $x^2-121$.
e $6x^2-9x-4x+6=6x^2-13x+6$.
f $25-30x+9x^2=9x^2-30x+25$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct expansion: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks).
