exam_questions.statement:
Factorise the following:
a $x^2-4x-77$
b $x^2-6x+9$
c $x^2-144$
d $3x^2+3x-18$
e $2x^2+5x-12$
f $4x^2-20x+25$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Need two numbers multiplying to $-77$ and summing to $-4$: $-11$ and $7$, so $(x-11)(x+7)$.
b Perfect square: $(x-3)^2$.
c Difference of two squares: $(x-12)(x+12)$.
d Take out factor 3 first: $3(x^2+x-6)=3(x+3)(x-2)$.
e $(2x-3)(x+4)=2x^2+8x-3x-12=2x^2+5x-12$. ✓
f Perfect square: $(2x-5)^2=4x^2-20x+25$. ✓
mark_scheme: B1 for each fully factorised form: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Make the letter in green the subject of the formula:
a $mf^2=p$ (subject $f$)
b $m=5t^2$ (subject $t$)
c $A=\pi r\sqrt{p+q}$ (subject $p$)
d $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{t}$ (subject $x$)
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Divide by $m$: $f^2=\frac{p}{m}$, take the square root: $f=\sqrt{\frac{p}{m}}$.
b Divide by 5: $t^2=\frac{m}{5}$, take the square root: $t=\sqrt{\frac{m}{5}}$.
c Divide by $\pi r$: $\sqrt{p+q}=\frac{A}{\pi r}$. Square both sides: $p+q=\frac{A^2}{\pi^2r^2}$, so $p=\frac{A^2}{\pi^2r^2}-q$.
d $\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{y}=\frac{y-t}{ty}$, so (taking reciprocals) $x=\dfrac{ty}{y-t}$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 isolate $f^2$, A1 $f=\sqrt{\frac{p}{m}}$; (b) M1 isolate $t^2$, A1 $t=\sqrt{\frac{m}{5}}$; (c) M1 square both sides to remove the root, A1 $p=\frac{A^2}{\pi^2r^2}-q$; (d) M1 write the left-hand side over a common denominator, A1 $x=\frac{ty}{y-t}$ (2 marks per part, 8 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following algebraic fractions:
a $\dfrac{x^7}{x^3}$
b $\dfrac{mn}{p}\times\dfrac{pq}{m}$
c $\dfrac{(y^3)^3}{(y^2)^3}$
d $\dfrac{28pq^2}{7pq^3}$
e $\dfrac{m^2n}{2}\div\dfrac{m^2}{n^2}$
f $\dfrac{7b^3}{c}\div\dfrac{4b^2}{3c^3}$
exam_questions.answer: a $x^4$  b $nq$  c $y^3$  d $\dfrac{4}{q}$  e $\dfrac{n^3}{2}$  f $\dfrac{21bc^2}{4}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $x^{7-3}=x^4$.
b $\frac{mn\times pq}{p\times m}=nq$ ($p$ and $m$ cancel).
c $\frac{y^9}{y^6}=y^3$.
d $\frac{28}{7}\times\frac{p}{p}\times\frac{q^2}{q^3}=\frac{4}{q}$.
e $\frac{m^2n}{2}\times\frac{n^2}{m^2}=\frac{n^3}{2}$.
f $\frac{7b^3}{c}\times\frac{3c^3}{4b^2}=\frac{21b c^2}{4}$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct simplified result: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following algebraic fractions:
a $\dfrac{m}{11}+\dfrac{3m}{11}-\dfrac{2m}{11}$
b $\dfrac{3p}{8}-\dfrac{9p}{16}$
c $\dfrac{4x}{3y}-\dfrac{7x}{12y}$
d $\dfrac{3m}{15p}+\dfrac{4n}{5p}-\dfrac{11n}{30p}$
e $\dfrac{2(y+4)}{3}-(y-2)$
f $3(y+2)-\dfrac{2y+3}{2}$
exam_questions.answer: a $\dfrac{2m}{11}$  b $-\dfrac{3p}{16}$  c $\dfrac{3x}{4y}$  d $\dfrac{6m+13n}{30p}$  e $\dfrac{14-y}{3}$  f $\dfrac{4y+9}{2}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Combine over a common denominator of 11: $\frac{m+3m-2m}{11}=\frac{2m}{11}$.
b Common denominator 16: $\frac{6p-9p}{16}=-\frac{3p}{16}$.
c Common denominator $12y$: $\frac{16x-7x}{12y}=\frac{9x}{12y}=\frac{3x}{4y}$.
d Common denominator $30p$: $\frac{6m}{30p}+\frac{24n}{30p}-\frac{11n}{30p}=\frac{6m+13n}{30p}$.
e $\frac{2y+8}{3}-(y-2)=\frac{2y+8-3(y-2)}{3}=\frac{2y+8-3y+6}{3}=\frac{14-y}{3}$.
f $3(y+2)=\frac{6(y+2)}{2}=\frac{6y+12}{2}$; subtract $\frac{2y+3}{2}$: $\frac{6y+12-2y-3}{2}=\frac{4y+9}{2}$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct simplified fraction: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following:
a $\dfrac{4}{x-5}+\dfrac{3}{x-2}$
b $\dfrac{a^2-b^2}{(a+b)^2}$
c $\dfrac{x-2}{x^2+x-6}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Common denominator $(x-5)(x-2)$: $\frac{4(x-2)+3(x-5)}{(x-5)(x-2)}=\frac{4x-8+3x-15}{(x-5)(x-2)}=\frac{7x-23}{(x-5)(x-2)}$.
b $a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$, so $\frac{(a-b)(a+b)}{(a+b)^2}=\frac{a-b}{a+b}$.
c $x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)$, so $\frac{x-2}{(x+3)(x-2)}=\frac{1}{x+3}$, cancelling the common factor $(x-2)$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 common denominator $(x-5)(x-2)$, A1 $\frac{7x-23}{(x-5)(x-2)}$; (b) M1 factorise $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$, A1 $\frac{a-b}{a+b}$; (c) M1 factorise $x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)$, A1 $\frac{1}{x+3}$ (2 marks per part, 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by the formula $V=\pi r^2 h$, where $h$ is the height of the cylinder and $r$ is the radius.
a Find the volume of a cylindrical post $6.5\,\text{m}$ long and with a diameter of $20\,\text{cm}$.
b Make $r$ the subject of the formula.
c A cylinder of height $60\,\text{cm}$ has a volume of $5500\,\text{cm}^3$: find its radius correct to 3 s.f.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Diameter $20\,\text{cm}\Rightarrow r=10\,\text{cm}=0.1\,\text{m}$, $h=6.5\,\text{m}$. $V=\pi(0.1)^2(6.5)=0.065\pi\approx0.204\,\text{m}^3$.
b Divide by $\pi h$: $r^2=\frac{V}{\pi h}$, so $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{\pi h}}$.
c $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{5500}{\pi\times60}}=\sqrt{29.18}\approx5.40\,\text{cm}$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 convert diameter to radius and units, A1 correct volume (a: 2 marks); B1 correct rearrangement (b: 1 mark); M1 substitute and solve, A1 radius to 3 s.f. (c: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The formula for the surface area of a closed cylinder is $A=2\pi r(r+h)$, where $r$ is the radius of the cylinder and $h$ is its height.
a Find the surface area of a cylinder of radius $12\,\text{cm}$ and height $20\,\text{cm}$, giving your answer to 3 s.f.
b Rearrange the formula to make $h$ the subject.
c What is the height of a cylinder of surface area $500\,\text{cm}^2$ and radius $5\,\text{cm}$? Give your answer to 3 s.f.
mark_scheme: M1 substitute, A1 answer to 3 s.f. (a: 2 marks); B1 correct rearrangement (b: 1 mark); M1 substitute and solve, A1 answer to 3 s.f. (c: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The formula for finding the length $d$ of the body diagonal of a cuboid whose dimensions are $x$, $y$ and $z$ is: $$d=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$$
a Find $d$ when $x=2$, $y=3$ and $z=4$.
b How long is the body diagonal of a block of concrete in the shape of a rectangular prism of dimensions $2\,\text{m}$, $3\,\text{m}$ and $75\,\text{cm}$?
c Rearrange the formula to make $x$ the subject.
d Find $x$ when $d=0.86$, $y=0.25$ and $z=0.41$.
mark_scheme: B1 $\sqrt{29}$ or $5.39$ (a); M1 convert $75\,\text{cm}=0.75\,\text{m}$ and substitute, A1 $3.68\,\text{m}$ (b); B1 $x=\sqrt{d^2-y^2-z^2}$ (c); M1 substitute, A1 $0.713$ (d)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A pendulum of length $l$ metres takes $T$ seconds to complete one full oscillation. The formula for $T$ is: $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$$ where $g\,\text{m/s}^2$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
a Find $T$ if $l=5$ and $g=10$.
b Rearrange the formula to make $l$ the subject of the formula.
c How long is a pendulum which takes 3 seconds for one oscillation, if $g=10$?
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{5}{10}}=2\pi\sqrt{0.5}\approx4.44\,\text{s}$.
b Divide by $2\pi$: $\frac{T}{2\pi}=\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$. Square both sides: $\frac{T^2}{4\pi^2}=\frac{l}{g}$, so $l=\dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2}$.
c $l=\dfrac{10\times3^2}{4\pi^2}=\dfrac{90}{39.48}\approx2.28\,\text{m}$.
mark_scheme: M1 substitute, A1 $T\approx4.44\,\text{s}$ (a); M1 divide by $2\pi$ and square both sides, A1 $l=\frac{gT^2}{4\pi^2}$ (b); B1 $l\approx2.28\,\text{m}$ (c)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following using indices:
a $a\times a\times a\times b\times b$
b $d\times d\times e\times e\times e\times e\times e$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Count the repeated factors of each letter and write as a power.
a Three $a$'s and two $b$'s: $a^3b^2$.
b Two $d$'s and five $e$'s: $d^2e^5$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct index form: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Write the following out in full:
a $m^3$
b $r^4$
exam_questions.answer: a $m\times m\times m$  b $r\times r\times r\times r$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Writing a power out in full means repeating the base as many times as the index indicates.
a $m^3=m\times m\times m$.
b $r^4=r\times r\times r\times r$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each product written out in full: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following using indices:
a $a^4\times a^3$
b $p^3\times p^2\times q^4\times q^5$
c $\dfrac{b^7}{b^4}$
d $\dfrac{(e^4)^5}{e^{14}}$
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct simplification: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following:
a $r^4\times t^0$
b $\dfrac{(a^3)^0}{b^2}$
c $\dfrac{(m^0)^5}{n^{-3}}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Use $x^0=1$ for any nonzero $x$, and $\frac{1}{n^{-3}}=n^3$.
a $t^0=1$, so $r^4\times1=r^4$.
b $(a^3)^0=1$, so the expression is $\frac{1}{b^2}$.
c $(m^0)^5=1^5=1$, so the expression is $\frac{1}{n^{-3}}=n^3$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct simplification: (a), (b), (c) (3 × B1 = 3 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following:
a $\dfrac{(p^2\times p^{-5})^2}{p^3}$
b $\dfrac{(h^{-2}\times h^{-5})^{-1}}{h^0}$
mark_scheme: (a) M1 apply the index laws inside the bracket, A1 $\frac{1}{p^9}$; (b) M1 apply the index laws inside the bracket, A1 $h^7$ (2 marks per part, 4 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
Rewrite the following in the form $a^{m/n}$:
a $\sqrt[8]{a}$
b $(\sqrt[5]{a})^{-2}$
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct fractional-index form: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
Rewrite the following in the form $\sqrt[n]{b^m}$:
a $b^{4/9}$
b $b^{-2/3}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
A fractional index $b^{m/n}$ is the $n$th root of $b^m$: $b^{m/n}=\sqrt[n]{b^m}$.
a $b^{4/9}=\sqrt[9]{b^4}$.
b $b^{-2/3}=\sqrt[3]{b^{-2}}$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct root form: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following algebraic expressions, giving your answer in the form $a^{m/n}$:
a $a^{1/3}\times a^{3/2}$
b $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{a}}{a^{-5/6}}\times a^2$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $a^{1/3}\times a^{3/2}=a^{1/3+3/2}$. Common denominator 6: $\frac{2}{6}+\frac{9}{6}=\frac{11}{6}$, so the answer is $a^{11/6}$.
b $\frac{a^{1/3}}{a^{-5/6}}\times a^2=a^{1/3}\times a^{5/6}\times a^2=a^{1/3+5/6+2}$. Common denominator 6: $\frac{2}{6}+\frac{5}{6}+\frac{12}{6}=\frac{19}{6}$, so the answer is $a^{19/6}$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 add the indices over a common denominator, A1 $a^{11/6}$; (b) M1 combine all three indices over a common denominator, A1 $a^{19/6}$ (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Simplify the following algebraic expressions, giving your answer in the form $(\sqrt[n]{t})^m$:
a $\dfrac{\sqrt{t}\times t^{2/3}}{t^{-1/3}}$
b $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{t}}{t^2\times t^{-2/5}}$
mark_scheme: (a) M1 combine the indices over a common denominator, A1 $(\sqrt{t})^3$; (b) M1 combine the indices over a common denominator, A1 $(\sqrt[15]{t})^{-19}$ (2 marks per part, 4 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following equations:
a $y+9=3$
b $3x-5=13$
c $12-5p=-8$
d $2.5y+1.5=7.5$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=3-9=-6$.
b $3x=18\Rightarrow x=6$.
c $-5p=-20\Rightarrow p=4$.
d $2.5y=6\Rightarrow y=2.4$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct solution: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following equations:
a $5-p=4+p$
b $8m-9=5m+3$
c $11p-4=9p+15$
d $27-5r=r-3$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $1=2p\Rightarrow p=0.5$.
b $3m=12\Rightarrow m=4$.
c $2p=19\Rightarrow p=9.5$.
d $30=6r\Rightarrow r=5$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct solution: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following equations:
a $\dfrac{p}{-2}=-3$
b $6=\dfrac{2}{5}x$
c $\dfrac{m-7}{5}=3$
d $\dfrac{4t-3}{3}=7$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Multiply by $-2$: $p=6$.
b Multiply by $\frac{5}{2}$: $x=15$.
c Multiply by 5: $m-7=15\Rightarrow m=22$.
d Multiply by 3: $4t-3=21\Rightarrow 4t=24\Rightarrow t=6$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct solution: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following equations:
a $\dfrac{2}{5}(t-1)=3$
b $5(3-m)=4(m-6)$
c $5=\dfrac{2}{3}(x-1)$
d $\dfrac{4}{5}(t-2)=\dfrac{1}{4}(2t+8)$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $t-1=7.5\Rightarrow t=8.5$.
b $15-5m=4m-24\Rightarrow39=9m\Rightarrow m=\frac{39}{9}=\frac{13}{3}$.
c $x-1=7.5\Rightarrow x=8.5$.
d Multiply both sides by 20: $16(t-2)=5(2t+8)\Rightarrow16t-32=10t+40\Rightarrow6t=72\Rightarrow t=12$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 multiply both sides by $\frac52$ (or expand the bracket), A1 $t=8.5$; (b) M1 expand both brackets, A1 $m=\frac{13}{3}$; (c) M1 multiply both sides by $\frac32$ (or expand the bracket), A1 $x=8.5$; (d) M1 multiply through by $20$ to clear both fractions, A1 $t=12$ (2 marks per part, 8 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following simultaneous equations:
a $x+y=11,\ x-y=3$
b $5p-3q=-1,\ -2p-3q=-8$
c $3x+5y=26,\ x-y=6$
d $2m-3n=-9,\ 3m+2n=19$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Adding the equations: $2x=14\Rightarrow x=7$, then $y=11-7=4$.
b Subtracting: $(5p-3q)-(-2p-3q)=-1-(-8)\Rightarrow7p=7\Rightarrow p=1$; then $5-3q=-1\Rightarrow q=2$.
c From the second equation $x=6+y$; substitute: $3(6+y)+5y=26\Rightarrow18+8y=26\Rightarrow y=1$, so $x=7$.
d Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3: $4m-6n=-18$ and $9m+6n=57$; add: $13m=39\Rightarrow m=3$; then $6-3n=-9\Rightarrow n=5$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 add the two equations to eliminate $y$, A1 $x=7,\ y=4$; (b) M1 subtract the equations to eliminate $q$, A1 $p=1,\ q=2$; (c) M1 eliminate one variable (e.g. substitute $x=y+6$), A1 $x=7,\ y=1$; (d) M1 scale and combine the equations to eliminate $n$, A1 $m=3,\ n=5$ (2 marks per part, 8 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=-3x+5$ and $y=4x^2+8x+2$
mark_scheme: M1 set the expressions equal and rearrange to $4x^2+11x-3=0$, M1 solve the quadratic (factorise or formula), A1 both pairs of $(x,y)$

exam_questions.statement:
The angles of a quadrilateral are $x$, $3x$, $(2x-40)$ and $(3x-50)$ degrees.
a Construct an equation in terms of $x$.
b Solve the equation.
c Calculate the size of the four angles.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a The angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$: $x+3x+(2x-40)+(3x-50)=360\Rightarrow9x-90=360$.
b $9x=450\Rightarrow x=50$.
c $x=50^\circ$, $3x=150^\circ$, $2x-40=60^\circ$, $3x-50=100^\circ$. Check: $50+150+60+100=360$. ✓
mark_scheme: M1 sum of angles $=360$ set up correctly (a: 1 mark); M1 solve linear equation, A1 $x$ value (b: 2 marks); A1 all four angles correct (c: 1 mark)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Three is subtracted from seven times a number. The result is multiplied by 5. If the answer is 55, calculate the value of the number by constructing an equation and solving it.
exam_questions.full_solution: Let the number be $n$: $5(7n-3)=55\Rightarrow7n-3=11\Rightarrow7n=14\Rightarrow n=2$.
mark_scheme: M1 correct equation $5(7n-3)=55$, A1 $n=2$
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: The interior angles of a pentagon are $9x$, $5x+10$, $6x+5$, $8x-25$ and $10x-20$ degrees. If the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon is $540^\circ$, find the size of each of the angles.
mark_scheme: M1 correct equation $38x-30=540$, A1 $x=15$, A1 all five angles correctly listed
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the following quadratic equation by factorisation: $x^2-x=20$
exam_questions.full_solution: $x^2-x-20=0\Rightarrow(x-5)(x+4)=0\Rightarrow x=5$ or $x=-4$.
mark_scheme: M1 rearrange to $x^2-x-20=0$ and factorise, A1 both solutions
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the following quadratic equation by using the quadratic formula: $2x^2-7=3x$
exam_questions.full_solution: Rearrange: $2x^2-3x-7=0$. Using $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ with $a=2,b=-3,c=-7$: discriminant $=9+56=65$, so $x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{65}}{4}\approx2.77$ or $-1.27$.
mark_scheme: M1 rearrange to $2x^2-3x-7=0$, M1 correctly apply the quadratic formula, A1 both solutions (exact or to 3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the following equations simultaneously: $y=\dfrac{2}{x}+1$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+2$
exam_questions.full_solution: Equate: $\dfrac{2}{x}+1=\dfrac{1}{2}x+2$. Multiply by $2x$: $4+2x=x^2+4x\Rightarrow x^2+2x-4=0$. Discriminant $=4+16=20$, so $x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{20}}{2}=-1\pm\sqrt5$. For $x=-1+\sqrt5$: $y=\frac12(-1+\sqrt5)+2=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\approx2.62$. For $x=-1-\sqrt5$: $y=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\approx0.38$.
mark_scheme: M1 set equal and clear fractions to get $x^2+2x-4=0$, M1 solve quadratic (formula), A1 both $x$ values, A1 corresponding $y$ values
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the inequality below and illustrate your answer on a number line: $6<2x\le10$
exam_questions.full_solution: Dividing every part of the inequality by 2: $3<x\le5$. On a number line this is shown with an open circle at $x=3$ (not included) and a filled/closed circle at $x=5$ (included), with the line between them shaded.
mark_scheme: M1 divide through by 2, A1 correct inequality and correct number-line sketch (open circle at 3, closed circle at 5, line shaded between)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: For what values of $x$ is the following inequality true? $\dfrac{7}{x-5}>0$
exam_questions.full_solution: Since the numerator $7$ is always positive, the fraction is positive exactly when the denominator is also positive: $x-5>0\Rightarrow x>5$.
mark_scheme: M1 recognise numerator positive so denominator must be positive, A1 correct inequality $x>5$
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The angles of a triangle are $x^\circ$, $y^\circ$ and $40^\circ$. The difference between the two unknown angles is $30^\circ$.
a Write down two equations from the information given above.
b What is the size of the two unknown angles?
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Angle sum of a triangle: $x+y+40=180\Rightarrow x+y=140$. The difference condition gives $x-y=30$ (taking $x$ as the larger angle).
b Adding the two equations: $2x=170\Rightarrow x=85$; then $y=140-85=55$. So the unknown angles are $85^\circ$ and $55^\circ$.
mark_scheme: B1 $x+y=140$, B1 $x-y=30$ (a: 2 marks); M1 solve simultaneously, A1 both angles (b: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The interior angles of a pentagon increase by $10^\circ$ as you progress clockwise.
a Illustrate this information in a diagram.
b Write an expression for the sum of the interior angles.
c The sum of the interior angles of a pentagon is $540^\circ$. Use this to calculate the largest **exterior** angle of the pentagon.
d Illustrate on your diagram the size of each of the five exterior angles.
e Show that the sum of the exterior angles is $360^\circ$.
exam_questions.answer: Interior angles $88^\circ,98^\circ,108^\circ,118^\circ,128^\circ$; largest exterior angle $=92^\circ$; exterior angles $92^\circ,82^\circ,72^\circ,62^\circ,52^\circ$ sum to $360^\circ$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Label the smallest interior angle $a$; the five interior angles going clockwise are $a,\ a+10,\ a+20,\ a+30,\ a+40$.
b Sum $=5a+100$.
c Set $5a+100=540\Rightarrow5a=440\Rightarrow a=88$. The smallest interior angle (88°) corresponds to the largest exterior angle, since exterior $=180-$ interior: $180-88=92^\circ$.
d The five interior angles are $88^\circ,98^\circ,108^\circ,118^\circ,128^\circ$, so the corresponding exterior angles ($180-$ interior) are $92^\circ,82^\circ,72^\circ,62^\circ,52^\circ$.
e $92+82+72+62+52=360^\circ$, as required for the exterior angles of any convex polygon.
mark_scheme: B1 correctly labelled diagram (a); B1 expression $5a+100$ for angles $a,a+10,\dots,a+40$ (b); M1 solve $5a+100=540$ and use exterior $=180-$ smallest interior, A1 $92^\circ$ (c); B1 all five exterior angles $92^\circ,82^\circ,72^\circ,62^\circ,52^\circ$ shown and their sum calculated as $360^\circ$ (d, e)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A flat sheet of card measures $12\,\text{cm}$ by $10\,\text{cm}$. It is made into an open box by cutting a square of side $x\,\text{cm}$ from each corner and then folding up the sides.
a Illustrate the box and its dimensions on a simple 3D sketch.
b Write an expression for the surface area of the outside of the box.
c If the surface area is $56\,\text{cm}^2$, form and solve a quadratic equation to find the value of $x$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a The open box has base $(12-2x)\times(10-2x)$ and height $x$.
b Outside surface area $=$ base $+$ four walls $=(12-2x)(10-2x)+2x(12-2x)+2x(10-2x)$. Expanding: $(120-44x+4x^2)+(44x-8x^2)=120-4x^2$. (This simplification makes sense: folding does not change the card's total area, so the outside area equals the original area minus the four $x\times x$ corner squares removed, i.e. $120-4x^2$.)
c $120-4x^2=56\Rightarrow4x^2=64\Rightarrow x^2=16\Rightarrow x=4$ (taking the positive root, and checking $0<x<5$ so the box dimensions stay positive).
mark_scheme: B1 correct 3D sketch with labelled dimensions $(12-2x),(10-2x),x$ (a: 1 mark); M1 correct expression for total surface area, A1 simplified $120-4x^2$ (b: 2 marks); M1 form $120-4x^2=56$ and solve, A1 $x=4$ (c: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Show that $x-2=\dfrac{4}{x-3}$ can be written as $x^2-5x+2=0$.
b Use the quadratic formula to solve $x-2=\dfrac{4}{x-3}$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Multiply both sides by $(x-3)$: $(x-2)(x-3)=4\Rightarrow x^2-5x+6=4\Rightarrow x^2-5x+2=0$.
b With $a=1,b=-5,c=2$: discriminant $=25-8=17$, so $x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}\approx4.56$ or $0.438$.
mark_scheme: M1 multiply both sides by $(x-3)$ and expand, A1 correctly shown (a); M1 apply quadratic formula, A1 both solutions $x\approx4.56$ and $x\approx0.438$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A right-angled triangle $ABC$ has side lengths as follows: $AB=x\,\text{cm}$, $AC$ is $2\,\text{cm}$ shorter than $AB$, and $BC$ is $2\,\text{cm}$ shorter than $AC$.
a Illustrate this information on a diagram.
b Using this information show that $x^2-12x+20=0$.
c Solve the above quadratic and hence find the length of each of the three sides of the triangle.
exam_questions.answer: b shown  c $x=10$: sides are $AB=10\,\text{cm},\ AC=8\,\text{cm},\ BC=6\,\text{cm}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $AB$ is the hypotenuse (the longest side), $AC=x-2$ and $BC=x-4$, with the right angle at $C$.
b By Pythagoras: $AB^2=AC^2+BC^2\Rightarrow x^2=(x-2)^2+(x-4)^2=x^2-4x+4+x^2-8x+16=2x^2-12x+20$. So $0=x^2-12x+20$, i.e. $x^2-12x+20=0$.
c Factorising or using the formula: $x^2-12x+20=0\Rightarrow(x-10)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=10$ or $x=2$. $x=2$ is rejected since it gives $BC=x-4=-2<0$ (impossible). So $x=10$, giving $AB=10$, $AC=8$, $BC=6$ — a $6$–$8$–$10$ right triangle, since $6^2+8^2=36+64=100=10^2$. ✓
mark_scheme: B1 correctly labelled right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $AB$ (a: 1 mark); M1 apply Pythagoras $x^2=(x-2)^2+(x-4)^2$, A1 shown to simplify to $x^2-12x+20=0$ (b: 2 marks); M1 solve quadratic, A1 correct side lengths, rejecting the invalid root (c: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following inequalities:
a $17+5x\le42$
b $3\ge\dfrac{y}{3}+2$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $5x\le25\Rightarrow x\le5$.
b $1\ge\frac{y}{3}\Rightarrow3\ge y$, i.e. $y\le3$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct inequality solution: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Find the range of values for which:
a $7<4y-1\le15$
b $18<3(p+2)\le30$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Add 1 throughout: $8<4y\le16$; divide by 4: $2<y\le4$.
b Divide by 3: $6<p+2\le10$; subtract 2: $4<p\le8$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct range: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A garage stocks two kinds of engine oil. They have $r$ cases of regular oil and $s$ cases of super oil. They have fewer than ten cases of regular oil in stock and between three and nine cases of super oil in stock. They also have fewer than 12 cases in stock altogether.
a Express the three constraints described above as inequalities.
b Draw an appropriate pair of axes and identify the region which satisfies all the inequalities by shading the unwanted regions.
c State two possible solutions for the number of each case in stock.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Fewer than 10 cases of regular: $r<10$ (with $r\ge0$). Between three and nine cases of super (inclusive): $3\le s\le9$. Fewer than 12 cases altogether: $r+s<12$.
b On axes of $r$ (horizontal) and $s$ (vertical), shade out $r\ge10$, $s<3$, $s>9$ and $r+s\ge12$, leaving the feasible (unshaded) region.
c Any integer point in the feasible region works, e.g. $r=5,s=3$ (total $8<12$) or $r=2,s=6$ (total $8<12$).
mark_scheme: B1 $r<10$, B1 $3\le s\le9$, B1 $r+s<12$ (a: 3 marks, allow $r,s\ge0$ implied); B1 correctly shaded graph identifying the feasible region (b: 1 mark); B1 two valid integer solutions satisfying all three inequalities (c: 1 mark)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Students from Argentina and students from England are meeting on a cultural exchange. In total there will be between 12 and 20 students. There are fewer than 10 students from Argentina, while the number from England cannot be more than three greater than the number from Argentina.
a Write inequalities for the number $(A)$ of students from Argentina and the number $(E)$ of students from England.
b On an appropriate pair of axes, graph the inequalities, leaving unshaded the region which satisfies all of them.
c State two of the possible combinations of $A$ and $E$ which satisfy the given conditions.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Total between 12 and 20: $12\le A+E\le20$. Fewer than 10 from Argentina: $A<10$ (with $A>0$). England no more than three greater than Argentina: $E\le A+3$.
b Draw axes for $A$ and $E$ and shade out the regions not satisfying each inequality, leaving the feasible region unshaded.
c Checking $A=5,E=8$: total $13$ (in range), $E=8\le A+3=8$ ✓. Checking $A=8,E=10$: total $18$ (in range), $E=10\le A+3=11$ ✓.
mark_scheme: B1 $12\le A+E\le20$, B1 $0<A<10$, B1 $E\le A+3$ (a: 3 marks); B1 correctly shaded/unshaded feasible region (b: 1 mark); B1 two valid integer combinations (c: 1 mark)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Solve the following inequalities:
a $5+6x\le47$
b $4\ge\dfrac{y+3}{3}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $6x\le42\Rightarrow x\le7$.
b $12\ge y+3\Rightarrow y\le9$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct inequality solution: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Find the range of values for which:
a $3\le3p<12$
b $24<8(x-1)\le48$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Divide by 3: $1\le p<4$.
b Divide by 8: $3<x-1\le6$; add 1: $4<x\le7$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct range: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).

exam_questions.statement:
A breeder of horses has $x$ stallions and $y$ mares. She has fewer than four stallions and more than two mares. She has enough room for a maximum of eight animals in total.
a Express the three conditions above as inequalities.
b Draw an appropriate pair of axes and leave unshaded the region which satisfies all the inequalities.
c State two of the possible combinations of stallions and mares which she can have.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Fewer than four stallions: $x<4$. More than two mares: $y>2$. Maximum eight animals: $x+y\le8$.
b Shade out $x\ge4$, $y\le2$ and $x+y>8$, leaving the feasible region unshaded.
c $x=2,y=3$: $x+y=5\le8$ ✓. $x=3,y=4$: $x+y=7\le8$ ✓.
mark_scheme: B1 $x<4$, B1 $y>2$, B1 $x+y\le8$ (a: 3 marks, with $x,y\ge0$ implied); B1 correct feasible region shown (b: 1 mark); B1 two valid integer combinations (c: 1 mark)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Antonio is employed by a company to do two jobs. He mends cars and he also repairs electrical goods. His terms of employment are listed below.
- He is employed for a maximum of 40 hours.
- He must spend at least 16 hours mending cars.
- He must spend at least 5 hours repairing electrical goods.
- He must spend more than twice as much time mending cars as repairing electrical goods.
a Express the conditions above as inequalities, using $c$ to represent the number of hours spent mending cars, and $e$ to represent the number of hours spent mending electrical goods.
b On an appropriate pair of axes, graph the inequalities, leaving unshaded the region which satisfies all four.
c State two of the possible combinations which satisfy the above conditions.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Maximum 40 hours total: $c+e\le40$. At least 16 hours cars: $c\ge16$. At least 5 hours electrical: $e\ge5$. More than twice as much time on cars: $c>2e$.
b Draw axes for $c$ and $e$ and shade out the complementary regions, leaving the feasible region unshaded.
c $c=20,e=8$: $c>2e=16$ ✓, total $28\le40$ ✓. $c=30,e=10$: $c>2e=20$ ✓, total $40\le40$ ✓.
mark_scheme: B1 $c+e\le40$, B1 $c\ge16$, B1 $e\ge5$, B1 $c>2e$ (a); B1 correct feasible region left unshaded (b); B1 two valid combinations (c)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For each of the sequences given below:
i calculate the next two terms,
ii explain the pattern in words.
a $9,\ 18,\ 27,\ 36,\ \ldots$
b $54,\ 48,\ 42,\ 36,\ \ldots$
c $18,\ 9,\ 4.5,\ \ldots$
d $12,\ 6,\ 0,\ -6,\ \ldots$
e $216,\ 125,\ 64,\ \ldots$
f $1,\ 3,\ 9,\ 27,\ \ldots$
exam_questions.answer: a $45,54$ (add 9 each time)  b $30,24$ (subtract 6 each time)  c $2.25,1.125$ (halve each time)  d $-12,-18$ (subtract 6 each time)  e $27,8$ (cubes of $6,5,4,3,2$ descending)  f $81,243$ (multiply by 3 each time)
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Arithmetic, common difference $+9$: next terms $45,54$.
b Arithmetic, common difference $-6$: next terms $30,24$.
c Geometric, common ratio $\frac12$: next terms $2.25,1.125$.
d Arithmetic, common difference $-6$: next terms $-12,-18$.
e These are cubes of descending integers $6^3,5^3,4^3,\ldots$: next terms $3^3=27,\ 2^3=8$.
f Geometric, common ratio $3$: next terms $81,243$.
mark_scheme: Each part (a) to (f): B1 the next two terms correct, B1 the pattern correctly described in words (2 marks per part, 6 parts, 12 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For each of the sequences shown below give an expression for the $n$th term:
a $6,\ 10,\ 14,\ 18,\ 22,\ \ldots$
b $13,\ 19,\ 25,\ 31,\ \ldots$
c $3,\ 9,\ 15,\ 21,\ 27,\ \ldots$
d $4,\ 7,\ 12,\ 19,\ 28,\ \ldots$
e $0,\ 10,\ 20,\ 30,\ 40,\ \ldots$
f $0,\ 7,\ 26,\ 63,\ 124,\ \ldots$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a,b,c,e are arithmetic: $n$th term $=$ first term $+(n-1)\times$common difference, rearranged to the forms shown.
d Second differences are constant ($2$), so it is quadratic: fitting $an^2+bn+c$ to the first three terms gives $a=1,b=0,c=3$, i.e. $n^2+3$ (checked against all given terms).
f Third differences are constant, so it is cubic: fitting $an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ gives $a=1,b=c=0,d=-1$, i.e. $n^3-1$ (checked: $1^3-1=0,\ 2^3-1=7,\ 3^3-1=26,\ 4^3-1=63,\ 5^3-1=124$ ✓).
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct $n$th-term expression: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) (6 × B1 = 6 marks). In (d) and (f) the mark is for the final expression, found from a difference table.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For each of the following arithmetic sequences:
i write down a formula for the $n$th term
ii calculate the 10th term.
a $1,5,9,13,\ldots$
b $1,-2,-5,-8,\ldots$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a First term 1, common difference 4: $u_n=1+4(n-1)=4n-3$. $u_{10}=4(10)-3=37$.
b First term 1, common difference $-3$: $u_n=1-3(n-1)=4-3n$. $u_{10}=4-30=-26$.
mark_scheme: Each part: B1 the correct $n$th-term formula, B1 the correct 10th term ((a) $u_n=4n-3$, $u_{10}=37$; (b) $u_n=4-3n$, $u_{10}=-26$) (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For both of the following, calculate $u_5$ and $u_{100}$:
a $u_n=6n-3$
b $u_n=-\dfrac{1}{2}n+4$
mark_scheme: Each part: B1 $u_5$, B1 $u_{100}$ ((a) $27$ and $597$; (b) $1.5$ and $-46$) (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Copy and complete both of the following tables of arithmetic sequences:
a

| Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 10 | | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Term | 17 | 14 | | | $-55$ | |

b

| Position | 2 | 6 | 10 | | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Term | $-4$ | $-2$ | | 35 | |
exam_questions.answer:
a nth term $=20-3n$; table: position $1,2,3,10,25,n$ gives term $17,14,11,-10,-55,20-3n$.
b nth term $=\dfrac{n}{2}-5$; table: position $2,6,10,80,n$ gives term $-4,-2,0,35,\dfrac{n}{2}-5$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a First term 17 (position 1), common difference $14-17=-3$, so term $=17-3(n-1)=20-3n$. Position 3: $20-9=11$. Position 10: $20-30=-10$. Term $=-55$: $20-3n=-55\Rightarrow n=25$.
b From position 2 (term $-4$) to position 6 (term $-2$), the term increases by 2 over 4 positions, so the common difference per position is $0.5$: term $=0.5\times\text{position}-5$ (since $0.5(2)-5=-4$ ✓). Position 10: $0.5(10)-5=0$. Term $=35$: $0.5p-5=35\Rightarrow p=80$.
mark_scheme: M1 find the rule $20-3n$, A1 all missing entries correct ($11$, $-10$, position $25$, $20-3n$) (a); M1 find the rule $\frac{n}{2}-5$, A1 all missing entries correct ($0$, position $80$, $\frac{n}{2}-5$) (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A girl deposits $\$300$ in a bank account. The bank offers 7% interest per year. Assuming the girl does not take any money out of the account, calculate:
a the amount of money in the account after 8 years
b the minimum number of years the money must be left in the account, for the amount to be greater than $\$350$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a This is a geometric (compound interest) sequence, amount after $n$ years $=300\times1.07^n$. After 8 years: $300\times1.07^8\approx\$515.46$.
b Try whole numbers of years: after 2 years $300\times1.07^2=\$343.47$ (not more than $\$350$); after 3 years $300\times1.07^3\approx\$367.51$ (more than $\$350$). The minimum number of years is therefore $3$.
mark_scheme: M1 use $300\times1.07^n$, A1 amount after 8 years to appropriate accuracy (a: 2 marks); M1 set up inequality $300\times1.07^n>350$ and solve/trial, A1 minimum whole number of years (b: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A computer loses 35% of its value each year. If the computer cost $\$600$ new, calculate:
a its value after 2 years
b its value after 10 years.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Losing 35% each year leaves 65% of the previous value, so value after $n$ years $=600\times0.65^n$.
a $600\times0.65^2=600\times0.4225=\$253.50$.
b $600\times0.65^{10}\approx\$8.08$.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Part of an exponential sequence is given below: $\ldots,\ \ldots,\ 27,\ \ldots,\ \ldots,\ -1$ where $u_3=27$ and $u_6=-1$. Calculate:
a the common ratio $r$
b the value $u_1$
c the value of $n$ if $u_n=-\dfrac{1}{81}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $u_6=u_3\times r^3\Rightarrow r^3=\dfrac{-1}{27}\Rightarrow r=-\dfrac13$ (the real cube root).
b $u_3=u_1\times r^2=u_1\times\frac19=27\Rightarrow u_1=243$.
c $u_n=243\times\left(-\frac13\right)^{n-1}=-\dfrac1{81}$. Since $243=3^5$ and $\frac1{81}=\frac1{3^4}$, we need $\left(-\frac13\right)^{n-1}=-\dfrac{1}{3^9}$. As $9$ is odd, $\left(-\frac13\right)^9=-\frac1{3^9}$, so $n-1=9\Rightarrow n=10$.
mark_scheme: M1 use $u_6=u_3 r^3$, A1 $r=-\frac13$ (a: 2 marks); M1 use $u_3=u_1r^2$, A1 $u_1=243$ (b: 2 marks); M1 set up and solve $243\times(-\frac13)^{n-1}=-\frac1{81}$, A1 $n=10$ (c: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Using a table of differences if necessary, calculate the rule for the $n$th term of the sequence $8,\ 24,\ 58,\ 116,\ 204,\ \ldots$
exam_questions.full_solution: First differences: $16,34,58,88$; second differences: $18,24,30$; third differences: $6,6$ (constant), so the sequence is cubic. Fitting $u_n=an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ to the first four terms gives $a=1,b=3,c=0,d=4$, i.e. $u_n=n^3+3n^2+4$. Check: $u_1=1+3+4=8$, $u_2=8+12+4=24$, $u_3=27+27+4=58$, $u_4=64+48+4=116$, $u_5=125+75+4=204$. ✓
mark_scheme: M1 identify constant third differences (cubic sequence), M1 fit $an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ to the data, A1 correct $n$th term
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Using a table of differences, calculate the rule for the $n$th term of the sequence $10,\ 23,\ 50,\ 97,\ 170,\ \ldots$
exam_questions.full_solution: First differences: $13,27,47,73$; second differences: $14,20,26$; third differences: $6,6$ (constant), so the sequence is cubic. Fitting $u_n=an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ gives $a=1,b=1,c=3,d=5$, i.e. $u_n=n^3+n^2+3n+5$. Check: $u_1=1+1+3+5=10$, $u_2=8+4+6+5=23$, $u_3=27+9+9+5=50$, $u_4=64+16+12+5=97$, $u_5=125+25+15+5=170$. ✓
mark_scheme: M1 identify constant third differences (cubic sequence), M1 fit $an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ to the data, A1 correct $n$th term
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$y=kx$. When $y=12$, $x=8$.
a Calculate the value of $k$.
b Calculate $y$ when $x=10$.
c Calculate $y$ when $x=2$.
d Calculate $x$ when $y=18$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 $k=1.5$; then B1 for each correct value: (b) $y=15$, (c) $y=3$, (d) $x=12$ (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$y=\dfrac{k}{x}$. When $y=2$, $x=5$.
a Calculate the value of $k$.
b Calculate $y$ when $x=4$.
c Calculate $x$ when $y=10$.
d Calculate $x$ when $y=0.5$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 $k=10$; then B1 for each correct value: (b) $y=2.5$, (c) $x=1$, (d) $x=20$ (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$p=kq^3$. When $p=9$, $q=3$.
a Calculate the value of $k$.
b Calculate $p$ when $q=6$.
c Calculate $p$ when $q=1$.
d Calculate $q$ when $p=576$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $k=\frac{9}{3^3}=\frac{9}{27}=\frac13$.
b $p=\frac13\times6^3=\frac13\times216=72$.
c $p=\frac13\times1^3=\frac13$.
d $576=\frac13q^3\Rightarrow q^3=1728\Rightarrow q=12$ (since $12^3=1728$).
mark_scheme: (a) B1 $k=\frac13$; then B1 for each correct value: (b) $p=72$, (c) $p=\frac13$, (d) $q=12$ (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$m=\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{n}}$. When $m=1$, $n=25$.
a Calculate the value of $k$.
b Calculate $m$ when $n=16$.
c Calculate $m$ when $n=100$.
d Calculate $n$ when $m=5$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $k=1\times\sqrt{25}=5$.
b $m=\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{5}{4}=1.25$.
c $m=\frac{5}{\sqrt{100}}=\frac{5}{10}=0.5$.
d $5=\frac{5}{\sqrt{n}}\Rightarrow\sqrt{n}=1\Rightarrow n=1$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 $k=5$; then B1 for each correct value: (b) $m=1.25$, (c) $m=0.5$, (d) $n=1$ (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$y=\dfrac{k}{x^2}$. When $y=3$, $x=\dfrac13$.
a Calculate the value of $k$.
b Calculate $y$ when $x=0.5$.
c Calculate both values of $x$ when $y=\dfrac{1}{12}$.
d Calculate both values of $x$ when $y=\dfrac13$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $k=3\times\left(\frac13\right)^2=3\times\frac19=\frac13$.
b $y=\dfrac{1/3}{0.25}=\dfrac43\approx1.33$.
c $\dfrac{1}{12}=\dfrac{1/3}{x^2}\Rightarrow x^2=\dfrac{1/3}{1/12}=4\Rightarrow x=\pm2$.
d $\dfrac13=\dfrac{1/3}{x^2}\Rightarrow x^2=1\Rightarrow x=\pm1$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 substitute $y=3$ and $x=\frac13$ into $y=\frac{k}{x^2}$, A1 $k=\frac13$ (2 marks); (b) B1 $y=\frac43$ (1 mark); (c) M1 solve $x^2=\frac{k}{y}=4$, A1 $x=\pm2$ (2 marks); (d) B1 $x=\pm1$ (1 mark). Total 6 marks.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$y$ is inversely proportional to $x$.
a Copy and complete the table below:
$x$: $1,2,4,8,16,32$; $y$: at $x=8$, $y=4$.
b What is the value of $x$ when $y=20$?
exam_questions.full_solution:
Since $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$ and $y=4$ when $x=8$: $k=4\times8=32$. So $y=\dfrac{32}{x}$.
a Table: $x=1\to y=32$, $x=2\to y=16$, $x=4\to y=8$, $x=8\to y=4$, $x=16\to y=2$, $x=32\to y=1$.
b $20=\dfrac{32}{x}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{32}{20}=1.6$.
mark_scheme: M1 find $k=32$ and complete table, A1 all table values correct (a); A1 (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Copy and complete the tables below:
a $y\propto x$: $x=1,2,4,5,10$, with $y=10$ when $x=2$.
b $y\propto\dfrac1x$: $x=1,2,4,5,10$, with $y=20$ when $x=1$.
c $y\propto\sqrt x$: $x=4,16,25,36,64$, with $y=4$ when $x=4$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=kx$ with $10=k(2)\Rightarrow k=5$, so $y=5x$: values $5,10,20,25,50$ for $x=1,2,4,5,10$.
b $y=\frac{k}{x}$ with $20=\frac{k}{1}\Rightarrow k=20$, so $y=\frac{20}{x}$: values $20,10,5,4,2$.
c $y=k\sqrt x$ with $4=k\sqrt4=2k\Rightarrow k=2$, so $y=2\sqrt x$: values at $x=4,16,25,36,64$ are $4,8,10,12,16$.
mark_scheme: Each table: M1 find the constant of proportionality ((a) $k=5$, (b) $k=20$, (c) $k=2$), A1 all five values correct (2 marks per table, 3 tables, 6 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The pressure $(P)$ of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume $(V)$ at a constant temperature. If $P=4$ when $V=6$, calculate:
a $P$ when $V=30$
b $V$ when $P=30$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
$P=\dfrac{k}{V}$ with $4=\dfrac{k}{6}\Rightarrow k=24$, so $P=\dfrac{24}{V}$.
a $P=\dfrac{24}{30}=0.8$.
b $30=\dfrac{24}{V}\Rightarrow V=\dfrac{24}{30}=0.8$.
mark_scheme: M1 use $P=\frac{k}{V}$ to find $k=24$, A1 $P=0.8$ (a); M1 rearrange to $V=\frac{24}{P}$, A1 $V=0.8$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The gravitational force $(F)$ between two masses is inversely proportional to the square of the distance $(d)$ between them. If $F=4$ when $d=5$, calculate:
a $F$ when $d=8$
b $d$ when $F=25$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
$F=\dfrac{k}{d^2}$ with $4=\dfrac{k}{25}\Rightarrow k=100$, so $F=\dfrac{100}{d^2}$.
a $F=\dfrac{100}{64}=1.5625$.
b $25=\dfrac{100}{d^2}\Rightarrow d^2=4\Rightarrow d=2$.
mark_scheme: M1 use $F=\frac{k}{d^2}$ to find $k=100$, A1 $F=1.5625$ (a); M1 obtain $d^2=\frac{100}{F}=4$, A1 $d=2$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Absolute zero $(0\,\text{K})$ is equivalent to $-273\,^\circ\text{C}$ and $0\,^\circ\text{C}$ is equivalent to $273\,\text{K}$. Draw a conversion graph which will convert K into $^\circ\text{C}$. Use your graph to estimate:
a the temperature in K equivalent to $-40\,^\circ\text{C}$,
b the temperature in $^\circ\text{C}$ equivalent to $100\,\text{K}$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
The relationship is linear: $K=C+273$ (equivalently $C=K-273$).
a $K=-40+273=233\,\text{K}$.
b $C=100-273=-173\,^\circ\text{C}$.
mark_scheme: B1 correct straight-line conversion graph through $(0\,\text{K},-273\,^\circ\text{C})$ and $(273\,\text{K},0\,^\circ\text{C})$; B1 $233\,\text{K}$ (a); B1 $-173\,^\circ\text{C}$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A Canadian plumber has a call-out charge of 70 Canadian dollars and then charges a rate of \$50 per hour.
a Draw a conversion graph and estimate the cost of the following:
i a job lasting $4\frac12$ hours,
ii a job lasting $6\frac34$ hours.
b If a job cost \$245, estimate from your graph how long it took to complete.
mark_scheme: B1 correct straight-line graph of cost $=70+50h$; B1 $\$295$ (a i); B1 $\$407.50$ (a ii); B1 $3.5$ hours (b) (accept values read sensibly from the graph)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A boy lives $3.5\,\text{km}$ from his school. He walks home at a constant speed of $9\,\text{km/h}$ for the first 10 minutes. He then stops and talks to his friends for 5 minutes. He finally runs the rest of his journey home at a constant speed of $12\,\text{km/h}$.
a Illustrate this information on a distance-time graph.
b Use your graph to estimate the total time it took the boy to get home that day.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a The graph has three stages: a straight line of gradient $9\,\text{km/h}$ for the first 10 minutes, then a horizontal (flat) section for 5 minutes (stationary), then a steeper straight line of gradient $12\,\text{km/h}$ until the distance reaches $3.5\,\text{km}$.
b Distance covered walking in 10 min $=9\times\frac{10}{60}=1.5\,\text{km}$. Remaining distance $=3.5-1.5=2\,\text{km}$. Time running $=\dfrac{2}{12}\,\text{h}=10$ minutes. Total time $=10+5+10=25$ minutes.
mark_scheme: B2 correct three-stage distance-time graph (walking, stationary, running), B1 for two stages correct (a); M1 calculate distance walked ($1.5\,\text{km}$) and running time ($10$ min), A1 total time $25$ minutes (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A car accelerates from rest. Its speed-time graph is a straight line from $(0,0)$ to $(15\,\text{s},\ 30\,\text{m/s})$.
a Calculate the car's acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$.
b Calculate, in metres, the distance the car travels in 15 seconds.
c How long did it take the car to travel half the distance?
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Acceleration $=\dfrac{30-0}{15-0}=2\,\text{m/s}^2$.
b Distance $=$ area under the graph (a triangle) $=\frac12\times15\times30=225\,\text{m}$.
c The distance travelled in the first $t$ seconds is the area of the triangle under the graph up to time $t$. The speed at time $t$ is $2t$, so this area is $\frac12\times t\times2t=t^2$. Half the total distance is $112.5\,\text{m}$, so $t^2=112.5\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{112.5}\approx10.6\,\text{s}$.
mark_scheme: M1 gradient $=\Delta v/\Delta t$, A1 $2\,\text{m/s}^2$ (a); M1 area under graph (triangle), A1 $225\,\text{m}$ (b); M1 area up to time $t$ ($=t^2$) set equal to $112.5$, A1 $t\approx10.6\,\text{s}$ (c)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A car decelerates to rest. Its speed-time graph is a straight line from $(0,\ 30\,\text{m/s})$ to $(12\,\text{s},\ 0)$.
a Calculate the car's deceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$.
b Calculate, in metres, the distance the car travels in 12 seconds.
c How long did it take the car to travel half the distance?
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Deceleration magnitude $=\dfrac{30-0}{12-0}=2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$ (gradient is $-2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$).
b Distance $=$ area under the graph (a triangle) $=\frac12\times12\times30=180\,\text{m}$.
c Speed at time $t$: $v=30-2.5t$. The distance travelled in the first $t$ seconds is the area of the trapezium under the graph: $\frac12\left(30+(30-2.5t)\right)t=30t-1.25t^2$. Half the total distance is $90\,\text{m}$: $30t-1.25t^2=90\Rightarrow t^2-24t+72=0\Rightarrow t=12\pm6\sqrt2$. Since the motion only lasts until $t=12\,\text{s}$, the valid root is $t=12-6\sqrt2\approx3.51\,\text{s}$ (the other root, $\approx20.5\,\text{s}$, is outside the domain).
mark_scheme: M1 gradient $=\Delta v/\Delta t$, A1 deceleration $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$ (a); M1 area under graph (triangle), A1 $180\,\text{m}$ (b); M1 area up to time $t$ set equal to $90$, i.e. $30t-1.25t^2=90$, A1 $t\approx3.51\,\text{s}$ (valid root) (c)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the graph of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$.
exam_questions.answer: A reciprocal (hyperbola) curve with two branches, one in the first quadrant and one in the third quadrant, approaching the asymptotes $x=0$ and $y=0$.
exam_questions.full_solution: $y=\dfrac1x$ is undefined at $x=0$ (vertical asymptote $x=0$) and $y\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ (horizontal asymptote $y=0$). For $x>0$, $y>0$ and decreases from $+\infty$ towards $0$ (branch in quadrant 1); for $x<0$, $y<0$ and the curve is the point-symmetric reflection through the origin (branch in quadrant 3).
mark_scheme: B1 correct two-branch shape (one branch in each of quadrants 1 and 3), B1 both asymptotes ($x=0$ and $y=0$) shown/implied
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Copy and complete the table below for the function $y=-x^2-7x-12$:
$x$: $-7,-6,-5,-4,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2$ (given: at $x=-6$, $y=-6$; at $x=-2$, $y=-2$)
b Plot a graph of the function.
mark_scheme: B3 all eight missing values correct (B2 for six or seven correct, B1 for four or five correct) (a); B1 correctly plotted smooth parabola (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Plot a graph of each of the functions below between the given limits of $x$:
a $y=x^2-3x-10$, $-3\le x\le6$
b $y=-x^2-4x-4$, $-5\le x\le1$
exam_questions.answer: a Roots at $x=-2,5$; vertex at $(1.5,-12.25)$ (minimum)  b Touches the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ (repeated root); vertex/maximum at $(-2,0)$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=x^2-3x-10=(x-5)(x+2)$, so the curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ and $x=5$, and (since the coefficient of $x^2$ is positive) has a minimum turning point at $x=1.5$: $y=1.5^2-3(1.5)-10=-12.25$, i.e. $(1.5,-12.25)$.
b $y=-x^2-4x-4=-(x+2)^2$, a downward parabola that just touches the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ (a repeated root), which is also its maximum turning point, $(-2,0)$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 table of values or key features ($x$-intercepts $-2$ and $5$, minimum $(1.5,-12.25)$), A1 correctly plotted curve; (b) M1 table of values or key features (repeated root at $x=-2$, maximum $(-2,0)$), A1 correctly plotted curve (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Plot the graph of the quadratic equation $y=-x^2-x+15$ for $-6\le x\le4$.
b Showing your method clearly, use your graph to solve the following equations:
i $10=x^2+x$
ii $x^2=x+5$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Plot $y=-x^2-x+15$ from a table of values for $-6\le x\le4$.
i $10=x^2+x$ can be rewritten as $-x^2-x+15=5$, so draw the line $y=5$ and read off the $x$-coordinates where it meets the curve: $x\approx2.7$ or $x\approx-3.7$. (Check with the formula: $x^2+x-10=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{41}}{2}\approx2.70$ or $-3.70$.)
ii $x^2=x+5$ can be rewritten as $-x^2-x+15=10-2x$, so draw the line $y=10-2x$ and read off where it meets the curve: $x\approx2.8$ or $x\approx-1.8$. (Check: $x^2-x-5=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{21}}{2}\approx2.79$ or $-1.79$.)
mark_scheme: B1 correctly plotted curve (a); M1 draw the line $y=5$, A1 $x\approx2.7$ and $x\approx-3.7$ (b i); M1 draw the line $y=10-2x$, A1 $x\approx2.8$ and $x\approx-1.8$ (b ii)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Plot the graph of $y=\dfrac2x$ for $-4\le x\le4$.
b Showing your method clearly, use your graph to solve the equation $x^2+x=2$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Plot $y=\frac2x$, a reciprocal curve with branches in quadrants 1 and 3 (asymptotes $x=0,y=0$).
b Divide both sides of $x^2+x=2$ by $x$ ($x\neq0$): $x+1=\dfrac2x$. So draw the line $y=x+1$ on the same axes and read off the $x$-coordinates where it meets the curve $y=\dfrac2x$: $x=1$ and $x=-2$. (Check: $x^2+x-2=(x+2)(x-1)=0$.)
mark_scheme: B1 correctly plotted reciprocal curve (a); M1 draw the line $y=x+1$ (from $x+1=\frac2x$), A1 both roots $x=1$ and $x=-2$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
In each of the following equations:
i State whether the turning point is a maximum or a minimum, giving a reason for your answer.
ii State the coordinate of the turning point.
a $y=-(x+3)^2-5$
b $y=\dfrac12(x-6)^2+2$
exam_questions.answer: a Maximum at $(-3,-5)$, since the coefficient of the squared term is negative.  b Minimum at $(6,2)$, since the coefficient of the squared term is positive.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=-(x+3)^2-5$ has a negative coefficient on the squared bracket, so the parabola opens downward and the turning point is a maximum, at $(-3,-5)$ (where the bracket is zero).
b $y=\frac12(x-6)^2+2$ has a positive coefficient, so the parabola opens upward and the turning point is a minimum, at $(6,2)$.
mark_scheme: B1 correct type with reason, B1 correct coordinate (a: 2 marks); B1 correct type with reason, B1 correct coordinate (b: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the function $y=\dfrac12x^2-2$, showing clearly where it intersects both axes and indicating the coordinates of the turning point.
exam_questions.full_solution: $x$-axis: $\frac12x^2-2=0\Rightarrow x^2=4\Rightarrow x=\pm2$. $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow y=-2$. Since the coefficient of $x^2$ is positive, the vertex $(0,-2)$ is a minimum turning point.
mark_scheme: B1 correct $x$-intercepts, B1 correct $y$-intercept, B1 correct turning point
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the function $y=(3x+2)(-x^2-x+2)$, indicating clearly the intersections with both axes.
exam_questions.full_solution: $x$-axis: either $3x+2=0\Rightarrow x=-\frac23$, or $-x^2-x+2=0\Rightarrow x^2+x-2=0\Rightarrow(x+2)(x-1)=0\Rightarrow x=-2$ or $x=1$. So the three $x$-intercepts are $x=-\frac23,-2,1$. $y$-axis: at $x=0$, $y=(2)(2)=4$.
mark_scheme: M1 factorise the quadratic factor, A1 all three $x$-intercepts, A1 $y$-intercept
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Name the types of graph i and ii shown in the diagram.
b Give a **possible** equation for each of the graphs drawn.
exam_questions.answer: i Linear graph, e.g. $y=-x+3$  ii Quadratic graph, e.g. $y=-x^2+4$
exam_questions.full_solution:
i A straight line with negative gradient is a linear function, e.g. $y=-x+3$ (any negative gradient and any intercept is acceptable).
ii A curve that is an upside-down 'n' shape, symmetric about a vertical line, crossing the $y$-axis above the origin, is a (downward) quadratic function, e.g. $y=-x^2+4$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 (i) linear graph (straight line), B1 (ii) quadratic graph; (b) B1 a valid equation for (i) — any line with a negative gradient, e.g. $y=-x+3$; B1 a valid equation for (ii) — any negative quadratic with a positive $y$-intercept, e.g. $y=-x^2+4$ (4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The two graphs of part a: i a straight line sloping downwards; ii a symmetrical curve with a maximum, crossing the $y$-axis above the origin. The axes carry no scale, so any equation of the right type is accepted.
assets.purpose: Restore the two graphs the question asks students to name (a line with negative gradient and a downward parabola).

exam_questions.statement:
For each of the functions below:
i draw up a table of values,
ii plot a graph of the function.
a $f(x)=x^2+3x$, $-5\le x\le2$
b $f(x)=\dfrac1x+3x$, $-3\le x\le3$ (excluding $x=0$)
exam_questions.answer: a Parabola with roots at $x=0,-3$ and minimum at $(-1.5,-2.25)$  b Curve with two branches (undefined at $x=0$), steep near the asymptote and roughly linear ($\approx3x$) for larger $|x|$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f(x)=x^2+3x=x(x+3)$ has roots at $x=0$ and $x=-3$, minimum at $x=-1.5$: $f(-1.5)=2.25-4.5=-2.25$. Tabulating $f(x)$ for $x=-5,\ldots,2$ and plotting gives an upward parabola.
b $f(x)=\frac1x+3x$ is undefined at $x=0$ and has a vertical asymptote there; for $|x|$ away from zero the curve behaves increasingly like $y=3x$. Tabulating values at $x=-3,-2,-1,-0.5,0.5,1,2,3$ (excluding 0) and plotting gives two branches, one for $x<0$ and one for $x>0$.
mark_scheme: M1 correct table of values, A1 correctly plotted curve (a: 2 marks); M1 correct table (noting $x=0$ excluded), A1 correctly plotted curve (b: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Plot the function $y=\dfrac12x^3+2x^2$ for $-5\le x\le2$.
b Calculate the gradient of the curve when:
i $x=1$
ii $x=-1$
mark_scheme: (a) B1 correctly plotted cubic curve (1 mark); (b) M1 differentiate to $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac32x^2+4x$, A1 gradient $5.5$ at $x=1$, A1 gradient $-2.5$ at $x=-1$ (3 marks). Total 4 marks.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Plot a graph of the function $y=2x^2-5x-5$ for $-2\le x\le5$.
b Use the graph to solve the equation $2x^2-5x-5=0$.
c Showing your method clearly, use the graph to solve the equation $2x^2-3x=10$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
b Read off where the curve crosses the $x$-axis ($y=0$): $x\approx3.3$ or $x\approx-0.8$. (Check with the formula: discriminant $=25+40=65$, $x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{65}}{4}\approx3.27$ or $-0.766$.)
c Note that $2x^2-3x-10=(2x^2-5x-5)+(2x-5)$, so solving $2x^2-3x=10$ is equivalent to finding where the plotted curve $y=2x^2-5x-5$ meets the line $y=5-2x$. Algebraically: discriminant of $2x^2-3x-10=0$ is $9+80=89$, so $x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{89}}{4}\approx3.11$ or $-1.61$.
mark_scheme: B1 correctly plotted curve (a); B1 both roots read where the curve crosses the $x$-axis (b); M1 draw the line $y=5-2x$ (since $2x^2-3x=10\Leftrightarrow2x^2-5x-5=5-2x$), A1 both roots $x\approx3.1$ and $x\approx-1.6$ (c)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the function $\dfrac{y+2}{3}=x$.
exam_questions.answer: $y=3x-2$: a straight line, gradient 3, $y$-intercept $-2$ (passing through $(0,-2)$ and $(\frac23,0)$)
exam_questions.full_solution: Rearranging: $y+2=3x\Rightarrow y=3x-2$. This is a straight line of gradient 3 and $y$-intercept $-2$, crossing the $x$-axis at $x=\frac23$.
mark_scheme: M1 rearrange to $y=3x-2$, A1 correct straight-line sketch with gradient 3 and $y$-intercept $-2$
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the function $y=-2x^2+x+15$, stating clearly where it intersects the axes and indicating the coordinates of the turning point.
exam_questions.full_solution: $x$-axis: $-2x^2+x+15=0\Rightarrow2x^2-x-15=0$. Discriminant $=1+120=121=11^2$, so $x=\dfrac{1\pm11}{4}$, giving $x=3$ or $x=-2.5$. $y$-axis: at $x=0$, $y=15$. Turning point: $x=\dfrac{-b}{2a}=\dfrac{-1}{2(-2)}=0.25$ (using $y=-2x^2+x+15$); $y=-2(0.25)^2+0.25+15=-0.125+0.25+15=15.125$. Since the coefficient of $x^2$ is negative, this is a maximum.
mark_scheme: B1 $x$-intercepts $x=3$ and $x=-2.5$; B1 $y$-intercept $15$; M1 $x=\frac{-b}{2a}=0.25$ for the turning point, A1 maximum at $(0.25,\ 15.125)$
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A builder is constructing a fenced yard off the side of a house, as shown in the diagram: the yard is an 'L' shape, with the house bordering the top part of its left edge. The top edge of the yard has length $x$, its right-hand edge has length $(x+2)$, and the lower part of its left edge (below where the house ends) has length $x$. The total length of the fence is $60\,\text{m}$.
a Write an expression for the length of the unmarked side (the bottom edge of the yard) in terms of $x$.
b Write an equation for the area $A$ of the yard.
c Sketch the graph of the function for the area $A$ of the yard.
d From your graph deduce the value of $x$ which gives the largest area for the yard.
e Calculate the largest area possible for the yard.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a The fence consists of four fenced sides: top ($x$), right ($x+2$), bottom (unmarked, call it $b$) and the lower-left vertical ($x$). Total: $x+(x+2)+b+x=60\Rightarrow b=58-3x$.
b Split the L-shaped yard into two rectangles: the right-hand rectangle (width $x$, height $x+2$, area $x(x+2)$) and the lower-left extension rectangle (width $b-x=58-4x$, height $x$, area $(58-4x)x$). Total area: $A=x(x+2)+(58-4x)x=x^2+2x+58x-4x^2=-3x^2+60x$.
c $A=-3x^2+60x=-3x(x-20)$ is a downward parabola with roots at $x=0$ and $x=20$.
d By symmetry the maximum occurs halfway between the roots, at $x=10$ (confirmed since $\frac{dA}{dx}=-6x+60=0\Rightarrow x=10$).
e $A(10)=-3(100)+600=300\,\text{m}^2$.
mark_scheme: M1 use total fence $=60$, A1 $58-3x$ (a); M1 split the L-shape into two rectangles and add areas, A1 $A=-3x^2+60x$ (b); B1 correctly sketched downward parabola with roots $0$ and $20$ (c); B1 $x=10$ (d); B1 largest area $300\,\text{m}^2$ (e)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For each of the functions below:
i draw up a table of values,
ii plot a graph of the function.
a $f(x)=2^x+x$, $-3\le x\le3$
b $f(x)=3^x-x^2$, $-3\le x\le3$
exam_questions.answer: a Values rise from about $-2.875$ at $x=-3$ to $11$ at $x=3$, combining exponential growth with the linear term  b Values combine exponential growth with a downward parabola, dominated by the exponential term for large $x$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Evaluate $f(x)=2^x+x$ at integer values from $-3$ to $3$ (e.g. $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=3$, $f(2)=6$, $f(3)=11$) and plot.
b Evaluate $f(x)=3^x-x^2$ at integer values from $-3$ to $3$ (e.g. $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=5$, $f(3)=18$) and plot.
mark_scheme: M1 correct table of values, A1 correctly plotted curve (a: 2 marks); M1 correct table of values, A1 correctly plotted curve (b: 2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Plot the function $y=-x^3-4x^2+5$ for $-5\le x\le2$.
b Calculate the gradient of the curve when:
i $x=0$
ii $x=-2$
mark_scheme: (a) B1 correctly plotted cubic curve (1 mark); (b) M1 differentiate to $\frac{dy}{dx}=-3x^2-8x$, A1 gradient $0$ at $x=0$, A1 gradient $4$ at $x=-2$ (3 marks). Total 4 marks.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Copy and complete the table below for the function $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}-5$:
$x$: $-3,-2,-1,-0.5,-0.25,0,0.25,0.5,1,2,3$ (given: at $x=-0.5$, $y=-1$; undefined at $x=0$).
b Plot a graph of the function.
c Use the graph to solve the equation $\dfrac{1}{x^2}=5$.
d Showing your method clearly, use your graph to solve the equation $\dfrac{1}{x^2}+x^2=7$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Substituting each value: e.g. $x=-3$: $\frac19-5=-\frac{44}9\approx-4.89$; $x=-0.25$: $16-5=11$; undefined at $x=0$ (division by zero). By symmetry (even function), values at $\pm x$ are equal.
b Plotting gives two symmetric branches either side of the vertical asymptote $x=0$, each approaching the horizontal asymptote $y=-5$.
c $\dfrac{1}{x^2}=5\Leftrightarrow\dfrac{1}{x^2}-5=0$, so read off where the curve crosses the $x$-axis: $x\approx\pm0.45$. (Check: $x^2=0.2\Rightarrow x=\pm\sqrt{0.2}\approx\pm0.447$.)
d $\dfrac{1}{x^2}+x^2=7\Leftrightarrow\dfrac{1}{x^2}-5=2-x^2$, so draw the curve $y=2-x^2$ on the same axes and read off the $x$-coordinates of the four intersection points: $x\approx\pm2.6$ and $x\approx\pm0.4$. (Algebraic check: let $u=x^2$: $\dfrac1u+u=7\Rightarrow u^2-7u+1=0\Rightarrow u=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{45}}{2}\approx6.854$ or $0.146$, so $x\approx\pm2.62$ or $\pm0.382$.)
mark_scheme: B2 all table values correct (B1 for at least six correct) (a); B1 correctly plotted two-branch curve (b); B1 $x\approx\pm0.45$ read where the curve crosses the $x$-axis (c); M1 draw $y=2-x^2$, A1 all four roots $x\approx\pm2.6$ and $\pm0.4$ (d)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Sketch the graph of $y=-2^x$ indicating clearly any intersections with either axis.
b Give the equation of any asymptote(s).
exam_questions.full_solution:
a Since $2^x>0$ for all $x$, $y=-2^x<0$ always; the curve crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,-1)$ and never crosses the $x$-axis, approaching $y=0$ from below as $x\to-\infty$.
b Horizontal asymptote: $y=0$.
mark_scheme: B1 correct shape with $y$-intercept $(0,-1)$ and no $x$-intercept (a: 1 mark); B1 asymptote $y=0$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Sketch the graph of $y=2^x-4$ indicating clearly any intersections with either axis.
b Give the equation of any asymptote(s).
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow y=1-4=-3$. $x$-axis: $2^x-4=0\Rightarrow2^x=4\Rightarrow x=2$.
b As $x\to-\infty$, $2^x\to0$, so $y\to-4$: horizontal asymptote $y=-4$.
mark_scheme: B1 correct $y$-intercept $(0,-3)$ and $x$-intercept $(2,0)$ (a: 1 mark); B1 asymptote $y=-4$ (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Find the gradient function of the following:
a $y=x^3$
b $y=2x^2-x$
c $y=-\dfrac12x^2+2x$
d $y=\dfrac23x^3+4x^2-x$
exam_questions.full_solution:
Differentiate term by term using $\frac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$.
a $3x^2$.
b $4x-1$.
c $-x+2$.
d $2x^2+8x-1$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct gradient function: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$:
a $f(x)=x(x+2)$
b $f(x)=(x+2)(x-3)$
c $f(x)=\dfrac{x^3-x}{x}$
d $f(x)=\dfrac{x^3+2x^2}{2x}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f(x)=x^2+2x\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x+2$.
b $f(x)=x^2-x-6\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x-1$.
c $f(x)=\dfrac{x(x^2-1)}{x}=x^2-1$ (for $x\neq0$) $\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x$.
d $f(x)=\dfrac{x(x+2)}{2}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x$ (for $x\neq0$) $\Rightarrow f'(x)=x+1$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct derivative, after expanding or simplifying first: (a), (b), (c), (d) (4 × B1 = 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Find the second derivative of the following functions:
a $y=x^4-3x^2$
b $s=2t^5-t^3$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4x^3-6x\Rightarrow\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x^2-6$.
b $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=10t^4-3t^2\Rightarrow\dfrac{d^2s}{dt^2}=40t^3-6t$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct second derivative: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:

c $f(x)=(x-3)(x+8);\ x=\dfrac14$
exam_questions.answer: a gradient $=2$  b gradient $=1$  c gradient $=\dfrac{11}{2}=5.5$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f'(x)=x+1\Rightarrow f'(1)=2$.
b $f'(x)=-3x^2+4x+1\Rightarrow f'(0)=1$.
c $f(x)=x^2+5x-24\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x+5\Rightarrow f'(0.25)=0.5+5=5.5$.

exam_questions.statement:
A stone is dropped from the top of a cliff. The distance $(s)$ it falls is given by the equation $s=5t^2$, where $s$ is the distance in metres and $t$ the time in seconds.
a Calculate the velocity $v$, by differentiating the distance $s$ with respect to time $t$.
b Calculate the stone's velocity after 3 seconds.
c The stone hits the ground travelling at $42\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, calculate:
i how long it took for the stone to hit the ground
ii the height of the cliff.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
The function $f(x)=x^3+x^2-1$ has a gradient of zero at points P and Q, where the $x$ coordinate of P is less than that of Q.
a Calculate the gradient function $f'(x)$.
b Calculate the coordinates of P.
c Calculate the coordinates of Q.
d Determine which of the points P or Q is a maximum. Explain your method clearly.
exam_questions.answer: a $f'(x)=3x^2+2x$  b P$=\left(-\dfrac23,-\dfrac{23}{27}\right)$  c Q$=(0,-1)$  d P is the maximum
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f'(x)=3x^2+2x$.
b,c $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow x(3x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ or $x=-\frac23$. Since $x_P<x_Q$: P has $x=-\frac23$, Q has $x=0$. $f(-\frac23)=-\frac{8}{27}+\frac{4}{9}-1=-\frac{8}{27}+\frac{12}{27}-\frac{27}{27}=-\frac{23}{27}$, so P$=(-\frac23,-\frac{23}{27})$. $f(0)=-1$, so Q$=(0,-1)$.
d $f''(x)=6x+2$. At P ($x=-\frac23$): $f''=-4+2=-2<0$, so P is a maximum. At Q ($x=0$): $f''=2>0$, so Q is a minimum. Hence P is the maximum.
mark_scheme: B1 $f'(x)=3x^2+2x$ (a); M1 solve $f'(x)=0$, A1 $P=\left(-\frac23,-\frac{23}{27}\right)$ (b); B1 $Q=(0,-1)$ (c); B1 P is the maximum, with a valid reason (second derivative $f''\left(-\frac23\right)=-2<0$, or the gradient either side) (d)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
a Explain why the point A$(1,1)$ lies on the curve $y=x^3-x^2+x$.
b Calculate the gradient of the curve at A.
c Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at A.
d Calculate the equation of the normal to the curve at A.
exam_questions.answer: a confirmed  b gradient $=2$  c $y=2x-1$  d $y=-\dfrac12x+\dfrac32$ (i.e. $x+2y=3$)
exam_questions.full_solution:
a At $x=1$: $y=1-1+1=1$, which matches the $y$-coordinate of A, so A lies on the curve.
b $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-2x+1$; at $x=1$: $3-2+1=2$.
c Tangent at A has gradient 2: $y-1=2(x-1)\Rightarrow y=2x-1$.
d Normal has gradient $-\frac12$ (negative reciprocal): $y-1=-\frac12(x-1)\Rightarrow y=-\frac12x+\frac32$.
mark_scheme: B1 substitute $x=1$ to show $y=1$ (a); M1 differentiate and substitute, A1 gradient $2$ (b); M1 use $y-1=2(x-1)$, A1 $y=2x-1$ (c); M1 use perpendicular gradient $-\frac12$, A1 $y=-\frac12x+\frac32$ (d)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For the function $f(x)=(x-2)^2+3$
a Calculate $f'(x)$.
b Determine the coordinates of the stationary point.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f(x)=x^2-4x+7\Rightarrow f'(x)=2x-4$.
b $2x-4=0\Rightarrow x=2$; $f(2)=(0)^2+3=3$, so the stationary point is $(2,3)$ (a minimum, since this matches the vertex of the squared-bracket form).
mark_scheme: M1 expand/differentiate, A1 $f'(x)=2x-4$ (a); M1 solve $f'(x)=0$, A1 coordinates (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
For the function $f(x)=x^4-2x^2$
a Calculate $f'(x)$.
b Determine the coordinates of any stationary points.
c Determine the nature of any stationary point.
d Find where the graph intersects or touches:
i the $y$-axis
ii the $x$-axis
e Sketch the graph of $f(x)$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $f'(x)=4x^3-4x$.
b $4x^3-4x=0\Rightarrow4x(x^2-1)=0\Rightarrow x=0,1,-1$. $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1-2=-1$, $f(-1)=1-2=-1$. Stationary points: $(0,0),(1,-1),(-1,-1)$.
c $f''(x)=12x^2-4$. At $x=0$: $f''=-4<0$, maximum. At $x=\pm1$: $f''=8>0$, minimum at each.
d i $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow y=0$, i.e. $(0,0)$.
ii $x$-axis: $x^4-2x^2=0\Rightarrow x^2(x^2-2)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ (touching, a repeated root) or $x=\pm\sqrt2$ (crossing).
e The curve is an even function (symmetric about the $y$-axis), a 'W' shape: it touches the origin (local maximum), dips to minima at $(\pm1,-1)$, and crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\pm\sqrt2\approx\pm1.41$ before rising steeply for larger $|x|$.
mark_scheme: B1 $f'(x)=4x^3-4x$ (a); M1 solve $f'(x)=0$, A1 all three stationary points (b); M1 use second derivative (or gradient either side), A1 correct nature at each point (c); B1 $y$-intercept, B1 all $x$-intercepts (d); B1 correct sketch (e)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
Find the inverse of each of the following functions:
a $f(x)=-x+4$
b $g(x)=\dfrac{3(x-6)}{2}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=-x+4\Rightarrow x=-y+4\Rightarrow f^{-1}(x)=4-x$.
b $y=\frac{3(x-6)}{2}\Rightarrow2y=3x-18\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{2y+18}{3}\Rightarrow g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{2x+18}{3}=\dfrac{2x}{3}+6$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 write $y=-x+4$ and rearrange for $x$, A1 $f^{-1}(x)=4-x$; (b) M1 write $y=\frac{3(x-6)}{2}$ and rearrange for $x$, A1 $g^{-1}(x)=\frac{2x}{3}+6$ (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:

exam_questions.full_solution:

b Solve $\frac32(-x+3)=\frac32\Rightarrow-x+3=1\Rightarrow x=2$.
mark_scheme: B1 for each correct value: (a), (b) (2 × B1 = 2 marks).

exam_questions.full_solution:
a $y=-3x+9\Rightarrow3x=9-y\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{9-y}{3}\Rightarrow f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{9-x}{3}$.
b $y=\dfrac{x-2}{4}\Rightarrow4y=x-2\Rightarrow x=4y+2\Rightarrow g^{-1}(x)=4x+2$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 write $y=-3x+9$ and rearrange for $x$, A1 $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{9-x}{3}$; (b) M1 write $y=\frac{x-2}{4}$ and rearrange for $x$, A1 $g^{-1}(x)=4x+2$ (2 marks per part, 4 marks).
